fields.title: Portraits of Courage – Samuel Ajayi Crowther
fields.subtitle: A Yoruba Captive Set Free, a Bishop on the Niger, and the Gospel in His Mother Tongue
fields.description: A Christian biography of Samuel Ajayi Crowther (c. 1807–1891), the Yoruba boy enslaved in 1821 and freed by a British warship, who became a Niger explorer, the translator who gave the Yoruba the Bible in their own language, and the first African bishop of the Anglican Church. Built on his own letters and journals and checked against the missionary records and modern historians, it tells the whole story, including the crisis of 1890, when young European missionaries overruled him and his clergy, and the Church of England’s later confession: “It was wrong.” All Scripture from the public-domain ASV (1901).

qa.question: What is this biography of Samuel Ajayi Crowther about?
qa.answer: It is a Christian biography of Samuel Ajayi Crowther (c. 1807–1891). It follows him from his Yoruba home at Osogun, through his capture in 1821 and rescue by HMS Myrmidon in 1822, his conversion and education in Sierra Leone, the Niger expeditions, the mission at Abeokuta and his reunion with his mother, to his consecration in 1864 as the first African Anglican bishop and his death at Lagos. It draws mainly on his own letters, journals and charges.

qa.question: Who was Samuel Ajayi Crowther?
qa.answer: He was a Yoruba man, sold into slavery as a boy and freed by the Royal Navy, who became a teacher, explorer, linguist and missionary. He led the translation of the Bible into Yoruba, began written work in Igbo, Nupe and other languages, founded the Niger Mission with an all-African staff in 1857, and was consecrated Bishop of the Niger in Canterbury Cathedral in 1864.

qa.question: Was he the first African bishop?
qa.answer: He was the first African bishop of the Anglican Church, consecrated in 1864. He was not the first African bishop in history, since the ancient churches of North Africa and Ethiopia had African bishops for centuries, and he was not the first African Anglican priest, since Philip Quaque of Cape Coast was ordained in 1765.

qa.question: What happened in the Niger Mission crisis of 1890?
qa.answer: After years of real problems in a thinly supervised mission, including a crime committed by two of its employees, a group of young English missionaries took control. At a committee meeting at Onitsha in August 1890, African agents and clergy were dismissed or suspended, among them his son, Archdeacon Dandeson Crowther. The bishop withdrew from the committee but remained bishop until his death. The missionary society’s own historian later called the young men ‘too severe,’ and in 2014 the Archbishop of Canterbury said of his treatment, ‘It was wrong.’

qa.question: Was the Niger Delta Pastorate a breakaway church?
qa.answer: Not from the Anglican Church. The Delta churches, under Archdeacon Dandeson Crowther, stopped taking the missionary society’s money and became a self-supporting pastorate, inaugurated at Bonny in April 1892 with Crowther’s approval. They remained part of the Church of England, and in time came back into closer relations with the society.

qa.question: How does the book handle the racism of his time?
qa.answer: Honestly. It shows the racial prejudice he faced from scientists, newspapers and some missionaries, and it notes where his own biographers used the language of racial superiority. It also looks at his deference to Europeans, including his 1884 letter beginning ‘I know my place as negro,’ and asks what it cost him.

qa.question: How is Scripture used in the book?
qa.answer: Each chapter opens with a passage from the American Standard Version (1901) that carries its theme, from ‘Thou hast been the helper of the fatherless’ to ‘a great multitude … out of every nation and of all tribes and peoples and tongues’, and further passages are woven through the story, including verses Crowther himself quoted. Every quotation was checked against the ASV text.

qa.question: Where should a reader begin?
qa.answer: At the beginning. The preface and introduction explain the sources and how the story has been told differently by his biographers; the chapters then follow his life in order. Appendix A gathers lessons from his life, Appendix B is a study guide for groups, Appendix C a chronology, and Appendix D a note on sources and on popular claims the book corrects.

fields.title: Preface
fields.body_html:
“Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall haste to stretch out her hands unto God.”

— Psalm 68:31, ASV

The first four volumes of this series told the stories of Watchman Nee in China, John Hyde in the Punjab, Corrie ten Boom in Haarlem, and Mary Slessor in the forests of south-eastern Nigeria. Mary Slessor’s story ended on the Cross River in 1915. This fifth volume goes back a generation and a little to the west, to a boy who was born in the Yoruba country of what is now south-western Nigeria some time around 1807, and who died in Lagos as a bishop of the Church of England on the last night of 1891.

His name at birth was Ajayi. When he was about thirteen, raiders burned his town, tied a rope around his neck, and led him away with his mother and sisters. He was sold six times. He tried, more than once, to kill himself. He was put in chains on a Portuguese slave ship bound for the Americas, and that same evening two British warships stopped it. He was landed in Sierra Leone, a colony for people rescued from the slave trade. There he learned to read, came to faith in Christ, and was baptised with the name of an English clergyman he never met: Samuel Crowther. Forty-two years later, in Canterbury Cathedral, he was consecrated the first African bishop of the Anglican Church. In the congregation that day sat the woman who had taught him the alphabet, and, according to his biographer, the naval captain who had freed him.

Why Courage?

It would be easy to tell his life as a story of rising, from the slave pen to the bishop’s chair. It was that. But it was not a story of arriving. Crowther spent almost his whole life on the move, by canoe and steamer and on foot, up the Niger River and its tributaries, in country where he was often a stranger and sometimes a prisoner. He was shipwrecked and lived for a year beside the wreck. He was kidnapped and held for ransom, and the man who rescued him was killed. He preached to kings and to slaves, to Muslim scholars and to worshippers of the old gods, and he did it with a patience that his European colleagues sometimes mistook for weakness.

His hardest courage was needed at the end. In his last years, a new generation of young European missionaries decided that African clergy could not be trusted with the church he had built. They dismissed and suspended his African clergy over his head, including his own son. He did not fight back with the weapons they used. He protested, withdrew from their committee, and went on being their bishop. He died some sixteen months later. The man chosen to succeed him was a European, and for decades afterwards the African bishops on the Niger served only as assistants. It took the Church of England until 2014 to say publicly, in Canterbury Cathedral, that he had been “betrayed and let down and undermined,” and that “it was wrong.”

How This Book Is Written

Unlike Mary Slessor, Samuel Crowther left a great deal of writing in his own words, and almost all of it is in the public domain. There is the letter he wrote in 1837, describing his capture and rescue, one of the most vivid accounts of the slave trade by anyone who survived it. There are his journals of three expeditions up the Niger, published in 1842, 1855, and 1859. There are his sermons and his charges to his clergy. This book quotes him freely, and wherever possible it lets him tell his own story.

There are also two biographies by an English writer, Jesse Page, published in 1888 and 1908, and the official history of the Church Missionary Society by Eugene Stock, published in 1899. These are valuable, and they are also partial. Page was an admirer who wrote in the racial language of his day, and both he and Stock took the side of the missionary society in the crisis that clouded Crowther’s last years. Modern historians, many of them Nigerian, have told that story very differently. This book draws on all of them, and it will tell the reader which is which.

Scripture in This Book

As in the earlier volumes, all Scripture quotations are from the American Standard Version of 1901, which is in the public domain. Each chapter opens with a passage that carries its theme, and further passages are woven through the narrative.

The verse at the head of this preface was one Crowther loved. In a letter he wrote in 1829, while he was still a young schoolmaster in Sierra Leone, he said he had hope “that Africa will soon stretch forth her hands unto God.” The psalm speaks of Ethiopia, which in the Bible stands for the peoples of Africa beyond Egypt. For nineteenth-century Christians it became a prophecy of Africa’s turning to Christ. Crowther lived to see the first small churches of the Niger, and to see them humbled. He did not live to see what came after: the growth of Christianity in Nigeria into one of the largest churches in the world, most of it led, as he always believed it should be, by Africans. Paul told the Athenians that God “made of one every nation of men to dwell on all the face of the earth … that they should seek God, if haply they might feel after him and find him” (Acts 17:26-27, ASV). This is the story of a man whom God found in a slave pen, and who spent his life helping his own people to find him too.

fields.title: Introduction: The Bishop and His Biographers
fields.body_html:
“And Jehovah answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tablets, that he may run that readeth it.”

— Habakkuk 2:2, ASV

A Man Who Wrote It Down

Most of the people in this series left little writing behind them. Samuel Crowther was different. He was a careful, methodical man who kept journals on every voyage, wrote long letters to the Church Missionary Society in London, compiled grammars and vocabularies, translated large parts of the Bible, and published his charges to his clergy. He was also, from his teens, a teacher, and he knew the value of writing things down so that others could read and act on them. The verse at the head of this chapter is God’s command to the prophet Habakkuk to write his vision plainly, so that anyone who read it could run with it. Crowther wrote plainly, and he meant to be read.

The most important document for his early life is a letter he wrote on 22 February 1837, from Fourah Bay in Sierra Leone, to the Rev. William Jowett, secretary of the Church Missionary Society. It tells the story of his capture, his sale, his rescue, and his conversion. It was printed in 1842 as an appendix to the journals of the Niger Expedition of 1841, and it has been reprinted many times since. This book quotes it from that 1842 printing. Later copies, including the one in Jesse Page’s 1908 biography, contain small errors, some of which change the meaning. In one place Page’s version says the rescued captives began to have a “poor opinion” of the British sailors who had freed them; what Crowther wrote was a “good opinion.”

Page and Stock

Jesse Page, an English writer of Christian biographies, published two lives of Crowther. The first, in 1888, was written while Crowther was still alive, and Page says that he read the proofs aloud to the bishop, who corrected some of the dates. The second, The Black Bishop, published in 1908, is much longer and was written with the help of Crowther’s son Dandeson and with access to the missionary society’s archives. Both books are full of Crowther’s letters and journals, and both are indispensable.

But Page wrote as an admirer and as a friend of the missionary society, and in the racial language of his age. He calls Crowther “a little black boy,” speaks of “the peculiar temperament of the negro race,” and in one passage makes a remark about Jews and Africans that would be unprintable today. This book does not repeat that language except where it is needed to show how Crowther’s contemporaries thought. Page also records, from family tradition, stories about Crowther’s childhood that have no other support: that his mother was descended from a king of Oyo, that a diviner foretold he would serve the high God, that he saved the household gods from a fire. Page himself warns that the family’s genealogy should not be taken “too seriously”; the other stories he tells without any caution at all. This book tells them as family memory, not as fact.

Eugene Stock’s History of the Church Missionary Society, published in 1899, is the society’s own history, written from its archives. It is reliable on dates and names. On the crisis that darkened Crowther’s last years, it is the society’s side of the story, and it too uses racial language that would not be used now. Yet Stock, writing only eight years after Crowther’s death, admits that the young missionaries who purged the Niger Mission were “too severe,” and he says of Crowther that no tongue, “however malicious,” ever ventured to whisper a word against his personal character.

The Historians

Since the 1960s, historians have told Crowther’s story afresh. The great Nigerian historian J. F. Ade Ajayi studied the Christian missions of Nigeria from 1841 to 1891 and edited Crowther’s 1837 letter. E. A. Ayandele, another Nigerian historian, wrote about the missionary impact on Nigeria and was frank about Crowther’s weaknesses as an administrator. Andrew Walls, a Scottish historian who spent much of his life studying Christianity in Africa, called him “probably the most widely known African Christian of the nineteenth century,” and described his legacy as a faith that was “essentially African and essentially missionary.” Lamin Sanneh, from the Gambia, saw in Crowther’s translation work a turning point in the history of Christianity, because it put the Bible into African languages and so gave those languages new dignity. Jehu Hanciles, from Sierra Leone, has written about the church that Crowther’s son led after his death.

This book has learned from all of them, and it will say where they disagree. It does not reproduce their books, which are in copyright.

What Is Uncertain

Some things about Crowther’s life cannot now be known. The most basic is the year he was born. He never gave it. His first biographer’s dates imply about 1808 or 1809; the missionary society in 1842 said he was about eleven when he was captured in 1821, which would make it about 1810; his gravestone says he died “aged about 89,” which would make it about 1802. Andrew Walls’s estimate of about 1807 is followed in this book, always with the word “about.”

It is uncertain, too, whether his people should be called Egba or Oyo, two branches of the Yoruba. The name of the slave ship on which he was captured, usually given as the Esperança Feliz, rests on mission tradition, not on any record of the ship itself. Page’s two books give different versions of what Crowther said when he met his mother again after twenty-five years. And his daughter’s account of his death, read carefully, places it at about a quarter to one in the morning of the first day of 1892, although every record gives the last day of 1891. This book notes such things as they arise, without making too much of them.

The Harder Story

The most important question on which the sources disagree is the story of Crowther’s last years. The older books, Page’s especially, tell of a saintly old man, a mission troubled by some unworthy African agents, and a painful but necessary discipline carried out by the society. Modern historians tell of a bishop whose clergy were dismissed and suspended over his head by young Europeans who had lost faith in African leadership, in a decade when the racial attitudes of the British Empire were hardening. The truth is not simple. Some of the charges against some of Crowther’s agents were true; one of them concerned a real and terrible crime. Crowther was, by common consent, too lenient a disciplinarian. But the way in which his work was taken from him was unjust, and it was shaped by a belief that Africans could not lead their own church. This book will tell that story as carefully as it can.

The psalmist promised that the people of God would not hide the works of God from their children, but would be “telling to the generation to come the praises of Jehovah, And his strength, and his wondrous works that he hath done” (Psalm 78:4, ASV). Crowther’s life is one of those wondrous works. It deserves to be told truthfully, with its sorrows as well as its triumphs.

fields.title: Ajayi of Osogun
fields.body_html:
“Thine eyes did see mine unformed substance; And in thy book they were all written, Even the days that were ordained for me, When as yet there was none of them.”

— Psalm 139:16, ASV

Osogun

The boy who became Samuel Crowther was born in the town of Osogun, in the Yoruba country of what is now south-western Nigeria, about the year 1807. No one wrote down the date. His own account, written thirty years later, does not give his age, and the guesses of his biographers range over eight years. It is fitting, in a way. He was born into a world that kept its history in memory and song rather than in registers, and the first written record of his life would be made by the people who bought and sold him.

Osogun lies today in Oyo State, near the town of Iseyin. In Crowther’s childhood it was a substantial place. He remembered it as a town of about twelve thousand people, able to put three thousand men into the field, surrounded by a wooden fence some four miles round, with six gates. The houses were built of mud, some of them twelve feet high to the eaves, with tall roofs, arranged in square compounds around open courtyards, several of them joined together and belonging to one family, with passages running from one to another. It was, in his words, “the place of my birth, the play-ground of my childhood, and the place which I thought would be the repository of my mortal body in its old age.”

He grew up, as he later wrote, “enjoying the comforts of father and mother, and the affectionate love of brothers and sisters.” We know a little about his family, and much of what we know comes from family memory recorded long afterwards by his biographer Jesse Page, with help from Crowther’s children. According to that tradition, his father carried on the family trade of weaving, farmed, and was a man of some standing in the town; his grandfather had come from Ketu, to the west. His mother, Page says, bore the title Afala, which marked her as a priestess of Obatala, the Yoruba deity of creation and purity, charged with keeping the god’s white cloths clean. Her own name was Ibisomi. Family tradition also held that she was descended from Abiodun, one of the great kings of Oyo. Page admits that these are traditions, and that he could not test them. This book follows his caution.

His name, Ajayi, was one of the names the Yoruba gave according to the circumstances of a child’s birth. Page says it was given to a child born face downward. A story in the family said that a diviner, consulted at his birth, declared that the boy must not be given to the service of any of the old gods, because he was destined to serve Olorun, the high God, alone, and that his parents were troubled by this. It is the kind of story that families tell about a child who has become famous, and it may or may not be true. What is certain is that the God who made him saw him before anyone else did. The prophet says, “Jehovah hath called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother hath he made mention of my name” (Isaiah 49:1, ASV). “Thine eyes did see mine unformed substance,” the psalmist writes; “in thy book they were all written, Even the days that were ordained for me, When as yet there was none of them.”

The World of Oyo

Osogun belonged to the Oyo empire, which for two centuries had been the greatest power in the Yoruba country. Its king, the Alaafin, ruled from the capital at Old Oyo, far to the north, over a network of towns that paid tribute and sent soldiers. Oyo’s strength lay in its cavalry and in its trade. Some of that trade was in human beings. Oyo had sold captives southward to the coast for generations, to the European ships that carried them to the Americas.

By the time Ajayi was born, Oyo was coming apart. Its rulers quarrelled among themselves. Around 1817 a general named Afonja, who governed the northern town of Ilorin, rebelled against the Alaafin and called on Muslim allies for help. Some of those allies were Fulani, part of the great Islamic movement that had swept across what is now northern Nigeria since 1804. Ilorin passed into Muslim hands and became a base for raiding. At about the same time the southern Yoruba towns fell to fighting among themselves in what became known as the Owu war. The result, over the next twenty years, was the ruin of much of the old Yoruba world. Towns were destroyed, their people scattered, killed, or enslaved. The refugees founded new towns, among them Abeokuta and Ibadan, which would become the centres of Yoruba life in the century to come.

Crowther himself described the wars that reached his town. “For some years,” he wrote in 1837, “wars had been carried on in my Eyo country, which was always attended with much devastation and bloodshed: the women, such men as had surrendered or were caught, with the children, were taken captives.” The raiders, he said, were Oyo Muslims, joined by Fulani and by escaped slaves, “making a formidable force of about 20,000, who annoyed the whole country. The Trade

It is important to understand what those last words meant. By 1821, when the raiders reached Osogun, Britain had outlawed its own slave trade for fourteen years, and was trying to stop other nations’ ships from carrying slaves. But the trade went on. Portuguese and Spanish ships, and ships sailing under other flags, still came to the coast of the Bight of Benin to buy captives for the plantations of Brazil and Cuba. Lagos, on its lagoon, was one of the busiest slave ports in West Africa. The wars in the Yoruba interior fed the trade, and the trade fed the wars. Every town that fell produced captives who could be sold for guns, cloth, tobacco, and rum.

Nobody in this story was innocent. African rulers and raiders captured and sold people. African traders marched them to the coast. European and Brazilian merchants bought them and shipped them across the Atlantic, where the plantations of the Americas worked them to death. Crowther, when he came to write about it, did not spare anyone: he described the cruelty of the raiders, the traders, and the Portuguese buyers with the same plain honesty. What he was chiefly concerned to describe, though, was not the system. It was what happened to one boy and his family on one morning in 1821.

A Childhood

Before that morning, he had been a child like others in a prosperous Yoruba town. Page records, again from family memory, that he was the leader of a club of about forty boys who worked the farms together, and that once, when fire broke out in the family compound, he carried the household gods out of the flames. If true, it is a telling detail. The boy who would one day preach against the worship of images was, as a child, devoted to them, as any Yoruba boy of his time would have been.

His family was a large one. He had an elder brother, whom Page calls Bola, and several sisters. His father’s house, his grandfather’s house, and the homes of his aunts and cousins stood near one another in the town. He knew the paths to the farms, the markets, the shrines, and the stream where the women drew water. He knew his own dialect of Yoruba, the one he would later call “my own,” and he knew no other. He had never seen the sea, a great river, or a white man.

He could not have imagined that he would one day stand in the presence of the Queen of England, preach in English cathedrals, and be consecrated a bishop. Nor could he have imagined the road by which he would get there. The psalm at the head of this chapter says that all his days were written in God’s book before one of them came to be. fields.title: The Unhappy, Blessed Day
fields.body_html:
“And as for you, ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.”

— Genesis 50:20, ASV

“Which I Shall Never Forget”

When Samuel Crowther sat down at Fourah Bay in February 1837 to tell the missionary society how he had come to Sierra Leone, he began with a day. “I suppose, some time about the commencement of the year 1821,” he wrote, “I was in my native country, enjoying the comforts of father and mother, and the affectionate love of brothers and sisters. From this period I must date the unhappy, but which I am now taught, in other respects, to call blessed day, which I shall never forget in my life.”

He explained the double name at once. It was an unhappy day “because it was the day in which I was violently turned out of my father’s house, and separated from my relations; and in which I was made to experience what is called to be in slavery.” It was a blessed day because it was “the day which Providence had marked out for me to set out on my journey” towards the place where the gospel was preached. He wrote those words sixteen years after the event, as a Christian, and the whole letter is shaped by that double vision. But he did not let the blessing cancel the grief. He told the story of the unhappy day in full.

The Morning of the Raid

“The morning in which my town, Ocho-gu, shared the same fate which many others had experienced, was fair and delightful; and most of the inhabitants were engaged in their respective occupations. We were preparing breakfast without any apprehension; when, about 9 o’clock a.m., a rumour was spread in the town, that the enemies had approached with intentions of hostility.”

The raiders surrounded the town before anyone could escape. The men of Osogun, many of them away and the rest surprised, had six gates and many weak places in the fence to defend. After three or four hours the enemy broke in. Crowther’s description of what followed is one of the most vivid eyewitness accounts of a slave raid ever written:

Here a most sorrowful scene imaginable was to be witnessed! — women, some with three, four, or six children clinging to their arms, with the infants on their backs, and such baggage as they could carry on their heads, running as fast as they could, through prickly shrubs, which, hooking their blies and other loads, drew them down from the heads of the bearers.

Mothers who could not carry both their children and their goods dropped the goods, and then found they could not save all the children either. The raiders caught them “with a noose of rope thrown over the neck of every individual, to be led in the manner of goats tied together, under the drove of one man.” Families were divided among different captors on the spot, “to see one another no more.”

Ajayi was caught with his mother, his two sisters, one of them a baby about ten months old, and a cousin. He had been carrying a bow and five arrows. He had lost the bow in the thorn bushes while trying to free himself, “before I could think of making any use of it against my enemies.” The last time he saw his father was when his father came from the fighting to tell them to run. Much later he learned that his father had been killed in another battle. “Here I must take thy leave, unhappy, comfortless father!” he wrote.

As they were led out through the burning town, some of the Fulani among the raiders took his cousin away from the group. They passed his grandfather’s house, already empty. They saw his grandmother at a distance in the crowd of captives for a few minutes, and then lost sight of her for ever. Old women who could not keep up were threatened with death on the spot. “O pitiful sight! whose heart would not bleed to have seen this?” That night, after a march of twenty miles past towns and villages already burned, they reached the raiders’ camp. “It was almost midnight before we reached the town, where we passed our doleful first night in bondage.”

Sold

The next morning the ropes were taken off their necks and the captives were brought to the chief of the raiders “as trophies at his feet.” The chief took Ajayi and one of his sisters. His mother and the baby went to others. “We dared not vent our grief by loud cries, but by very heavy sobs.” Within a few hours it was agreed that Ajayi should be traded for a horse. “Thus, in the space of twenty-four hours, being deprived of liberty and all other comforts, I was made the property of three different persons.”

The horse was taken on trial and turned out to be unsatisfactory, and after about two months Ajayi was returned to the chief, who took him to his own town. There, to his joy, he found his mother and the baby again. For three months he cut grass for the chief’s horses and visited his mother in her captor’s house, “without any fears or thoughts of being separated any more.” His mother told him that she had heard news of his other sister. He never saw her again.

Then, one evening, he was sent with a man to fetch some money from a neighbouring house, and found himself chained with other captives to be taken to market in the morning. His mother was in the same town, and he had not seen her for a day or two. He lay awake all night. At first cock-crow the traders set out with the captives, “with one hand chained to the neck.” Another boy in the chain, whose mother was also in the town, cried and begged to be allowed to see her, and was beaten into silence. “Seeing this, I dared not speak, although I thought we passed by the very house my mother was in. Thus was I separated from my mother and sister, my then only comforts, to meet no more in this world of misery.” He was wrong about that, as we shall see. But it would be twenty-five years.

The Dark Months

At the market town he was sold to a Muslim woman, who took him with her son southward through many towns towards the coast. He found himself among people who spoke another dialect, “a perfect stranger, having left the Eyo country far behind.” He lived about three months in a town called Toko, where he saw the heads of executed people nailed to the trees in the market-place, and heard of a woman shot for bewitching her husband.

His mistress spoke cheerfully of going on to the Popo country on the coast to buy tobacco and other fine things. Ajayi understood what that meant. It was where the Portuguese bought slaves. He lost his appetite and fell ill with dysentery. And then he did something that he confessed, sixteen years later, with a candour that is still startling:

I determined with myself that I would not go to the Popo country; but would make an end of myself, one way or another. In several nights I attempted strangling myself with my band; but had not courage enough to close the noose tight, so as to effect my purpose. May the Lord forgive me this sin! I determined, next, that I would leap out of the canoe into the river, when we should cross it in our way to that country.

Before he could try, his owner, seeing how he had changed, sold him on. Crowther’s comment on this is one of the most remarkable sentences in the letter: “Thus the Lord, while I knew Him not, led me not into temptation, and delivered me from evil.” He was quoting the Lord’s Prayer, which he would not have known until years later: “And bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one” (Matthew 6:13, ASV). Looking back, he saw that the petition had been answered for him before he had ever prayed it.

At the next town he tried again to strangle himself, several times, and failed. “It was very singular,” he wrote, “that no thought of making use of a knife ever entered my mind.” He was traded again for tobacco, rum, and other goods, and kept in chains alone for some time until his new owner had collected enough slaves. He was taken to another town, and after two months more, to a slave market on the shore of a great lagoon. He had never seen so much water. “The sight of the river terrified me exceedingly, for I had never seen any thing like it in my life.” There he was sold again, for tobacco, and taken across the water by canoe at night to Lagos. “Nothing now terrified me more than the river, and the thought of going into another world.”

Ye Meant Evil

It is worth pausing at this point in the story, as Crowther himself did in writing it. A boy of about thirteen had in little more than a year lost his father, his home, his town, his grandmother, his sisters, and twice his mother. He had been sold or bartered at least six times. He had tried to kill himself, and failed. And he was now on the edge of the sea, among people whose language he did not speak, waiting to be sold to white men he had never seen.

Christians have often compared Crowther to Joseph, the son of Jacob, whose brothers sold him to traders for twenty pieces of silver, and who was carried into Egypt as a slave (Genesis 37:28). His first biographer made the comparison, and so do many sermons. It is a true comparison, and Crowther himself would not have objected to it. Years later, when Joseph had become the second man in Egypt and his brothers were afraid of his revenge, he told them: “ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.”

But the comparison can be made too quickly. Joseph did not say that what his brothers did was good. He said they meant it for evil, and it was evil. What he said was that God had been at work in it, for purposes they could not see. Crowther said the same. He called the day of his capture blessed, but he never called slavery good, and he never pretended that his losses were not losses. At the end of his letter he wrote: “Thus the day of my captivity was to me a blessed day, when considered in this respect; though certainly it must be unhappy also, in my being deprived on it of my father, mother, sisters, and all other relations.”

That double sentence is the key to his whole life. He held on to both halves of it, the grief and the gratitude, to the end.

fields.title: Myrmidon
fields.body_html:
“The Spirit of the Lord Jehovah is upon me; because Jehovah hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the broken-hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound”

— Isaiah 61:1, ASV

Lagos

Lagos in 1822 was an island town on a lagoon, ruled by its own king and full of slave-traders. The Portuguese and Spanish buyers lived in one part of it. Ajayi was there more than three months before he saw one of them. Then one evening a group of about six white men walked down the street where he was living. He did not dare to look at them properly, “being always suspicious that they had come for me: and my suspicion was not a fanciful one; for, in a few days after, I was made the eighth in number of the slaves of the Portuguese.”

By now he had stopped resisting. “Being a veteran in slavery, if I may be allowed the expression, and having no more hope of ever going to my country again, I patiently took whatever came; although it was not without a great fear and trembling that I received, for the first time, the touch of a White Man, who examined me whether I was sound or not.”

The Portuguese kept their captives in a room with one door and no windows. The men and boys were chained together by the neck, on a chain about six fathoms long, padlocked at both ends. The boys suffered most. When the men grew angry, or wanted to ease the weight of the chain to lie down at night, they pulled it tight, and the boys’ necks were bruised. “We were almost suffocated, or bruised to death.” When one or two fought in the night, all of them were punished. Eventually, when more men arrived and there was no chain to spare, the boys were separated and tied together with cord instead. “The female sex fared not much better.” They were kept like this for nearly four months.

Among the captives brought in at this time was another Yoruba boy named Joseph Bartholomew. The two would sail together, be freed together, and years later serve together as agents of the Church Missionary Society.

War on the Sea

Then a rumour went round that the English were cruising the coast. To the captives this was one more cause of dread. They had never heard of war at sea, or imagined it possible. It delayed their embarkation for some weeks. At last they were taken by canoe at night from Lagos to the beach, and in the morning put on board the ship, which sailed at once. There were 187 of them. The crew, busy with loading, gave them nothing to eat that day, and most of them were seasick.

“On the very same evening,” Crowther wrote, “we were surprised by two English men-of-war; and on the next morning found ourselves in the hands of new conquerors, whom we at first very much dreaded, they being armed with long swords.” When they were brought up from the hold, they found themselves surrounded by two large warships and several smaller vessels. The warships were His Majesty’s ships Myrmidon, under Captain H. J. Leeke, and Iphigenia, under Captain Sir Robert Mends, “who captured us on the 7th of April 1822, on the river Lagos.”

Mission tradition gives the name of the Portuguese ship as the Esperança Feliz, which means “Happy Hope.” Crowther’s letter does not name it, and no independent record of the ship has been found. The name may be right. It would be a fitting one.

The Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron had been patrolling the coast since 1808, trying to enforce the laws against the slave trade. It was a small force for a long coast, and most slave ships got through. The sailors were driven partly by conviction and partly by prize money, which was paid for every captive freed. Many of them died of fever. It was, whatever its motives, one of the few things the British Empire did in West Africa in those years that was simply good, and for the 187 people in the hold of that ship it was the difference between the plantations of Brazil or Cuba and a chance of life.

Hogs and Cannon-Shot

The Portuguese owner and his sailors were tied up. The cook was left free to make breakfast. The captives, hungry and not threatened, began to help themselves to fruit from the stern, and then to wander over the ship looking for anything they could take. “Now we began to entertain a good opinion of our conquerors.”

After breakfast they were divided among the ships. Ajayi and five friends, among them Joseph Bartholomew, kept close together so as to be taken to the same vessel, and were rowed across to the Myrmidon. They could find no trace there of the captives who had been taken over before them. Then they saw parts of a pig hanging up, with white skin, which they had never seen, since in their country a pig was always roasted in the fire to remove the hair. And along the deck they saw rows of cannon-balls. They drew the obvious conclusion. The white men had killed and eaten the others, and the round shot were their heads. “But we were soon undeceived, by a close examination of the flesh with cloven foot, which resembled that of a hog; and, by a cautious approach to the shot, that they were iron.”

It is a story that Crowther clearly enjoyed telling against himself, and it says a great deal about what the captives believed. Many Africans in the era of the slave trade believed that Europeans bought people to eat them. The fear was not foolish. People taken to the coast by the white men never came back.

Within a few days the six boys were “quite at home in the man-of-war.” The sailors took them as their own boys and gave them clothes. The Portuguese owner and his son were brought on board in fetters. Ajayi, sure now that he would never again be in the man’s power, walked up to him while he was being shaved by his son and struck him on the head. He recorded it honestly, and judged it honestly: “an act, however, very wicked and unkind in its nature.”

Freetown

The slave ship was towed along for a time and then, being a slow sailer and not worth the trouble, stripped and abandoned at sea. Not all the captives who had been freed with Ajayi survived. One of the vessels carrying them was wrecked on a sandbank, though everyone aboard was saved. Another sank in a storm with all the captives and all but five of the sailors, who were found days later in a boat, reduced to skeletons. A hundred and two of the people from the slave ship were lost.

After about two and a half months cruising, the Myrmidon landed its rescued captives at Sierra Leone on 17 June 1822. Sierra Leone had been founded on the peninsula around Freetown in 1787 as a settlement for freed Black people from Britain and later from Nova Scotia and Jamaica, and since 1808 it had been a British colony and the place where the Navy landed the people it took from slave ships. They were known as “recaptives” or “liberated Africans,” and by 1822 there were thousands of them, from dozens of peoples and languages, settled in villages in the hills around the town.

That same day Ajayi and his companions were sent to one of those villages, Bathurst, and put in the care of the missionary there, Mr. Davey. They found many of their own countrymen, though none they had known before. The people assured them that they were free, “and we very soon believed them.”

But a few days later they were sent for to go to Freetown, to give evidence against their Portuguese owner in the court that dealt with captured slave ships. Someone hinted to them that they would be handed back to him. They refused to go unless they were carried, and in the end they were whipped into going. It was, Crowther wrote, “not a small joy to us to return to Bathurst again, in the evening, to our friends.” He admitted that he had been afraid, partly because of the blow he had given the man on the ship.

Liberty to the Captives

The verse at the head of this chapter was read by Jesus in the synagogue at Nazareth, at the beginning of his ministry. He unrolled the scroll of Isaiah and read that the Spirit of the Lord had anointed him “to proclaim release to the captives … to set at liberty them that are bruised” (Luke 4:18, ASV). Then he rolled up the scroll and said that the scripture had been fulfilled that day.

The captain of the Myrmidon did not know that he was setting free a future bishop. He was doing his duty. But the boy with the bruised neck whom his sailors fed and clothed would spend the rest of his life proclaiming a greater release, from a deeper bondage, to the people of his own land. Forty-two years later, according to Page, Leeke, by then an admiral, was in Canterbury Cathedral to see the boy he had freed consecrated a bishop. For Crowther, the day of his rescue was the day the psalmist describes: “Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: The snare is broken, and we are escaped” (Psalm 124:7, ASV).

fields.title: Samuel Crowther
fields.body_html:
“Wherefore if any man is in Christ, he is a new creature: the old things are passed away; behold, they are become new.”

— 2 Corinthians 5:17, ASV

Bathurst

Bathurst was one of the villages in the hills above Freetown where the colony settled the people the Navy rescued. It had been called Leopold; the government renamed it after a British minister. Its people came from dozens of African nations and spoke dozens of languages. They had been torn from their homes, marched to the coast, chained in holds, and set down in a strange land by strangers. Many of them were children. The Church Missionary Society, which had worked in Sierra Leone since 1804, ran the schools and churches in several of the villages, and at Bathurst the missionary was a man named Davey.

Ajayi was put into the school. He learned fast. “In about six months after my arrival at Sierra Leone,” he wrote, “I was able to read the New Testament with some degree of freedom; and was made a Monitor, for which I was rewarded with sevenpence-halfpenny per month.” A monitor was an older pupil who taught younger ones; the system allowed a single master to teach a large school. It is the first sign of the gift that would mark his whole life. As soon as he had learned something, he began to teach it.

At Bathurst he lived in the house of the missionary, Mr. Davey, and his wife. According to Page, he served as their pantry-boy, and in return his mistress taught him for half an hour every evening. Years later, widowed twice, she married another Bathurst missionary, John Weeks, a Cornish mechanic who had reached the colony in 1824 and who taught Crowther carpentry. It is as Mrs. Weeks that she appears later in this story, and she would remember those evening lessons forty years afterwards.

Samuel Crowther

The next part of his story he told in two sentences. “The Lord was pleased to open my heart to hearken to those things which were spoken by His servants; and being convinced that I was a sinner, and desired to obtain pardon through Jesus Christ, I was baptized on the 11th of December 1825, by the Rev. J. Raban.”

It is a very plain account. There is no vision, no crisis, no dramatic moment. He heard the gospel preached, he came to see that he was a sinner, and he wanted the forgiveness that Christ offered. The words “the Lord was pleased to open my heart” echo the story of Lydia in the Acts of the Apostles, “whose heart the Lord opened to give heed unto the things which were spoken by Paul.” That was how he understood it: not as something he had achieved, but as something God had done for him.

At his baptism he took a new name. He was named after Samuel Crowther, the vicar of Christ Church, Newgate Street, in the City of London, who had been one of the founding members of the Church Missionary Society. Henry Venn, the society’s great secretary, later said that it was Mrs. Davey, the later Mrs. Weeks, who chose the name. Before she came to Africa she had taught in Mr. Crowther’s Sunday school in London, and she gave the boy the name of her own pastor. The English clergyman died in 1829. He never met the African boy who carried his name, and could not have known what that boy would do with it.

The name was common among recaptives. Rescued Africans in Sierra Leone were often given the names of missionaries, benefactors, or English clergymen, and many of them, like Crowther, kept their African names alongside. For the rest of his life he signed himself Samuel Crowther, and later Samuel Adjai Crowther, using the old spelling of his Yoruba name. The African name was never lost.

Paul says that if anyone is in Christ, “he is a new creature: the old things are passed away; behold, they are become new.” For Ajayi of Osogun that was true in a literal way. He had a new name, a new language, a new faith, and a new country. But it would be a mistake to think that the old things were simply thrown away. The boy who had been a Yoruba did not stop being one. As we shall see, he would spend much of his life studying the language, the proverbs, and the customs of his own people, and insisting that the gospel should come to them in their own tongue. What passed away was the old slavery. What remained, and was made new, was Ajayi.

A Visit to England

In 1826 Mr. Davey returned to England on leave, and took Crowther with him. They landed at Portsmouth in August. For a few months Crowther attended the parish school in Liverpool Road, Islington, in north London. “It was my desire,” he wrote later, “to remain for a good while, to be qualified as a Teacher to my fellow-creatures; but Providence ordered it so, that, at my return, I had the wished-for instruction.” In another letter he admitted that he had “begged very hard” to stay, and that when he found it was not God’s will, “I cast myself upon Him, because He knows best.”

He came back to Sierra Leone in 1827 with some English clothes, including a blue suit and a beaver hat, and a mattress that someone in England had given him. Mr. Davey, recommending him as the one lad fit to be sent back to England for training, described him as a boy of “abilities far surpassing any I have met with before,” who “appears to be truly pious.” His only fear was that Crowther “should be lifted up too much” by his visit to England.

Fourah Bay

That same year the society opened a training institution at Fourah Bay, on the edge of Freetown, to prepare African teachers and ministers. It would become Fourah Bay College, for many years the only institution of higher education in West Africa. The first name on its roll of students was Samuel Crowther.

The principal was a German missionary, the Rev. C. L. F. Haensel, a strict and devout man who made his students clean their own rooms, wash their own clothes, and carry loads of rice on their heads, “just to remind them that they are not above” it. When Crowther arrived with his English mattress, Haensel forbade it. “This was too great a luxury,” he reported, “I at once forbade its entrance, to which he readily consented. I wish for the good of his own soul to see him in that state of lowliness of mind which Africans so easily lose by visits to England.” Haensel’s remark about Africans says more about Haensel than about Crowther. But Crowther took the mattress away without complaint, and years later he spoke of Haensel with admiration as “a peculiar person altogether; we could never find one to match him.”

Haensel, for his part, soon recognised what he had. “He is a very clever lad,” he wrote, “and it is a real pleasure to instruct him.” Later: “He is a lad of uncommon ability, steady conduct, a thirst for knowledge, and indefatigable industry.”

There was one complication. Haensel reported to his committee in March 1827 that Crowther was being admitted only on probation, “owing to the information which is received of an attachment entertained by him towards a girl who is schoolmistress at Bathurst.” Crowther said it would not interfere with his studies. Haensel was ready to trust him, but doubted “whether he knows himself sufficiently.”

Asano

The girl was named Asano. She was a Yoruba like him, and had also been rescued from a slave ship, captured by HMS Bann on 31 October 1822 and landed at Freetown the same year as Crowther. Page says that she had learned her letters at his side at Bathurst. At her baptism she took the name Susan Thompson. By the time Crowther went to Fourah Bay she was herself teaching in the school at Bathurst.

Crowther did not let her go. Two years later, when he was schoolmaster at the village of Regent, earning twenty-four pounds a year, he applied to the missionaries in council for permission to marry her. The council recorded that it had received “a satisfactory account … of the girl’s suitableness for a fellow-worker with him,” and gave its consent. They were married on 21 September 1829. The marriage lasted fifty-one years, until her death in 1880. By 1837 they had a son and two daughters; in the end there were six children.

Some popular accounts say that Crowther and Asano met on the slave ship. They did not. They were freed from different ships, six months apart. They met as two recaptive children in a mission school, two survivors of the same catastrophe, who had lost their homes and families and found each other.

“Pray for Africa”

In January 1829, while he was an assistant to Haensel at Fourah Bay, Crowther wrote a letter to the society in London. It is the earliest of his letters to survive in any length, and it shows a young man already thinking about his calling. He was not satisfied, he wrote, to be an assistant: “I am desiring to be instructed by God’s Holy Spirit that I may soon rise up and become a teacher to the others. I have hope that Africa will soon stretch forth her hands unto God.” He asked for prayer for a few African teachers who felt very few against so great a task. He reminded his readers that Elijah had stood alone against four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, and that God had answered him (1 Kings 18:22). And he ended: “Pray for Africa is the prayer of your most humble, thankful, and obliged servant, Samuel Crowther.”

Over the next twelve years he taught at Regent and then at Wellington, and from 1834 he was a tutor at Fourah Bay. He studied Greek and theology. He began to collect words and phrases in Yoruba, the language of his childhood, which many of the recaptives in the colony spoke, and which had hardly yet been written down. He preached and taught in the villages. He was a respected member of the small African Christian community of Sierra Leone, a schoolmaster and a family man. It might have been his whole life.

He ended his 1837 letter to Mr. Jowett with a sentence from the Book of Common Prayer, where the service of God is called “perfect freedom.” “May I ever have a fresh desire to be engaged in the service of Christ,” he wrote, “for it is perfect freedom!” For a man who had been chained by the neck in a Lagos slave pen fifteen years earlier, the phrase was not a cliché. He had known the other kind of service. He knew what freedom was. And he had found, as Jesus promised, that “If therefore the Son shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed” (John 8:36, ASV).

The council recorded that it had received “a satisfactory account … of the girl’s suitableness for a fellow-worker with him,” and gave its consent. They were married on 21 September 1829. He reminded his readers that Elijah had stood alone against four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, and that God had answered him (1 Kings 18:22). He studied Greek and theology. He began to collect words and phrases in Yoruba, the language of his childhood, which many of the recaptives in the colony spoke, and which had hardly yet been written down. He preached and taught in the villages. He was a respected member of the small African Christian community of Sierra Leone, a schoolmaster and a family man. It might have been his whole life. He ended his 1837 letter to Mr. Jowett with a sentence from the Book of Common Prayer, where the service of God is called “perfect freedom.” “May I ever have a fresh desire to be engaged in the service of Christ,” he wrote, “for it is perfect freedom!” For a man who had been chained by the neck in a Lagos slave pen fifteen years earlier, the phrase was not a cliché. He had known the other kind of service. He knew what freedom was. And he had found, as Jesus promised, that “If therefore the Son shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed” (John 8:36, ASV).

fields.title: The Niger, 1841
fields.body_html:
“But ye shall receive power, when the Holy Spirit is come upon you: and ye shall be my witnesses both in Jerusalem, and in all Judæa and Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.”

— Acts 1:8, ASV

A Great Expedition

In 1841 the British government sent an expedition up the Niger River. It was the idea of Sir Thomas Fowell Buxton, who had led the campaign to abolish slavery in the British colonies. Buxton believed that the slave trade could not be ended by the Navy alone. It had to be undermined at its source, by making treaties with the rulers of the interior, by introducing honest trade to replace the trade in people, and by bringing the gospel. Three iron steamers were built for the purpose, the Albert, the Wilberforce, and the Soudan, under the command of Captain H. D. Trotter of the Royal Navy. They carried treaty commissioners, scientists, a company of settlers to start a model farm, and, at the request of the Church Missionary Society, two missionaries.

One was a German clergyman, the Rev. J. F. Schön, who had worked in Sierra Leone for ten years and was a gifted linguist. The other was “Mr. Samuel Crowther,” a catechist and schoolmaster of Fourah Bay. Afterwards the society would invite him to England with a view to his ordination “for Missionary labours in his own country, should the Bishop of London deem him qualified.” He was in his early thirties. He had a wife who was expecting another child, and four children. He had lived in Sierra Leone for nineteen years, which he called “the happiest part of my life, because there I was brought acquainted with the saving knowledge of Jesus Christ.”

He went aboard the Soudan on 1 July 1841, after taking “affectionate leave of my wife, children, and friends.” His prayer as he went was characteristic: “May the Lord, who has been my guide from my youth up until now, keep them and me, and make me neither barren nor unfruitful in His service!”

On Board

His journal of the voyage, published the next year with Schön’s, is the first long piece of writing we have from him, and it shows a man at ease in any company. The captain of the Soudan, Bird Allen, was a devout man who held services and an officers’ Bible class, and invited Crowther to join it. He lent Crowther his cabin to write in. Crowther made a first attempt to teach the Kru sailors their alphabet, led evening prayers when asked, “I hope with all lowliness and self-abasement before God,” and worked with the Yoruba interpreter on a vocabulary of his mother tongue.

At Cape Coast, on the Gold Coast, he spent a day at the house of the Wesleyan missionary Thomas Birch Freeman, himself the son of an African father, and visited a government school of 170 boys taught by an African master. He also copied, for a Dr. Marshall, the memorial of the Rev. Philip Quaque, a native of Cape Coast who had been ordained in the Church of England in 1765 and had served his people for fifty years. Crowther copied it without comment, but it was proof that an African could be a clergyman of the Church of England. Crowther would follow him.

He listened to a sermon preached through an interpreter, and came away convinced of something he would say for the rest of his life: “The plan of studying the language of the people, and translating the Scriptures into it, ought to be immediately adopted by every Missionary sent into the heathen world.”

Up the River

They crossed the bar at the mouth of the Niger on 13 August. “Hitherto hath the Lord helped us!” Crowther wrote, using Samuel’s words when he set up a stone of remembrance after a victory: “Hitherto hath Jehovah helped us” (1 Samuel 7:12, ASV). He would use the phrase again and again.

The steamers pushed slowly up through the mangrove swamps of the Delta and into the broad river beyond. At Aboh, the king, Obi Ossai, signed a treaty against the slave trade and asked for teachers. At Idda, the capital of the Igala people, there were long negotiations with the Attah, the king, who thought it beneath his dignity to step into a canoe. The day before they reached Idda, at the village of Doko Abbokkoh, Crowther had acted as interpreter in Hausa for the first time. At the confluence of the Niger and the Benue, the expedition bought land for its model farm at the foot of a hill, and left a company of settlers there under a superintendent, Mr. Carr, with the schoolmaster Thomas King to teach them.

At Gori, Crowther watched three slaves, two women and a man, freed after a trial before the Attah’s son. They were given new clothes, and their old clothes were thrown into the river. At Egga, further up, he went ashore and found himself among Yoruba people for the first time since he had been taken from his home twenty years before. They gave him news of the wars: Old Oyo deserted, the new capital moved south, the new towns of Ibadan and Abeokuta rising. He argued with Yoruba Muslims who said that God had sanctioned the slave trade, and then let the argument drop; “I waived all disputes whether God sanctioned the slave-trade or not,” he wrote, and simply told them that the God who had brought him so far could do greater things. He asked Yoruba traders whether it was better to trade in goods, “or to trade in slaves, when the buyer and seller rejoice, and the purchased, our fellow-creatures, enshackled, sit mournfully.”

When he told the people of Egga how the liberated Africans lived in Sierra Leone, many of them said, he wrote, “that they could judge of their happy state merely by my appearance.” He was, without meaning to be, the expedition’s best argument.

The Fever

Then the fever came. It had already begun at the Confluence. Within weeks almost every European on the expedition was ill. The Soudan was sent back down the river as a hospital ship, and Crowther moved to the Albert, which pushed on a little further under Trotter before he too fell ill and the ship turned back. The officers were all sick. The mate worked the ship, and Dr. Stanger took a turn in the engine room. Two men, delirious, jumped overboard; one was saved by a Black sailor, and the other drowned. At the Confluence the three Europeans in charge of the model farm were all ill. Crowther sat up with Captain Bird Allen until midnight.

They reached the island of Fernando Po in the Gulf of Guinea on 17 October. On 25 October Bird Allen died. “Captain Trotter, with tears, closed the eyes of his departed friend.” Others followed. Of about 150 Europeans on the expedition, Macgregor Laird later wrote, 42 died within about two months. The model farm was abandoned the next year. By any measure, the expedition was a disaster, and the society itself called it an “admitted failure.”

But the Africans on the expedition had mostly stayed well. Crowther’s biographer says that he escaped the fever altogether, though his own journal records a bout of ague on the way out. Whatever the reason, and no one at the time really understood malaria, the lesson seemed obvious. At Fernando Po, while the survivors recovered, Crowther gathered a class of people who wanted to be baptised. By mid-November it had grown from seven to thirty-six. And he wrote a letter to the society in London.

Her Own Children

The letter, written on 2 November 1841, is the first statement of the idea that would govern his life. “I do not limit the power of the Lord of the Vineyard,” he wrote, and he did not want to seem to say that European missionaries were not needed. “Still, I am reluctantly led to adopt the opinion, that Africa can chiefly be benefitted by her own Children.”

He did not write it proudly. In the same letter he said: “I always feel that myself and my Brethren of the Natives are not sufficiently qualified for so great a work.” He added that “human learning will be of very little avail, if the heart is not inspired by the Holy Spirit from above.” He was not claiming that Africans were better missionaries than Europeans. He was saying that Africans could live where Europeans died, could speak the languages that Europeans had to learn, and could go where Europeans could not. The question was whether they would be trained, trusted, and sent.

Schön, writing his own report, drew the same conclusion and put a name to it. Might not Samuel Crowther, he asked, “a Native of the same country, and held in high estimation by his brethren, be sent thither, after he shall have received Ordination?” By “thither” Schön meant the Yoruba country, by way of Badagry.

The verse at the head of this chapter records the last words of Jesus before his ascension. The apostles were to be his witnesses in Jerusalem, and Judea, and Samaria, and to the uttermost part of the earth. The order is worth noticing. The witness was to begin at home and spread outward, carried by people in their own land before it was carried to others. The disaster of 1841 persuaded the Church Missionary Society, in a way that no argument had, that the uttermost parts of Africa would be reached chiefly by Africans. Samuel Crowther would be the first of them.

fields.title: “Who Maketh Thee to Differ?”
fields.body_html:
“For who maketh thee to differ? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? but if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory as if thou hadst not received it?”

— 1 Corinthians 4:7, ASV

Islington

Crowther arrived in England in September 1842, bringing with him a manuscript grammar and vocabulary of the Yoruba language. The society sent him to its training college at Islington, in north London, to prepare for ordination. He was there for about nine months. James Scholefield, a Cambridge professor who examined him on Paley’s Evidences, praised his work. When his Yoruba vocabulary was published in 1843, it was, as Andrew Walls says, the first such work by a native speaker of the language.

On Trinity Sunday, 11 June 1843, Charles Blomfield, Bishop of London, ordained him deacon. As Page tells it, Henry Venn, the society’s secretary, had taken him to the bishop to be examined, and how the bishop had questioned him “pretty smartly.” When he had left the room, Blomfield said to Venn: “He’ll do, he’ll do, only polish him up a bit.” At breakfast after the ordination, the bishop told another of the new deacons that Crowther was “no mean scholar; his examination papers were capital, and his Latin remarkably good.” In October the same bishop ordained him priest.

Eugene Stock, the society’s historian, records a story that on the day of the ordination the English candidates “waited for the Negro to go first.” Stock tells it as a mark of respect. Stock called him “the first African clergyman of our day,” adding in a footnote that he had not forgotten Philip Quaque. He was not, as popular accounts sometimes claim, the first African Anglican priest. That honour belongs to Philip Quaque, whose memorial he had copied at Cape Coast.

Home Again

He sailed back to Sierra Leone and landed at Freetown on Saturday, 2 December 1843. The next morning he preached his first sermon in Africa as a clergyman, in English, to a crowded church. His text was from the parable of the great supper, where the servant reports to his master: “Lord, what thou didst command is done, and yet there is room” (Luke 14:22, ASV).

He wrote afterwards:

The novelty of seeing a native clergyman performing Divine Service excited a very great interest among all who were present. But the question, “Who maketh thee to differ?” filled me with shame and confusion of face.

The question is Paul’s, from the verse at the head of this chapter. Paul was writing to Christians in Corinth who had begun to boast about their teachers and their gifts. “Who maketh thee to differ? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? but if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory as if thou hadst not received it?” Crowther, standing in the pulpit as the first African clergyman many of his hearers had ever seen, felt the force of it. He had been a slave boy in a Lagos pen twenty-one years before. Everything that now set him apart, his education, his ordination, his place in the pulpit, he had received. There was nothing to boast of.

That sense of having received everything never left him. It was the root of his humility, and it made him patient with others. A man who knows that his own gifts were given is less likely to despise people who have not been given the same.

In His Own Tongue

A few weeks later he did something that had probably never been done before. Many of the people of Freetown were Yoruba recaptives like himself, and he announced that he would hold a service in the Yoruba language. He visited homes to invite people, especially those who never came to church. He called on the headman of the Yoruba Muslims who lived near Fourah Bay, and told him about it. He described the conversation: “I did not raise any objections to their faith nor attack it, but endeavoured to show them the great blessings Christianity bestowed on mankind wherever it was embraced.” To his surprise, the Muslims were proud that one of their own countrymen had become a clergyman of the Church of England.

On 9 January 1844, at half past four in the afternoon, he opened the first Yoruba service in the mission church in Freetown. A large crowd came, Yoruba, Igbo, and people from Calabar and elsewhere, drawn by the novelty of hearing the gospel preached in an African language in an English church. He wrote:

Although the language is my native tongue, with which I am well acquainted, yet on this occasion it appeared as if I were a babe just learning to utter my mother tongue. The work in which I was engaged, the place where I stood, and the congregation before me were altogether so new and strange that the whole proceeding seemed to myself like a dream. But the Lord supported me.

He read the prayers that had not yet been translated in English, and a portion of Luke’s Gospel in Yoruba, which he had translated himself on the voyage home. Three young Muslims, sent by their headman, were in the congregation. He preached on the angel’s words to Mary: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee: wherefore also the holy thing which is begotten shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35, ASV). It was the lesson he had just read, and with Muslims present it was a pointed one, since it concerns the very point on which Christians and Muslims most disagree. Afterwards the young Muslims followed him home, said they were glad of what they had heard, and wished God would help him in his work.

The Shango Drummer

Not every encounter went so well. In February 1844 he visited a house in Freetown where worshippers of Shango, the Yoruba god of thunder, were holding a ceremony. The head drummer said something obscene in his hearing, and when Crowther rebuked him he rose in anger and turned on him. The Christians of the colony, he said, were the worst adulterers in the place. He himself had once gone to church and found no good in it.

Crowther recorded what happened next with an honesty that few missionaries of his time would have allowed themselves:

To my great mortification, shame, and regret I was silenced — the charge was too true.

The Christians of Freetown were not all saints, and the drummer knew it. Crowther did not pretend otherwise. When he tried to speak to the owner of the house, the worshippers pulled the man away, and drummed and chanted to drown his voice. They asked him whether his own forefathers had not worshipped the orisha for thirty generations, whether he had not been born and kept alive by their gods, and told him that if his forefathers had gone to hell, he must go too.

“The only weapons I used on this occasion,” he wrote, “were patience and an even temper, which the Lord has pleased to grant me.” When he left, two of the worshippers ran after him into the street to say how surprised they were that he had kept his temper while he was insulted. “I told them it was the religion of Christ only which could make the temper of man sweet and amiable.”

Three things in this story would mark his whole ministry. The first is that he spoke to people in their own language and about their own religion, from inside their world. The second is that he did not answer anger with anger. And the third is that he admitted the truth of a charge against Christians when it was true. The drummer’s rebuke stayed with him. A church whose members did not live as Christians would not persuade anyone, however well it was preached.

“Pray Upon Her Lap”

He loved the Church of England, and he loved its Book of Common Prayer. Later he wrote: “I have considered the Church as my mother, which has taught me to pray, as it were, upon her lap by the Prayer Book.” It was the Prayer Book that had given him the phrase “perfect freedom.” It was the Prayer Book he would translate into Yoruba, and whose services he would carry up the Niger.

It may seem strange that a man with such a deep sense of his own African identity should love so English a book. But Crowther did not see a contradiction. The Prayer Book, for him, was not English. It was the prayer of the Church, drawn from Scripture and from centuries of Christian worship, and it could be prayed in any language. His life’s work would be to make it pray in his own.

Three young Muslims, sent by their headman, were in the congregation. He preached on the angel’s words to Mary: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee: wherefore also the holy thing which is begotten shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35, ASV). It was the lesson he had just read, and with Muslims present it was a pointed one, since it concerns the very point on which Christians and Muslims most disagree.
