fields.title: The Helper of the Fatherless
fields.body_html:
“Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: The helpless committeth himself unto thee; Thou hast been the helper of the fatherless.”

— Psalm 10:14, ASV

Going Home

In the late 1830s something unexpected began to happen in Sierra Leone. Some of the recaptives, having saved a little money by trade, bought ships and sailed back down the coast to the places from which they had been taken. Many of them were Egba Yoruba, and they found that their scattered people had built a new city, Abeokuta, among great granite rocks in the forest north of Lagos. Some of the returnees were Christians. They sent word back to Sierra Leone asking for missionaries to come and teach their people.

The Wesleyan missionary T. B. Freeman reached Abeokuta in 1842, and Henry Townsend of the Church Missionary Society visited soon afterwards. The society decided to open a mission to the Yoruba. It was the obvious work for its new African clergyman. On 18 December 1844 Crowther sailed from Freetown with Townsend and his wife, a German clergyman named C. A. Gollmer and his wife, and several African assistants, among them Mark Willoughby, who had been freed from the same slave ship on the same day as Crowther twenty-two years before.

They landed at Badagry, on the coast west of Lagos, on 17 January 1845. There they were held up for eighteen months. The chief of Abeokuta who had invited them, Shodeke, died just before they landed, and his successors hesitated. Mrs. Gollmer died. A Brazilian slave-trader named Domingo, who had no wish to see missionaries in the interior, did his best to block the road. The missionaries used the time to build, to preach, and to study. Crowther translated parts of the Prayer Book into Yoruba. At last the chiefs of Abeokuta sent word that they would receive them, and in the last days of July 1846 Crowther and Townsend set out along the forest road. They entered Abeokuta on 3 August 1846.

Twenty-Five Years

Crowther had been in the city less than three weeks when he received news he could hardly believe. His mother was alive. She was living with his sisters in a nearby town. He sent for them. His sisters, Page says, would not believe the message, but his mother came, with one of his half-brothers.

On 21 August 1846 he wrote in his journal:

The text for to-day in the Christian Almanac is “Thou art the Helper of the fatherless.” I have never felt the force of this text more than I did this day, as I have to relate that my mother, from whom I was torn away about five-and-twenty years ago, came with my brother in quest of me. When she saw me she trembled. She could not believe her own eyes. We grasped one another, looking at one another in silence and great astonishment, while the big tears rolled down her emaciated cheeks.

She held his hand and called him by the pet names his grandmother had used for him as a child. “We could not say much,” he wrote, “but sat still, casting many an affectionate look towards each other, a look which violence and oppression had long checked.” The two sisters who had been captured with him were living with her, with their children. “I cannot describe my feelings. I had given up all hope, and now, after a separation of twenty-five years, without any plan or device of mine, we were brought together again.”

There is a small puzzle in the sources. Jesse Page printed this journal entry twice, in 1888 and in 1908, and in one version Crowther speaks of “an affection which twenty-five years had not extinguished,” while in the other it had “nearly been extinguished.” We cannot now tell which is right. Both are true enough. Twenty-five years of separation, in which each believed the other lost for ever, would test any love. It had not died.

Her Story

His mother had her own story to tell, and it was a hard one. The two main sources tell it slightly differently. According to Eugene Stock, she had never been sold to the coast, but had remained a slave in the interior until her daughters were able to redeem her. According to Page’s 1908 account, she and her daughters had first regained their freedom through a half-brother. Years later, going to market, she and her eldest daughter had been kidnapped again. The daughter was ransomed by her husband, but the old woman was dragged from market to market, and sold as a domestic slave. She was sent by her mistress towards Abeokuta, captured again on the road, and sold again into hard bondage, until her daughter managed to scrape together enough cowrie shells to buy her back for four pounds ten shillings.

Whichever version is right in its details, the outline is the same. The woman who had been led away with a rope round her neck from the burning town of Osogun had spent a large part of the next twenty-five years as a slave. She was now old and thin. Her husband was dead, and so was the grandmother whose pet names for the boy she still remembered. And she had found her son again, not as the boy who had been taken, but as a clergyman in the dress of a white man, who had come back to her people with a message about a God she did not know.

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from a psalm that cries out against the violent and the oppressor, the men who lie in wait to catch the poor and drag them off in their net. “Thou hast seen it,” the psalmist says to God; “for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: The helpless committeth himself unto thee; Thou hast been the helper of the fatherless.” Crowther read it on the morning of the day his mother came back to him, and it described his life exactly. He had been fatherless and helpless, and God had helped him. God had seen the raiders, the traders, and the slave-dealers, and had not forgotten.

Hannah

His mother came to live with him. At first she still worshipped the old gods. She believed that the spirit of her dead husband had brought her son back to her. Crowther was grieved to see her, as Page puts it, still without knowledge of the true God. She attended the services at the mission. Then she fell ill, and afterwards she told her son: “Had I been left alone I should have attributed my sickness to this or that deity, and should have made sacrifices accordingly; but now I have seen the folly of so doing, all my hopes are in the Lord Jesus Christ, whom now I serve.”

In February 1848 she was baptised, among the first converts of the Abeokuta mission. Page says it was on the 5th, and that her son baptised her himself; Stock says the 6th, and names only Henry Townsend as her teacher. What is agreed is the name she took. She was baptised Hannah, the name of the mother of the prophet Samuel.

The choice was deliberate. In the Bible, Hannah was a woman who had prayed for a son, and when her prayer was answered she gave him to the service of God. “For this child I prayed; and Jehovah hath given me my petition which I asked of him: therefore also I have granted him to Jehovah; as long as he liveth he is granted to Jehovah” (1 Samuel 1:27-28, ASV). Hannah Crowther had not given her son to God. He had been taken from her by force. But now she was given back to him, and she gave him, as it were, a second time. When he warned her that his work would keep him travelling, and that he could not stay at home with her as other members of the family might, she told him: “You are no longer my son, but the servant of God, whose work you must attend unto without any anxiety for me.” He recalled the words after her death, nearly forty years later.

She lived for another thirty-seven years, her last ones in Lagos, where she kept her Yoruba dress and sat in the market “like a true Yoruba woman,” as Page puts it. She died in October 1883, aged about ninety-seven, “as was supposed.” No one knew her real age either.

Abeokuta

The mission at Abeokuta grew. By August 1849 Crowther could report five hundred regular worshippers, eighty communicants, and two hundred people preparing for baptism. Other missionaries joined them, among them a German, David Hinderer, who came in 1849 and was later joined by his English wife Anna; they would work in Ibadan. In May 1849 a letter from Queen Victoria to the chief of Abeokuta was read in the town, sent with two Bibles and, from Prince Albert, a corn mill. Crowther’s daughter Julianna, then a girl, dictated a letter from Abeokuta, written out in her father’s hand, that survives. The family was together, in the Yoruba country, among his own people.

It was not a peaceful place. The Egba of Abeokuta had powerful enemies, among them the kingdom of Dahomey to the west, whose army raided for slaves to sell at the coast. In March 1851 the Dahomean army attacked Abeokuta. The Egba drove them off. Crowther knew as well as anyone what would have happened to the city’s people if they had not.

He had read the psalmist’s words on the morning his mother came back, and they had proved true. God had been the helper of the fatherless. He had seen the mischief and spite. He had given a Yoruba slave boy back to his mother, and a Yoruba mother back to her son, and both of them to himself.

fields.title: In Our Own Language
fields.body_html:
“And how hear we, every man in our own language wherein we were born?”

— Acts 2:8, ASV

Writing Down a Language

When Samuel Crowther was born, Yoruba had hardly ever been written, except here and there by Muslim scholars in Arabic script. It was a rich language, full of proverbs, poetry, praise-songs, and the verses of the Ifa diviners, but all of it lived in memory and speech. By the time he died, there was a Yoruba Bible, a Yoruba Prayer Book, grammars, dictionaries, schoolbooks, and newspapers, and the language had a standard written form that is still, with changes, the basis of the one used today. Crowther was not the only person responsible for that change, but he was, as Andrew Walls puts it, the principal influence in it.

He had begun collecting Yoruba words in Sierra Leone in the 1830s. On the 1841 voyage he filled in the Yoruba column of the government’s vocabulary. In 1843, while he was studying for ordination, the society published his Vocabulary of the Yoruba Language, with a short grammar. It was the first such work by a native speaker. An enlarged grammar and vocabulary followed in 1852. He translated parts of the Bible and the Prayer Book, beginning with Luke’s Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles on his voyage home in 1843, and he never stopped.

Writing down a language is harder than it sounds. Yoruba is a tonal language, in which the same syllable spoken on a high, middle, or low pitch may have entirely different meanings. It has sounds that the English alphabet has no letters for. Missionaries in different places had been spelling it in different ways. In the 1850s the society brought together Crowther, Henry Townsend, and several European scholars to settle a common system, with marks under certain letters and tone marks over vowels. The system owed much to Henry Venn and to the German scholar Richard Lepsius, and to careful proof-reading by others. The resulting orthography was not perfect, and it has been revised since, but it made possible a Yoruba literature.

The translation of the whole Bible was a team effort, over forty years. Townsend, Hinderer, Gollmer, the Yoruba clergyman Thomas King, and others all took part. Crowther’s part was the largest, and his instinct for the living language shaped the whole. The complete Yoruba Bible was published in 1884, a few years before his death. Popular accounts sometimes say that he translated it alone. He would have been the first to correct them.

Listening to the Elders

He was a native speaker, working in his mother tongue, and that was his great advantage over every European translator. He noticed that some Yoruba customs resembled those of the Old Testament, and wondered at it. And he insisted, all his life, that missionaries must do the same. “The plan of studying the language of the people, and translating the Scriptures into it,” he had written in 1841, “ought to be immediately adopted by every Missionary.”

The historian Lamin Sanneh, from the Gambia, argued that this commitment to translation was one of the most important things that ever happened to African Christianity. When the Bible is translated into a people’s language, he pointed out, that language is declared worthy to carry the word of God. The people who speak it are no longer required to become someone else in order to become Christians. Crowther did not use those words, but he acted on the idea. For him the gospel was not an English possession that Africans had to learn English to receive. It could speak Yoruba.

The verse at the head of this chapter describes the day of Pentecost. The disciples, filled with the Spirit, began to speak, and a crowd of Jews from all over the world, from Parthia and Mesopotamia, from Egypt and Libya and Rome, heard them in their own languages. “And how hear we,” they asked in amazement, “every man in our own language wherein we were born?” The first sign of the Spirit’s coming was that the gospel was heard in many languages at once. From that day, Christianity has been a translated faith, never bound to the language of its founders. Crowther’s work stood in that tradition.

England, 1851

In 1851 Crowther returned to England. Henry Venn, the society’s secretary, wanted him to help persuade the British government to act against the slave trade at Lagos, where a ruler named Kosoko was protecting the slave-dealers. Crowther met the Foreign Secretary, Lord Palmerston, at his house in August. The society remembered, and Stock repeated, that Palmerston asked him in astonishment whether he meant to say that he had himself been a slave. Palmerston afterwards wrote him a letter promising the government’s concern for Abeokuta.

In November he went to Windsor Castle. He had an appointment to see Prince Albert, who was interested in Africa and in the campaign against slavery, and he went with Lord Wriothesley Russell, a clergyman and friend of the society. He left an account of the day, and it is one of the pleasantest things he ever wrote.

He talked with Prince Albert about Abeokuta and Lagos, and showed him a small map that his eldest son, Samuel, had drawn. While they were talking, a lady came quietly into the room and joined them. She was dressed simply, and Crowther did not at first realise who she was. It was Queen Victoria. “She did not come in state,” he wrote, “but simply like any other lady.” When the lamp by which they were looking at the maps went out, the Queen herself lit candles. Lord Wriothesley Russell asked Crowther to say something in Yoruba. He repeated a Yoruba proverb, and then, so that the Queen could hear the language better, the Lord’s Prayer. The Queen said it was “soft and melodious.” She stayed nearly half an hour. Crowther was with the Prince for an hour and a quarter.

This story has often been embellished, with the Queen summoning the former slave to her throne and demanding to hear the prayer. The truth, as he told it, is gentler and more human: a lady “simply dressed,” a lamp that went out, and a Yoruba clergyman saying “Our Father” in his own language to the Queen of England by candlelight.

Lagos

There is another side to the story. Prince Albert, looking at the map, remarked that Lagos “ought to be knocked down.” A month later, in December 1851, the Royal Navy attacked Lagos, drove out Kosoko, and put his rival Akitoye on the throne, on condition that he end the slave trade. Crowther’s visit was one of many voices urging action, and it would be wrong to say that it caused the attack. But he was part of the campaign that brought it about, and he welcomed the result. Ten years later, in 1861, Britain annexed Lagos as a colony. It was the beginning of British rule in what would become Nigeria.

Crowther, like most African Christians of his generation, saw British power as a protection against the slave trade that had destroyed his childhood. He was not wrong about the slave trade. He could not foresee what British rule would become. This book will return to that tension more than once.

“A Real Man of Africa”

Before he left England, Crowther spoke to students at Cambridge. He reminded them of Paul’s vision of a man of Macedonia standing and begging him, “Come over into Macedonia, and help us” (Acts 16:9, ASV). Then he said: “It is no vision that you see now; it is a real man of Africa that stands before you.” He met again the naval captain who had freed him, Henry Leeke, now Sir Henry, and embraced him, and preached in his parish church in Kent. At a farewell meeting in Islington in December, the society sent him back to Africa with its blessing.

He had been a slave boy who could not speak English. He had now spoken, in his own language, before the Queen. But what mattered to him was not that he had been heard at Windsor. It was that the people of the Yoruba country, and of the Niger beyond it, should hear the gospel in the language wherein they were born.

For him the gospel was not an English possession that Africans had to learn English to receive. It could speak Yoruba. The verse at the head of this chapter describes the day of Pentecost. The disciples, filled with the Spirit, began to speak, and a crowd of Jews from all over the world, from Parthia and Mesopotamia, from Egypt and Libya and Rome, heard them in their own languages. “And how hear we,” they asked in amazement, “every man in our own language wherein we were born?” The first sign of the Spirit’s coming was that the gospel was heard in many languages at once. From that day, Christianity has been a translated faith, never bound to the language of its founders. Crowther’s work stood in that tradition. England, 1851 In 1851 Crowther returned to England. Henry Venn, the society’s secretary, wanted him to help persuade the British government to act against the slave trade at Lagos, where a ruler named Kosoko was protecting the slave-dealers. Crowther met the Foreign Secretary, Lord Palmerston, at his house in August. The society remembered, and Stock repeated, that Palmerston asked him in astonishment whether he meant to say that he had himself been a slave. Palmerston afterwards wrote him a letter promising the government’s concern for Abeokuta. In November he went to Windsor Castle. He had an appointment to see Prince Albert, who was interested in Africa and in the campaign against slavery, and he went with Lord Wriothesley Russell, a clergyman and friend of the society. He left an account of the day, and it is one of the pleasantest things he ever wrote. He talked with Prince Albert about Abeokuta and Lagos, and showed him a small map that his eldest son, Samuel, had drawn. While they were talking, a lady came quietly into the room and joined them. She was dressed simply, and Crowther did not at first realise who she was. It was Queen Victoria. “She did not come in state,” he wrote, “but simply like any other lady.” When the lamp by which they were looking at the maps went out, the Queen herself lit candles. Lord Wriothesley Russell asked Crowther to say something in Yoruba. He repeated a Yoruba proverb, and then, so that the Queen could hear the language better, the Lord’s Prayer. The Queen said it was “soft and melodious.” She stayed nearly half an hour. Crowther was with the Prince for an hour and a quarter. This story has often been embellished, with the Queen summoning the former slave to her throne and demanding to hear the prayer. The truth, as he told it, is gentler and more human: a lady “simply dressed,” a lamp that went out, and a Yoruba clergyman saying “Our Father” in his own language to the Queen of England by candlelight. Lagos There is another side to the story. Prince Albert, looking at the map, remarked that Lagos “ought to be knocked down.” A month later, in December 1851, the Royal Navy attacked Lagos, drove out Kosoko, and put his rival Akitoye on the throne, on condition that he end the slave trade. Crowther’s visit was one of many voices urging action, and it would be wrong to say that it caused the attack. But he was part of the campaign that brought it about, and he welcomed the result. Ten years later, in 1861, Britain annexed Lagos as a colony. It was the beginning of British rule in what would become Nigeria. Crowther, like most African Christians of his generation, saw British power as a protection against the slave trade that had destroyed his childhood. He was not wrong about the slave trade. He could not foresee what British rule would become. This book will return to that tension more than once. “A Real Man of Africa” Before he left England, Crowther spoke to students at Cambridge. He reminded them of Paul’s vision of a man of Macedonia standing and begging him, “Come over into Macedonia, and help us” (Acts 16:9, ASV). Then he said: “It is no vision that you see now; it is a real man of Africa that stands before you.” He met again the naval captain who had freed him, Henry Leeke, now Sir Henry, and embraced him, and preached in his parish church in Kent. At a farewell meeting in Islington in December, the society sent him back to Africa with its blessing. He had been a slave boy who could not speak English. He had now spoken, in his own language, before the Queen. But what mattered to him was not that he had been heard at Windsor. It was that the people of the Yoruba country, and of the Niger beyond it, should hear the gospel in the language wherein they were born.

fields.title: The Pleiad
fields.body_html:
“Jehovah will keep thee from all evil; He will keep thy soul. Jehovah will keep thy going out and thy coming in From this time forth and for evermore.”

— Psalm 121:7-8, ASV

The Pleiad

For thirteen years after the disaster of 1841, no great expedition went up the Niger. Then, in 1853, a Liverpool shipbuilder and merchant named Macgregor Laird, who had himself been up the river in the 1830s and believed passionately in its future, made a contract with the government. He would build a small steamer, the Pleiad, to explore the great eastern branch of the Niger, the Benue, which the explorers called the Tshadda, and to look for news of the German explorer Heinrich Barth, who was somewhere in the interior. Laird offered Crowther a free passage.

Crowther joined the expedition at Fernando Po in June 1854. Before he joined it, at Lagos, he learned that the British consul, John Beecroft, who was to have led it, had died. He wrote simply that he “resigned everything to God’s good and unerring providence.” He visited Beecroft’s grave and preached in his house on Paul’s words about the earthly tent that is dissolved and the building from God that is eternal. Command of the expedition passed to the ship’s doctor, a young Scot named William Balfour Baikie.

They crossed the bar into the Niger on 12 July. From the beginning, Crowther noticed signs of change since 1841. There were English shirts on the riverbanks, bought with palm oil, not with people. He suggested to Baikie and the ship’s officers that the green firewood they were burning, stacked in the bunkers, might be breeding the “miasma” that caused fever, and they agreed to tow it in canoes instead. It was the wrong theory; malaria is carried by mosquitoes, which no one then knew. Historians have usually credited the expedition’s health instead to Baikie’s regular doses of quinine. Crowther’s journal does not mention quinine. But whatever the reason, something was different this time.

Aboh and Idda

At Aboh, the old king Obi Ossai, who had signed the treaty in 1841 and asked for teachers, was dead, and his sons were quarrelling over the succession. Crowther talked with the eldest, Tshukuma, about the gospel. It was the middle of the day, and the sun was blazing. Would anyone, he asked, light lamps in broad daylight like this to help the sun to shine? The sacrifices the people offered to their gods were like lamps lit at noon. The sacrifice of Jesus Christ, once offered, alone could take away the sin of the world. Before he left, he arranged for Simon Jonas, an Igbo interpreter from Sierra Leone who had been on the 1841 expedition, to stay at Aboh and teach.

At Idda he had to go through a long and tedious ordeal before he was allowed to see the Attah, the same king Captain Trotter had treated with in 1841, who agreed again that his people might “learn the white man’s book.” Crowther used homely stories in his talks with rulers, about a boil that needs a salve, or a friend carrying a heavy load. He learned to wait. “The native chiefs always take more time to think and arrange their plans and settle their affairs than we are aware of,” he wrote on one occasion; and on another, “A prudent man will not consider an hour or two wasted, … rather than risk the painful result of misunderstandings which may never be remedied.”

At the Confluence, where the model farm had been, the site was overgrown. Old people on the hill asked him whether they had come back to rebuild it. He preached on board that Sunday on Paul’s words to Timothy, “God gave us not a spirit of fearfulness,” and admitted in his journal that he preached “in much weakness.”

Up the Benue

Then the Pleiad turned east, up the Benue, far beyond the point where the one earlier expedition had turned back. Crowther found towns destroyed by Fulani raiders and heard stories of treachery and slaughter. He saw Tiv people at their markets, armed and suspicious, and went ashore among them. “What is generally related of the natives of Africa as to their hostility to Europeans is not strictly correct,” he wrote. “If feelings of confidence and friendship are left to arise gradually … we shall soon come to a mutual understanding.” At one town a chief offered to sell a boy to the interpreter. At another, a Muslim scholar named Imoru asked him to pray for his wives, who had no children. Crowther read him the psalm that says children are a heritage from the Lord, and showed him his bare arms and neck to prove that Christians wore no charms: “we resign all our affairs to the hand of God.”

On 22 September he walked twelve miles through mud to Hamaruwa, the town of a Fulani ruler named Mohamma. It was a long way from the Yoruba country, among a Muslim people who had been raiding their neighbours for slaves. Crowther asked the ruler’s permission to teach the non-Muslim people of his territory, and Mohamma smiled and gave it. Crowther took out a pencil and wrote in front of him, and the king was astonished. Four days later, out of fuel, the Pleiad turned back.

Brethren

On the way down, at Agberi below Aboh, he sat with a headman named Agbekun and pointed to himself, to Simon Jonas, and to Dr. Baikie. “Look at me, a Yoruba by birth; Simon Jonas, an Ibo; and Dr. Baikie, an Englishman; though of different nations, we live together as brethren.” It was a picture of what he believed the gospel could do among the nations of the Niger, who had been at war with one another for generations.

At Aboh, one of the quarrelling princes, Aje, freed two prisoners at his request. Agbekun, just back from consulting the famous oracle at Aro, had asked how to pray to the Great God, and Crowther told him “to do so, just as a little child would ask his father.” Earlier, on the way up the Benue, when the Krumen were set to cut wood on a Sunday, he had written in his journal: “It is a reproach to us, who profess to observe the Lord’s-day, and teach others to sanctify it, thus to violate it ourselves.”

On the 101st day in the river, he wrote: “It is a hundred and one days to-day since we entered the river, and no death has taken place.” He did not take the credit. “Not unto us, but unto God, we give praise.” He was echoing the psalm: “Not unto us, O Jehovah, not unto us, But unto thy name give glory, For thy lovingkindness, and for thy truth’s sake” (Psalm 115:1, ASV). That Sunday he preached on the stone that Samuel set up, called Ebenezer, “Hitherto hath Jehovah helped us.”

They reached the sea on 4 November 1854, “just sixteen weeks, this very day,” Crowther noted, after they had entered the river. Crowther wrote to Henry Venn that they had returned “without any death, either among the Europeans, twelve in number, or among the fifty-four Africans.” In 1841, forty-two Europeans had died. In 1854, none.

The Lesson

Baikie wrote to Crowther afterwards: “It is nothing more than a simple fact, that no slight portion of the success we met with in our intercourse with the tribes is due to you.” Crowther wrote to Venn with his own conclusions. He had marked Onitsha and Asaba as the two most promising places for a mission to the Igbo. Aboh, he wrote, “can only be occupied by native teachers. I cannot recommend it for the residence of European Missionaries.” And he wrote: “I believe the time is fully come when Christianity must be introduced on the banks of the Niger.” He knew the men he would have to send were not perfect. “As pioneers,” he told Venn, “we must not look for instruments of the keenest edge.”

The psalm at the head of this chapter is one of the Songs of Ascents, sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. “Jehovah will keep thy going out and thy coming in.” It is a traveller’s psalm, a prayer for the road. Crowther spent most of his life on the road, and on the river, and he trusted that promise. It did not mean that he would never suffer; he would be wrecked, kidnapped, and bereaved. It meant that his going out and his coming in were in God’s hands. In 1854, on the Pleiad, he had seen it proved in the plainest way. Every man who went up the river came back.

fields.title: Wrecked at Jebba
fields.body_html:
“we are pressed on every side, yet not straitened; perplexed, yet not unto despair; pursued, yet not forsaken; smitten down, yet not destroyed”

— 2 Corinthians 4:8-9, ASV

The Dayspring

In 1857 Macgregor Laird signed a new contract with the government, for five years of regular voyages up the Niger. The first ship sent out under it was the Dayspring, commanded by Dr. Baikie, with a naval officer, Lieutenant John Glover, to survey the river. The Church Missionary Society decided that the time had come to plant a permanent mission on the Niger, and that it would be staffed entirely by Africans. Crowther was to lead it.

With him went the Rev. John Christopher Taylor, a young clergyman born in Sierra Leone to Igbo parents who had been sold as slaves, and Simon Jonas, the Igbo interpreter who had stayed at Aboh in 1854. And Crowther did something unusual. He hired, on purpose, a Yoruba Muslim named Kasumo as his teacher of Arabic, so that he could read and discuss the Qur’an with the Muslim rulers of the upper river. It was a mark of the way he meant to work.

They sailed from Fernando Po on 29 June 1857. At Fernando Po the first Igbo primer had just arrived from England, and Crowther started a class to teach it. At Umuoru, on 19 July, he gave the Lord’s Supper on board to twelve Africans and three Europeans. Everywhere in the Delta he noted the villages where African teachers might be placed.

Onitsha

On 26 July they reached Onitsha, the town on the east bank of the Niger that Crowther had marked in 1854 as the best place for an Igbo mission. At first the people armed themselves in fear. Then the king, Obi Akazua, received them, and agreed that a teacher should live among his people.

While they were there, the family of a local notable was preparing a funeral, and a slave woman was to be killed to accompany the dead. Crowther and Simon Jonas protested. The family agreed to sacrifice a bullock instead. The people then offered to sell the woman to the missionaries. “We refused to do,” Crowther wrote, “as we were not slave-traders.” She was sold to someone else, but she was “loosed from her bonds” and lived. The king promised to abolish human sacrifices. It would take much longer than that.

On 31 July Crowther left Taylor and Jonas at Onitsha with a letter of instructions. “Cultivate friendship with all the people as much as possible, so as to gain their goodwill and confidence. … You will have to teach more by conversation when you visit the people … than by direct service.” He told Taylor to learn the language and translate as much as he could. And he added a sentence that shows his realism: “Be not disappointed if you find the people do not act up to their engagement: it is rather a matter of surprise that they do so much. They must be taught the lesson of justice and truth, and that by our own example.” He called the founding of Onitsha “the first important move of the Church Missionary Society in planting a Mission from a native ministry, and an entire native offshoot from the colony of Sierra Leone.”

Gbebe and Bida

Further up, at Gbebe near the Confluence, he chose a site for a second station. He was clear about where it should be: “the Mission station must be in the midst of the people, because we can never expect them to go the distance of a mile to receive religious instruction before they know its real benefits.” When he tried to buy land, a local leader told him it could not be sold, “because the land is God’s,” and the matter dragged on. On 16 August, in the ante-room of a local chief, he gave what he called the first public Christian instruction at Gbebe, reading the third chapter of John in Hausa and giving the chief an Arabic Bible. Three days later a school opened with five boys.

In September he rode with Baikie and Glover to the war camp of the Nupe kingdom, whose rulers, a Fulani dynasty, controlled much of the middle Niger. The king, Sumo Zaki, received them, and so did his half-brother Dasaba, who, Crowther wrote, “rolled on his mat for joy.” In the camp market Crowther counted forty slaves for sale. He passed the body of a slave who had died in the night, neglected, by the road.

The Wreck

On 7 October 1857, near the town of Jebba, far up the Niger, the Dayspring struck rocks in a narrow channel and heeled over. Local canoes came out to help, and everyone was brought ashore. “We were thankful that, in the midst of the hurry and bustle … no life was lost.” But the ship could not be saved. Word was sent overland to the coast asking for another steamer. It would be a year before one came.

Fifty people camped on the riverbank at Jebba: twelve Europeans and thirty-eight Africans. Crowther held morning and evening prayers in his tent of mats, and opened it to the sick. He kept night watches with the others, and when a leopard raided the camp in January he admitted cheerfully, “I am no gunner.” On 25 October, soon after the wreck, he had preached on Paul’s words, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21, ASV). Before the wreck, on board off the ruins of Rabba, he had preached on another verse from Paul: “ye received not the spirit of bondage again unto fear; but ye received the spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15, ASV). A former slave was telling his hearers that they were not slaves to fear.

The people of Jebba believed that the god of the great rock by the river hated red cloth and had wrecked the ship. Crowther answered that the god’s law bound its own worshippers, not strangers. He told them about the great God “who made of one blood all nations,” and took the hands of Lieutenant Glover and his Nupe interpreter, “three different nations,” to show what he meant.

A Year by the River

He did not waste the year. He began to reduce the Nupe language to writing, working with a Muslim teacher from Jebba named Ibrahima and a young man named Henry George, who had once been a Sunday-school pupil at Abeokuta and had become a soldier in the Nupe army. “They felt very much interested,” Crowther wrote, “in seeing their language being reduced to writing.” He studied the religion of the Nupe, their farming, their trade, their ferries, and the work of their women in the markets, and wrote it all down.

When a Fulani chief let one of his followers rob a Nupe woman in front of him, Crowther “seriously told him that God would plead the cause of the oppressed,” and took the woman to safety in the mission’s boat. When the Nupe official in charge of the district asked him for charms, he “showed him my hands and neck, that I had never used charms, and told him I never should, because there is no help to be had from them.” In the spring of 1858 the official gave him land on the cliff above the ruins of Rabba, and Crowther built five round huts there for six pounds. “Though I was the only Christian in the village, with my servant, yet I was greatly respected.” In July a hostile letter came from the king, ordering him to leave because he was not of the same faith; it turned out to be the work of a mischief-making interpreter, and the king later cleared him. “Thus the Lord has silenced the mouths of my enemies for a time.”

One night in January, sitting up with Kasumo and another Muslim companion, he talked until late about whether Christ had really died on the cross, as Christians believe and the Qur’an denies. “If Christ himself had not died,” he told them, “then we are found false witnesses, because then he had never shed His blood, which is the price of our redemption.”

How to Deal With Muslims

At the end of his journal of these years he wrote a short essay, “How to deal with Mohammedans,” which sums up his method. He had spent some months as the only Christian, apart from his servant, in his village at Rabba, and he had no illusions about how quickly Muslims would change. Already at the Bida camp in 1857 he had written: “A Mohammedan can never be brought round by his religion being quarrelled with, and abusively charged with falsehood and imposition; but by kind treatment he may be led to read and study the Christian’s Bible.” He warned against “undue rashness in quarrelling with, and our untimely exposure of, Mohammedanism,” which could do no good. And he ended with a sentence of great patience: “God, who has permitted the religion of Mohammed to remain so long … can easily remove it when He pleases, without violence or rash proceedings on our part.”

He believed that Islam was wrong about Christ, and he said so, gently and clearly, when he was asked. But he believed that the way to reach Muslims was friendship, the Arabic Bible, and time. It was a view that many missionaries of his age did not share.

Onitsha Without Him

Meanwhile, at Onitsha, Taylor and Jonas were at work. Taylor held his first service “in my fatherland” to hundreds of people in the king’s yard. After hearing a sermon on the third chapter of John, the king said that Jesus, the Son of God, “surpasses him in speaking.” Taylor persuaded one man to free a girl held as a debt-slave. He reconciled four chiefs who had not spoken to each other for seven years. He built the first mission house in the town. In February 1858 he watched helplessly as the annual human sacrifice was carried out, two sick people drowned “one for the land, and one for the river,” and the king fined the mission for interfering. The first man to ask for baptism was admitted as a candidate on condition that he keep to one wife.

In October 1858 a relief steamer at last reached the camp at Jebba and took the party down the river. Crowther found Taylor at Onitsha and was welcomed as “my friend Mr. Crowther.” The people who had first called Taylor “a spirit without toes” wept when he left. A month later Simon Jonas died at Fernando Po. His last words were: “this is the third time I have gone up the Niger … and the last was the best I have spent in my fatherland.”

Crowther went back up the river by canoe, and then overland through the Yoruba country, past Ilorin, where he argued with the Muslim scholars from the Qur’an as well as the Bible, and they wondered at his learning. On the way he fell ill with dysentery and was nursed back to health at Ijaye, and he reached Abeokuta in March 1859. He had been away nearly two years.

Paul, describing his own missionary life, wrote: “we are pressed on every side, yet not straitened; perplexed, yet not unto despair; pursued, yet not forsaken; smitten down, yet not destroyed.” It is as good a summary of the years 1857 to 1859 as any. The ship was lost. The plans were ruined. And by the end of it, there was a mission at Onitsha, another at Gbebe, the beginnings of a Nupe grammar, and a small company of African Christians who had shown that they could plant the church on the Niger without anyone else’s help.

And Crowther did something unusual. He hired, on purpose, a Yoruba Muslim named Kasumo as his teacher of Arabic, so that he could read and discuss the Qur’an with the Muslim rulers of the upper river. It was a mark of the way he meant to work. They sailed from Fernando Po on 29 June 1857. At Fernando Po the first Igbo primer had just arrived from England, and Crowther started a class to teach it. At Umuoru, on 19 July, he gave the Lord’s Supper on board to twelve Africans and three Europeans. Everywhere in the Delta he noted the villages where African teachers might be placed. Onitsha On 26 July they reached Onitsha, the town on the east bank of the Niger that Crowther had marked in 1854 as the best place for an Igbo mission. At first the people armed themselves in fear. Then the king, Obi Akazua, received them, and agreed that a teacher should live among his people. While they were there, the family of a local notable was preparing a funeral, and a slave woman was to be killed to accompany the dead. Crowther and Simon Jonas protested. The family agreed to sacrifice a bullock instead. The people then offered to sell the woman to the missionaries. “We refused to do,” Crowther wrote, “as we were not slave-traders.” She was sold to someone else, but she was “loosed from her bonds” and lived. The king promised to abolish human sacrifices. It would take much longer than that. On 31 July Crowther left Taylor and Jonas at Onitsha with a letter of instructions. “Cultivate friendship with all the people as much as possible, so as to gain their goodwill and confidence. … You will have to teach more by conversation when you visit the people … than by direct service.” He told Taylor to learn the language and translate as much as he could. And he added a sentence that shows his realism: “Be not disappointed if you find the people do not act up to their engagement: it is rather a matter of surprise that they do so much. They must be taught the lesson of justice and truth, and that by our own example.” He called the founding of Onitsha “the first important move of the Church Missionary Society in planting a Mission from a native ministry, and an entire native offshoot from the colony of Sierra Leone.” Gbebe and Bida Further up, at Gbebe near the Confluence, he chose a site for a second station. He was clear about where it should be: “the Mission station must be in the midst of the people, because we can never expect them to go the distance of a mile to receive religious instruction before they know its real benefits.” When he tried to buy land, a local leader told him it could not be sold, “because the land is God’s,” and the matter dragged on. On 16 August, in the ante-room of a local chief, he gave what he called the first public Christian instruction at Gbebe, reading the third chapter of John in Hausa and giving the chief an Arabic Bible. Three days later a school opened with five boys. In September he rode with Baikie and Glover to the war camp of the Nupe kingdom, whose rulers, a Fulani dynasty, controlled much of the middle Niger. The king, Sumo Zaki, received them, and so did his half-brother Dasaba, who, Crowther wrote, “rolled on his mat for joy.” In the camp market Crowther counted forty slaves for sale. He passed the body of a slave who had died in the night, neglected, by the road. The Wreck On 7 October 1857, near the town of Jebba, far up the Niger, the Dayspring struck rocks in a narrow channel and heeled over. Local canoes came out to help, and everyone was brought ashore. “We were thankful that, in the midst of the hurry and bustle … no life was lost.” But the ship could not be saved. Word was sent overland to the coast asking for another steamer. It would be a year before one came. Fifty people camped on the riverbank at Jebba: twelve Europeans and thirty-eight Africans. Crowther held morning and evening prayers in his tent of mats, and opened it to the sick. He kept night watches with the others, and when a leopard raided the camp in January he admitted cheerfully, “I am no gunner.” On 25 October, soon after the wreck, he had preached on Paul’s words, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21, ASV). Before the wreck, on board off the ruins of Rabba, he had preached on another verse from Paul: “ye received not the spirit of bondage again unto fear; but ye received the spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15, ASV). A former slave was telling his hearers that they were not slaves to fear. The people of Jebba believed that the god of the great rock by the river hated red cloth and had wrecked the ship. Crowther answered that the god’s law bound its own worshippers, not strangers. He told them about the great God “who made of one blood all nations,” and took the hands of Lieutenant Glover and his Nupe interpreter, “three different nations,” to show what he meant. A Year by the River He did not waste the year. He began to reduce the Nupe language to writing, working with a Muslim teacher from Jebba named Ibrahima and a young man named Henry George, who had once been a Sunday-school pupil at Abeokuta and had become a soldier in the Nupe army. “They felt very much interested,” Crowther wrote, “in seeing their language being reduced to writing.” He studied the religion of the Nupe, their farming, their trade, their ferries, and the work of their women in the markets, and wrote it all down. When a Fulani chief let one of his followers rob a Nupe woman in front of him, Crowther “seriously told him that God would plead the cause of the oppressed,” and took the woman to safety in the mission’s boat. When the Nupe official in charge of the district asked him for charms, he “showed him my hands and neck, that I had never used charms, and told him I never should, because there is no help to be had from them.” In the spring of 1858 the official gave him land on the cliff above the ruins of Rabba, and Crowther built five round huts there for six pounds. “Though I was the only Christian in the village, with my servant, yet I was greatly respected.” In July a hostile letter came from the king, ordering him to leave because he was not of the same faith; it turned out to be the work of a mischief-making interpreter, and the king later cleared him. “Thus the Lord has silenced the mouths of my enemies for a time.” One night in January, sitting up with Kasumo and another Muslim companion, he talked until late about whether Christ had really died on the cross, as Christians believe and the Qur’an denies. “If Christ himself had not died,” he told them, “then we are found false witnesses, because then he had never shed His blood, which is the price of our redemption.” How to Deal With Muslims At the end of his journal of these years he wrote a short essay, “How to deal with Mohammedans,” which sums up his method. He had spent some months as the only Christian, apart from his servant, in his village at Rabba, and he had no illusions about how quickly Muslims would change. Already at the Bida camp in 1857 he had written: “A Mohammedan can never be brought round by his religion being quarrelled with, and abusively charged with falsehood and imposition; but by kind treatment he may be led to read and study the Christian’s Bible.” He warned against “undue rashness in quarrelling with, and our untimely exposure of, Mohammedanism,” which could do no good. And he ended with a sentence of great patience: “God, who has permitted the religion of Mohammed to remain so long … can easily remove it when He pleases, without violence or rash proceedings on our part.” He believed that Islam was wrong about Christ, and he said so, gently and clearly, when he was asked. But he believed that the way to reach Muslims was friendship, the Arabic Bible, and time. It was a view that many missionaries of his age did not share. Onitsha Without Him Meanwhile, at Onitsha, Taylor and Jonas were at work. Taylor held his first service “in my fatherland” to hundreds of people in the king’s yard. After hearing a sermon on the third chapter of John, the king said that Jesus, the Son of God, “surpasses him in speaking.” Taylor persuaded one man to free a girl held as a debt-slave. He reconciled four chiefs who had not spoken to each other for seven years. He built the first mission house in the town. In February 1858 he watched helplessly as the annual human sacrifice was carried out, two sick people drowned “one for the land, and one for the river,” and the king fined the mission for interfering. The first man to ask for baptism was admitted as a candidate on condition that he keep to one wife. In October 1858 a relief steamer at last reached the camp at Jebba and took the party down the river. Crowther found Taylor at Onitsha and was welcomed as “my friend Mr. Crowther.” The people who had first called Taylor “a spirit without toes” wept when he left. A month later Simon Jonas died at Fernando Po. His last words were: “this is the third time I have gone up the Niger … and the last was the best I have spent in my fatherland.” Crowther went back up the river by canoe, and then overland through the Yoruba country, past Ilorin, where he argued with the Muslim scholars from the Qur’an as well as the Bible, and they wondered at his learning. On the way he fell ill with dysentery and was nursed back to health at Ijaye, and he reached Abeokuta in March 1859. He had been away nearly two years. Paul, describing his own missionary life, wrote: “we are pressed on every side, yet not straitened; perplexed, yet not unto despair; pursued, yet not forsaken; smitten down, yet not destroyed.” It is as good a summary of the years 1857 to 1859 as any. The ship was lost. The plans were ruined. And by the end of it, there was a mission at Onitsha, another at Gbebe, the beginnings of a Nupe grammar, and a small company of African Christians who had shown that they could plant the church on the Niger without anyone else’s help.

fields.title: Africa’s Own Children
fields.body_html:
“The little one shall become a thousand, and the small one a strong nation; I, Jehovah, will hasten it in its time.”

— Isaiah 60:22, ASV

Henry Venn

Behind almost every step of Crowther’s career stood one man. Henry Venn was the honorary secretary of the Church Missionary Society from 1841 until shortly before his death in 1873. He was a clergyman from a famous evangelical family, a tireless organiser, and a thinker about missions whose ideas were far ahead of his time.

Venn believed that the goal of a mission was to make itself unnecessary. Missionaries from abroad should plant churches, train local leaders, and then step aside. The new churches should become, in the phrase later associated with his name, self-supporting, self-governing, and self-extending. They should pay their own clergy, run their own affairs, and send out their own missionaries. When that had happened, the foreign mission could be withdrawn, like scaffolding from a finished building. Venn called this, with a phrase that has become famous, the “euthanasia” of a mission: its good and peaceful death, because its work was done.

In the middle of the nineteenth century, when most Europeans assumed that Africans and Asians would need European guidance for generations, this was a radical idea. Venn meant it seriously. And Samuel Crowther was, for him, its living proof. Here was an African who had been a slave, who had become a scholar, a translator, a clergyman, and a leader. If the Niger Mission could be run by Africans under an African, then the principle was established.

The Native Agents

Crowther had been saying the same thing since 1841, and he said it again, more sharply, in 1857. The Church had been slow to trust its African members. “Had not our candles been long kept under a bushel,” he wrote, “and the smoking flax long suppressed, surely the number of faithful native preachers would have been twice as many.” The images are from the Gospels. Jesus said that no one lights a lamp to put it under a bushel (Matthew 5:15), and Isaiah’s servant of the Lord would not quench “a dimly burning wick” (Isaiah 42:3, ASV). Crowther was saying, as politely as he could, that the Church had hidden its African lamps and quenched its African wicks.

The men he sent up the Niger were almost all, like himself, recaptives or the children of recaptives from Sierra Leone. They were Africans, but they were not natives of the Niger. Most of them had to learn the languages of the peoples they served, and some were as foreign in Onitsha as an Englishman would have been. The historian Andrew Walls points out that the Niger Mission was therefore “a compromise, rather than the full expression” of Venn’s principles. It was African, but it was not yet a church of the people of the soil. Crowther knew this. His aim was to train men from the Niger peoples themselves, and in time he would.

Nor were the agents perfect. Crowther had told Venn in 1854 that pioneers could not expect “instruments of the keenest edge.” Some of the men he sent were poorly educated. Some were more interested in trade than in teaching. A few would prove unworthy. But many were faithful, and they went, with their families, to places where no European could live, and stayed.

A Closed River

After the wreck at Jebba, the river was hard to reach. In 1859 a trading steamer, the Rainbow, was fired on from the banks in the Delta, and two men were killed. The trading houses of the coast, the African middlemen who had controlled the trade of the lower river for generations, did not want Laird’s steamers cutting them out, and they were willing to fight. Laird himself died in January 1861. In retaliation for the attack, a British warship shelled and burned the villages that had fired on the steamer. It was an early example of a pattern that would become familiar: trade followed by gunboats.

In the same year Britain annexed Lagos as a colony. The mission, like everything else on the coast, was becoming entangled with British power, whether it wished to be or not.

In 1862 a naval vessel, HMS Investigator, took Crowther up the river again, with a party of about thirty African teachers, wives, and children. They reached Onitsha on 5 September. The mission there had held on through the years when no ship could come. They reached Onitsha on 5 September, but the ship steamed on within hours and Crowther was not allowed to land. The mission there had held on alone.

The First Fruits

Nine days later, on 14 September 1862, at Gbebe near the Confluence, he baptised eight adults and one infant. They were the first people baptised anywhere on the Niger. Crowther called them “the first-fruits of the Niger Mission.”

It is hard now to feel how much that meant. The first European expedition up the Niger with missionaries had been in 1841. For twenty-one years men had died, ships had been wrecked and fired on, stations had been opened and left, and at the end of it nine people of the Niger had been baptised. By the standards of the societies in London it was a small result for a great cost. By the standards of the kingdom of God it was a beginning. The verse at the head of this chapter is God’s promise to Israel in exile: “The little one shall become a thousand, and the small one a strong nation; I, Jehovah, will hasten it in its time.” Crowther believed it. It would take longer than he lived to see it fulfilled, but it would be fulfilled beyond anything he imagined.

The Gbebe station did not last. When its protector, the local king Ama Abokko, died, the town was attacked and the station destroyed, and the Christians moved across the river to Lokoja, where the British had a small post. It was to become one of the centres of the mission.

“By Her Own Sons and Daughters”

J. C. Taylor, the young clergyman at Onitsha, had put the principle in a single sentence. After preaching at Nsube in 1857, Taylor wrote in his journal of Africa’s need to hear the gospel. And how was it to hear? “It cannot be otherwise but by her own sons and daughters.” Before he sailed, an old communicant in Sierra Leone had asked him in wonder, “our children too can go out like white men and preach the gospel?” The answer was yes.

In the Yoruba country, the king of Ketu, whom Crowther visited in 1853, had put it another way. “Hitherto I have had no helper,” he said; “now I have found one, I will hold it fast.” He meant the mission. But the helper he had found was an African, speaking his own language, who had once been carried through that country in chains.

By 1864 the Niger Mission had stations at Onitsha, Lokoja, and Akassa at the mouth of the river, with more planned. It was run, entirely, by Africans. Its leader was a priest who had been in orders for twenty-one years and was now in his late fifties. Henry Venn had a plan for him, and Crowther did not like it at all.

fields.title: “I Am Not Worthy”
fields.body_html:
“He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, He lifteth up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes, And inherit the throne of glory: For the pillars of the earth are Jehovah’s, And he hath set the world upon them.”

— 1 Samuel 2:8, ASV

Venn’s Plan

By 1864 the Niger Mission had African clergy and catechists at several stations, and more were needed. But the only bishop who could ordain them, confirm converts, and consecrate churches was the Bishop of Sierra Leone, far away on the coast, who could rarely come. The Niger lay outside any British territory, so no colonial bishop had authority there. And it was plain after 1841 that a European bishop would be unlikely to survive the climate for long.

Henry Venn saw the answer. The mission should have a bishop of its own, and he should be an African. The society’s magazine set out the case in May 1864. The African church in Sierra Leone was already largely self-supporting. The Niger converts needed a chief pastor who could live among them. And “to delay any longer the native episcopate would be unduly to retard the development of the native Church.” The obvious man was Samuel Crowther.

Not everyone agreed. Some of the European missionaries in West Africa had grave doubts about an African bishop, and said so. Whether their objections were practical or something more, they would echo later. Venn pressed on. The government, through the Foreign Secretary, and the Archbishop of Canterbury were consulted, and a royal licence was prepared.

“I Am Not Worthy”

The one person who most strongly opposed the plan was Crowther himself. Many years later his son Dandeson told Jesse Page the story, which Crowther could never tell without emotion. He came to the society’s committee in London in a heavy old pilot’s coat with brass buttons, and some of the members laughed at his appearance. When Venn told him what they proposed, he refused. “I am not worthy,” he said. “No, sir, I am their servant in the field; I cannot accept it.”

Venn prayed with him and sent him away for two days to stay with his old friend J. F. Schön, to think it over. When he came back, he refused again. Then, the family remembered, Venn made one last appeal. “Samuel Adjai, my son, will you deny me my last wish asked of you before I die?” Crowther answered in the words of old Eli when Samuel brought him hard news: “It is the Lord; let Him do what seemeth Him good.” The two men knelt together, Venn weeping.

We should hold this story a little lightly. It comes from the family, decades later, and it has the shape of a story that has been told many times. But it fits everything else we know of Crowther. He had a genuine horror of self-importance. Afterwards he asked, through his son, to be addressed as “Right Reverend Bishop, and never as My Lord.” And before he left England he told the committee that he knew his new position made him “a kind of landmark,” and that “any false step taken by me will be injurious to all the Native Churches.”

Oxford

Before the consecration Venn wanted him to have a doctorate, as English bishops usually did. The Archbishop wrote to the Vice-Chancellor of Oxford. Crowther’s Yoruba grammar, his dictionary, and his translations of the Scriptures were submitted as evidence of his learning. One leading member of the university opposed the degree. The rest voted for it almost unanimously, and the Regius Professor of Divinity composed the Latin speech presenting him. Samuel Crowther, who, the family remembered, had been taught his letters by a missionary’s wife in exchange for keeping her pantry clean, became a Doctor of Divinity of the University of Oxford.

Canterbury, 1864

He was consecrated in Canterbury Cathedral on St. Peter’s Day, 29 June 1864, by Archbishop Charles Longley. Two English clergymen were consecrated with him, as Bishops of Peterborough and Tasmania. Special trains ran from London. The sermon was preached by H. L. Mansel of Oxford, on the words of Peter to the elders of the church: “Tend the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not of constraint, but willingly … neither as lording it over the charge allotted to you, but making yourselves ensamples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:2-3, ASV). Two colonial bishops were meant to present Crowther to the Archbishop, but the Bishop of Winchester, it was said, stepped in to take the place of one of them, so that the African should receive, as Page put it, “a double honour.”

Two people had a special claim to be there. According to Page, one was Admiral Sir Henry Leeke, who forty-two years earlier, as captain of HMS Myrmidon, had taken the boy Ajayi from the slave ship off Lagos. The other, whose presence Henry Venn himself recorded, was an elderly lady. Page tells a story that she arrived to find her seat reserved for someone else, and refused to move. “I think I have a right equally to this seat,” she said, “because that black minister to be consecrated Bishop this morning was taught the alphabet by me.” She was Mrs. Weeks, widow of the Bishop of Sierra Leone, who, as Mrs. Davey, had taught him in her house at Bathurst. The Dean, Page says, let her stay. When Crowther returned to London afterwards, his first two calls were on Mrs. Weeks and on Admiral Leeke.

The Book of Samuel preserves the song of Hannah, the mother of the prophet Samuel, after she had given her son to God. It is the verse at the head of this chapter. “He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, He lifteth up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes.” Hannah Crowther was still alive. Her son, the slave she had lost in 1821, now sat among the bishops of the Church of England.

What the Newspapers Said

The event was widely reported. The evangelical newspaper The Record called the consecration a “practical refutation … to the taunts of certain professors who maintain that the cerebral development of the negro shows that he is disqualified for intellectual pursuits.” It is a revealing sentence. In 1864 there were respected scientists in Britain who argued that Africans were a lesser branch of humanity, incapable of higher learning. The consecration of an African bishop was, for some, a public rebuttal of that belief. But the sentence also shows how deeply the idea had taken hold. Even Crowther’s supporters felt it necessary to argue that an African could think.

There were limits, too, to what the Church was prepared to do. The royal licence made Crowther bishop “in the said countries of Western Africa beyond the limits of our dominions.” His diocese lay entirely outside British territory. He was not given authority over the European missionaries in the British colonies of Sierra Leone or Lagos. Andrew Walls notes that this limit was deliberate. An African bishop over African clergy in an African land was acceptable. An African bishop over Englishmen in a British colony was not yet contemplated. The question would return.

“Can This Be Real?”

He sailed from England on 24 July and reached Freetown on 10 August 1864, where crowds turned out to welcome him. In his reply to the addresses of welcome, he used his favourite phrase: “Here we pause and raise our Ebenezer to God’s praise. Hitherto the Lord has helped us.” He told them that the weapon which prevailed most in the ministry was “the habit of prayer for help from above,” and that “we are better fitted when we feel our incompetency to change a sinner’s heart.” He reminded the students of Fourah Bay that in 1841 his friends had called him “a fool for joining the expedition without any guarantee of good pay like the Europeans.” And when a friend asked whether he meant to rest, he said: “I shall only rest when I have no more work to do.”

At Lagos on 22 August he held his first ordination. Then he went up the Niger. At Onitsha he held another ordination. That an African bishop should be ordaining African clergy on the banks of the Niger seemed to him almost beyond belief. “Can this be real?” he wrote.

At the same time, in the same town, a prince had died, and there were human sacrifices at his funeral, among them a girl of eight who was buried alive. The bishop’s consecration had changed his title. It had not changed the Niger.
