Venn pressed on. The government, through the Foreign Secretary, and the Archbishop of Canterbury were consulted, and a royal licence was prepared. “I Am Not Worthy” The one person who most strongly opposed the plan was Crowther himself. Many years later his son Dandeson told Jesse Page the story, which Crowther could never tell without emotion. He came to the society’s committee in London in a heavy old pilot’s coat with brass buttons, and some of the members laughed at his appearance. When Venn told him what they proposed, he refused. “I am not worthy,” he said. “No, sir, I am their servant in the field; I cannot accept it.” Venn prayed with him and sent him away for two days to stay with his old friend J. F. Schön, to think it over. When he came back, he refused again. Then, the family remembered, Venn made one last appeal. “Samuel Adjai, my son, will you deny me my last wish asked of you before I die?” Crowther answered in the words of old Eli when Samuel brought him hard news: “It is the Lord; let Him do what seemeth Him good.” The two men knelt together, Venn weeping. We should hold this story a little lightly. It comes from the family, decades later, and it has the shape of a story that has been told many times. But it fits everything else we know of Crowther. He had a genuine horror of self-importance. Afterwards he asked, through his son, to be addressed as “Right Reverend Bishop, and never as My Lord.” And before he left England he told the committee that he knew his new position made him “a kind of landmark,” and that “any false step taken by me will be injurious to all the Native Churches.” Oxford Before the consecration Venn wanted him to have a doctorate, as English bishops usually did. The Archbishop wrote to the Vice-Chancellor of Oxford. Crowther’s Yoruba grammar, his dictionary, and his translations of the Scriptures were submitted as evidence of his learning. One leading member of the university opposed the degree. The rest voted for it almost unanimously, and the Regius Professor of Divinity composed the Latin speech presenting him. Samuel Crowther, who, the family remembered, had been taught his letters by a missionary’s wife in exchange for keeping her pantry clean, became a Doctor of Divinity of the University of Oxford. Canterbury, 1864 He was consecrated in Canterbury Cathedral on St. Peter’s Day, 29 June 1864, by Archbishop Charles Longley. Two English clergymen were consecrated with him, as Bishops of Peterborough and Tasmania. Special trains ran from London. The sermon was preached by H. L. Mansel of Oxford, on the words of Peter to the elders of the church: “Tend the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not of constraint, but willingly … neither as lording it over the charge allotted to you, but making yourselves ensamples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:2-3, ASV). Two colonial bishops were meant to present Crowther to the Archbishop, but the Bishop of Winchester, it was said, stepped in to take the place of one of them, so that the African should receive, as Page put it, “a double honour.” Two people had a special claim to be there. According to Page, one was Admiral Sir Henry Leeke, who forty-two years earlier, as captain of HMS Myrmidon, had taken the boy Ajayi from the slave ship off Lagos. The other, whose presence Henry Venn himself recorded, was an elderly lady. Page tells a story that she arrived to find her seat reserved for someone else, and refused to move. “I think I have a right equally to this seat,” she said, “because that black minister to be consecrated Bishop this morning was taught the alphabet by me.” She was Mrs. Weeks, widow of the Bishop of Sierra Leone, who, as Mrs. Davey, had taught him in her house at Bathurst. The Dean, Page says, let her stay. When Crowther returned to London afterwards, his first two calls were on Mrs. Weeks and on Admiral Leeke. The Book of Samuel preserves the song of Hannah, the mother of the prophet Samuel, after she had given her son to God. It is the verse at the head of this chapter. “He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, He lifteth up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes.” Hannah Crowther was still alive. Her son, the slave she had lost in 1821, now sat among the bishops of the Church of England. What the Newspapers Said The event was widely reported. The evangelical newspaper The Record called the consecration a “practical refutation … to the taunts of certain professors who maintain that the cerebral development of the negro shows that he is disqualified for intellectual pursuits.” It is a revealing sentence. In 1864 there were respected scientists in Britain who argued that Africans were a lesser branch of humanity, incapable of higher learning. The consecration of an African bishop was, for some, a public rebuttal of that belief. But the sentence also shows how deeply the idea had taken hold. Even Crowther’s supporters felt it necessary to argue that an African could think. There were limits, too, to what the Church was prepared to do. The royal licence made Crowther bishop “in the said countries of Western Africa beyond the limits of our dominions.” His diocese lay entirely outside British territory. He was not given authority over the European missionaries in the British colonies of Sierra Leone or Lagos. Andrew Walls notes that this limit was deliberate. An African bishop over African clergy in an African land was acceptable. An African bishop over Englishmen in a British colony was not yet contemplated. The question would return. “Can This Be Real?” He sailed from England on 24 July and reached Freetown on 10 August 1864, where crowds turned out to welcome him. In his reply to the addresses of welcome, he used his favourite phrase: “Here we pause and raise our Ebenezer to God’s praise. Hitherto the Lord has helped us.” He told them that the weapon which prevailed most in the ministry was “the habit of prayer for help from above,” and that “we are better fitted when we feel our incompetency to change a sinner’s heart.” He reminded the students of Fourah Bay that in 1841 his friends had called him “a fool for joining the expedition without any guarantee of good pay like the Europeans.” And when a friend asked whether he meant to rest, he said: “I shall only rest when I have no more work to do.” At Lagos on 22 August he held his first ordination. Then he went up the Niger. At Onitsha he held another ordination. That an African bishop should be ordaining African clergy on the banks of the Niger seemed to him almost beyond belief. “Can this be real?” he wrote. At the same time, in the same town, a prince had died, and there were human sacrifices at his funeral, among them a girl of eight who was buried alive. The bishop’s consecration had changed his title. It had not changed the Niger.

fields.title: A Bishop in a Canoe
fields.body_html:
“But I hold not my life of any account as dear unto myself, so that I may accomplish my course, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.”

— Acts 20:24, ASV

A Diocese Without Roads

The new bishop’s diocese had no boundaries anyone could draw and no roads to travel. It stretched along more than three hundred miles of the Niger and into the Delta, among a dozen peoples speaking a dozen languages, and the only way to reach most of it was by water. For many years Crowther had no boat of his own able to make the journey. He went up the river once a year, when a trading steamer or a naval gunboat happened to be going, and came down when it did.

He knew the danger in this. To the people of the Niger, a man who arrived every year on a trading ship or a warship must be connected with the traders or the government. In February 1868 he wrote to Henry Venn about it. As long as he had to travel in such ships, “it will take a very long time to dissuade the natives from the old belief that I am interested in those ships.” He had tried travelling independently in his own small boat, and had been attacked for his pains. “Of two evils I must choose the least for safety’s sake, and must either move in a trading steamer or in a gunboat whenever an opportunity presents itself, whether I be called the proprietor, though I do not own a pennyworth of her, or be called a warrior from being associated with the ship, although I may not fire a blank shot.”

It is a frank letter. Crowther saw clearly that the gospel he preached was being associated with trade and with British power, and he did not like it. He also saw no alternative. It was a dilemma that the missions in Africa never fully escaped.

Bonny

His first new work as bishop was in the Niger Delta, at Bonny, one of the great trading towns of the coast, where European ships loaded palm oil brought down from the interior by African middlemen. In the days of the slave trade Bonny had been one of the busiest slave ports in Africa. Its king, William Pepple, had lived in England for five years in exile, and on his return had written to the Bishop of London asking for a mission. Crowther arrived in 1864 and made an agreement with the king and chiefs.

The land they offered for the mission was a patch of “bad bush” where the bodies of sacrificed people and abandoned twins had been thrown, and where no one would live. Crowther accepted it with a joke that became famous: “Give us the ground, and leave us and juju to settle the remaining palaver.” The king’s son asked for Scripture and prayer before they began to clear it. They found an old copper bell in the town, cast in England in 1824, and one of the chiefs paid to hang it on the mission’s chapel.

The people of Bonny held the monitor lizard, the iguana, sacred. It was the town’s great juju. The lizards wandered the streets and houses, and no one could harm them. On Easter Day 1867 the king and chiefs publicly renounced its worship. Crowther reported that fifty-seven carcasses of the lizards were counted in one market afterwards, and compared the event to Moses grinding the golden calf to powder and making the Israelites drink it (Exodus 32:20). It was a dramatic public change. It did not mean that the people of Bonny had become Christians.

Some did, and in the persecution that came to Bonny in the 1870s they paid for it. Page calls a young man named Joshua Hart, martyred in November 1875, “the protomartyr of Bonny.” His master, a chief, tried to make him eat food offered to the idols. Hart replied: “If he even requires me to carry the world itself on my head, I will try. … But if he requires me to partake of things sacrificed to the gods, I will never do it.” He was thrown into the river, beaten with a paddle, and run through with a pointed pole. Other converts were persecuted, and one was starved to death over six days. At a prayer meeting in 1878 the Bonny Christians prayed for their persecutors: “We beseech Thee not to rain down fire and brimstone … but we pray Thee to rain down Thy love on them, as in the case of Saul.”

Seized

In September 1867, going up the Niger in his own boat with his son Dandeson and an English bricklayer named Moore, Crowther stopped at a village near Idda to visit a chief named Abokko, whom he had known for years. Abokko had quarrelled with his own king, and he believed, like many on the river, that Crowther owned the trading ships and the trading posts. He seized the bishop’s boat, plundered his luggage, and held him and his party prisoner. He demanded three boatloads of goods as ransom. (Ten years later, in a lecture, Crowther himself dated these events to 1868, but his diary and the letters written at the time place them in 1867.)

Crowther kept a diary of his captivity, and it is one of the most revealing documents of his life. He could not make Abokko understand the difference between a mission and a trading company. “A pure missionary object,” he wrote, “unconnected with any selfish object, is beyond the comprehension of such avaricious men as Abokko.” The first night they slept on a mat on the damp ground with nothing to eat. One of Abokko’s slaves, pitying them, offered Crowther his own cloth as a blanket. A boatman gave him his robe as a pillow, and Crowther gave it to Dandeson, and slept himself on a small ridge of earth with his cap under his head. “I need not say sleeplessly,” he wrote, “for my thoughts were full of these unexpected trials. … But the God of mercies will interpose.”

For days the chief gave them almost nothing. The slaves of the household fed them secretly from their own scanty food. “I often told Dandeson,” Crowther wrote, “that these slave boys and tender-feeling females were our ravens which brought us daily food as it was needed.” He was thinking of Elijah in the wilderness, when “the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening” (1 Kings 17:6, ASV). He added that if God gave him the chance, “these small acts of kindness of these poor oppressed slaves shall not pass unrewarded.” The man who had once been a slave was being kept alive by slaves.

On the Sunday he had no Bible. “No Bible, no scraps of any book whatever in hand to read, I felt what it was to be deprived of the means of grace.” He and his son repeated from memory passages of Scripture that fitted their situation. At noon he went to Abokko and told him that it was the day when the people of God throughout the world met to read and pray, and he had no book. The chief, startled, said he never hindered the worship of God, and had his box brought out. Crowther took out his Bible and Prayer Book. A Muslim visitor begged him for some paper, and Crowther, “stripped of everything as I was,” tore a leaf from his notebook and gave it to him. Two days later Abokko sent him some fish that had been offered to his idol. Crowther sent it back, saying that he never ate anything offered to an idol. That day was Dandeson’s birthday.

The ransom demanded rose to a thousand bags of cowries, worth a thousand pounds, and Abokko talked of another thousand for Dandeson. It was proposed that Dandeson should be allowed to leave with a messenger. He refused to leave his father.

Fell

On 28 September a steamer arrived unexpectedly, carrying W. Fell, the British vice-consul at Lokoja, with some of Crowther’s sons and men sent by the Nupe king. Fell tried to negotiate, and then decided that paying such a ransom would only encourage more kidnappings. He urged Crowther and his party to run for the ship’s boat. As they pushed off, Abokko’s men opened fire with muskets and poisoned arrows. Fell was hit in the side by a barbed arrow. He died as the ship came near Lokoja.

Crowther wrote: “It would have been more satisfactory to me, had such been the will of God, had I been shot and my dead body taken to Lokoja instead of his.”

It was not a pious phrase. He meant it. He had not planned an escape by force; others arranged it, and he “yielded.” He had been ready to wait, and to trust God for his release. Another man had died for him. Paul told the elders of Ephesus, in the verse at the head of this chapter: “I hold not my life of any account as dear unto myself, so that I may accomplish my course.” Crowther held his own life cheaply. He found it much harder to accept that someone else had given his.

A Year of Troubles

The kidnapping was one of a series of blows. Not long before, the station at Gbebe had been destroyed in a local war, and a grass fire had burned the mission buildings at Onitsha. At Idda it turned out that the king had been bought off by Abokko and had been promised a share of the ransom, and the station there was abandoned. And in October 1867, at Abeokuta, where Crowther had begun his work twenty years earlier, the Egba, angry at British policy in Lagos, turned on the missionaries and expelled them from the city. Churches were sacked. The converts were scattered.

“Though the last year was closed with a chapter of most painful events in connection with our mission,” Crowther wrote to Venn, “yet I look above to the Hand which has ever overruled similar affairs which had happened in times past to His honour and the advancement of His own cause. May He give us more faith to trust Him.” Of the scattered Christians of Abeokuta he said: “they are all scattered; but though it is night with us now daylight shall come.”

fields.title: Sympathy with All Classes
fields.body_html:
“but sanctify in your hearts Christ as Lord: being ready always to give answer to every man that asketh you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, yet with meekness and fear”

— 1 Peter 3:15, ASV

A Bishop’s Charge

In the Church of England a bishop gives his clergy, from time to time, a formal address called a charge, setting out his teaching on the work of the ministry. Crowther’s first charge was printed in London in 1866. Its title page calls it “A Charge delivered on the banks of the River Niger in West Africa, by Samuel Adjai Crowther, D.D. Oxon. (Native Missionary Bishop).” It begins “My dear beloved Brethren,” and calls the occasion “the first gathering together of the Bishop and Clergy in this Mission.” There were only a handful of them, and every one was an African.

It is a remarkable document. In a few dozen pages, Crowther set out what he had learned in twenty-five years of mission work about how the gospel should be preached to the peoples of West Africa. Later charges, in 1869, 1874, and 1885, filled out the picture. Together they are the nearest thing we have to his theology of mission, and much of what they say still repays reading.

The Gospel First

He began with the history of the mission and its modest results: after nine years on the Niger, a hundred and forty-six baptisms, eighty-nine communicants, and a hundred and forty-nine children in school. He quoted Thomas Fowell Buxton’s watchword, “the Gospel and the Plough,” and called it “worthy to be written in letters of gold.” He believed in teaching crafts, farming, and trade alongside the gospel. But he was firm about the order: “the Gospel primarily; Industry, as the hand-maid to the Gospel.”

He had been told by some Europeans that he should stop teaching Africans to read and write and teach them carpentry and cooking instead, and that once their material lives were improved they would be ready for Christianity. One adviser had told him that unless he did so, he would never give a farthing to the mission. Crowther answered with a sharp irony. Look at England, he said, the first nation in the world in wealth, science, and invention. Had all these advantages made the men who gave such advice more willing to receive the gospel? “I fear there are no such effects. Neither themselves, nor many who maintain such an opinion, are found near the doors of the places where the Gospel is preached: it is to them foolishness.” Material progress did not make people Christians. Only “the faithful preaching of the Gospel, which is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth,” could change hearts, “both at home and abroad.”

Preaching Like Christ

How should the gospel be preached? His model was Christ himself: the Sermon on the Mount, the parables, the discourses. “Sublime and lofty as the sentiments therein expressed are; yet they are so simple, that every heathen can understand them; and so appropriate, that every one can see himself represented in them.” He told his clergy: “Imitate Christ, then, to reach the understanding, and not to move the feelings only; speak to the people as they are able to bear it.”

Then came the heart of his method:

Again, in preaching, divest yourself of a disposition to dispute with Mahometans, or to censure heathens; rather be possessed with the feelings of sympathy with all classes of hearers.

And of the worshippers of the old gods, among whom most of his clergy worked: “them you must not censure as ignorant, stupid, and foolish idolators; your dealing with them must be that of sympathy and love, as you would deal with the blind who errs out of the way.”

He went further. The missionary should “take advantage of any principles which they themselves admit.” The sacrifices that the people offered to their gods, which many missionaries simply condemned, were for Crowther “a foundation for our preaching.” People who already understood that sin required a sacrifice could be shown the sacrifice of Christ. Paul had done the same at Athens, when he began from an altar “To an Unknown God.”

The verse at the head of this chapter is Peter’s advice to Christians living among people who did not share their faith: “being ready always to give answer to every man that asketh you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, yet with meekness and fear.” Paul put it another way: “Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer each one” (Colossians 4:6, ASV). That was Crowther’s method exactly. He was ready to give an answer, and he gave it with meekness.

The Muslims

He applied the same principle to Islam, which was spreading southward from the Fulani states of the north into the lands of the Niger. He did not believe that Islam was true. He believed that Muhammad was not a prophet and that the Qur’an was wrong about Christ. But he believed that argument and abuse would never win a Muslim. The missionary should preach Christ fully and plainly to Muslims and leave the result to God. “We must leave the results to the Disposer of all hearts.”

He was scathing about Christians who tried to compete with Muslim scholars on their own ground. Many Africans wore charms made by Muslim teachers, scraps of paper with verses of the Qur’an written on them, sewn into leather pouches. People asked him for scraps of the Bible to wear in the same way, and some Europeans told him it would do no harm to give them. He refused. At a great missionary meeting in Exeter Hall, London, in 1873, Crowther said: “I would rather let the Mohammedans take possession of the field … than that we should use cunningly devised frauds to deceive souls.” When an old chief at Bida asked him for paper charms to protect his horse, Crowther told him he had ridden the same horse for twelve years without a single charm, only washing, grooming, and feeding it well.

Polygamy

On one subject Crowther was unbending. Most of the men of the Niger who were wealthy enough had several wives. Some Europeans, among them the explorer Richard Burton, defended the custom as suited to Africa, and some churchmen had argued that a man with several wives should be baptised, so long as he took no more. Crowther rejected this. He argued at length, from Genesis and from the teaching of Christ and Paul, that marriage was the union of one man and one woman.

His main argument, though, was not only from Scripture. It was about women. The system, he said, “has enslaved the female population of the countries where it prevails.” Of the women of the harems he wrote: “They are reasonable beings, in whom God has planted certain rights and feelings.” He would not baptise a man with several wives, but he would baptise the wives of such a man, since they had not chosen the arrangement.

This is one of the hardest questions in the history of African Christianity, and Christians have answered it differently. Some African churches later came to accept polygamous converts. It is fair to note that Crowther’s position meant, in practice, that some men who wanted to be baptised were refused. He held his position out of conviction, not convenience, and he held it for African women’s sake as much as for any other reason.

No Compulsion

He was insistent that no one should be forced. “They are never compelled to do anything,” he said of the people among whom his clergy worked; “we leave the matter to their own deliberate consideration; they are never urged to cast away their idolatrous objects of worship.” Converts must come of their own will, or not at all.

And he was humble about the hardest question a missionary is asked: what becomes of those who die without ever hearing the gospel? He refused to pronounce. “With all submission, I will remark that it is not the will of God to reveal unto us what shall become of such persons.” He pointed his clergy instead to Abraham’s question: “shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” (Genesis 18:25, ASV). Their task was not to judge the dead but to go to the living.

Africa and Its Customs

In later charges he spoke about African culture. “Christianity does not undertake to destroy national assimilation,” he said in one; “where there are any degrading superstitious defects, it corrects them.” The gospel did not require Africans to become Europeans. It required them to become Christians, and a great deal of their own way of life could remain.

He also warned against the opposite mistake. By 1869 the cry “Africa for the Africans” was being raised in Sierra Leone and Lagos, and some were saying that the missions should be handed over entirely to Africans, with no more European help. Crowther called the slogan “Africa for the Africans alone” “great ignorance, not to say unpardonable selfishness.” He believed that Africa still needed European men and money, and that the young African churches were not yet strong enough to stand alone. “We are but a Church in embryo,” he told his clergy at Onitsha in 1874; “we must derive nourishment from the mother.” It is a striking position, given what would happen later. He did not want Europeans out. He wanted them as partners.

It would be wrong to present Crowther’s charges as modern documents. He shared many of the assumptions of his time. Crowther’s first charge was printed in London in 1866. Its title page calls it “A Charge delivered on the banks of the River Niger in West Africa, by Samuel Adjai Crowther, D.D. Oxon. (Native Missionary Bishop).” It begins “My dear beloved Brethren,” and calls the occasion “the first gathering together of the Bishop and Clergy in this Mission.” There were only a handful of them, and every one was an African. It is a remarkable document. In a few dozen pages, Crowther set out what he had learned in twenty-five years of mission work about how the gospel should be preached to the peoples of West Africa. Later charges, in 1869, 1874, and 1885, filled out the picture. Together they are the nearest thing we have to his theology of mission, and much of what they say still repays reading. The Gospel First He began with the history of the mission and its modest results: after nine years on the Niger, a hundred and forty-six baptisms, eighty-nine communicants, and a hundred and forty-nine children in school. He quoted Thomas Fowell Buxton’s watchword, “the Gospel and the Plough,” and called it “worthy to be written in letters of gold.” He believed in teaching crafts, farming, and trade alongside the gospel. But he was firm about the order: “the Gospel primarily; Industry, as the hand-maid to the Gospel.” He had been told by some Europeans that he should stop teaching Africans to read and write and teach them carpentry and cooking instead, and that once their material lives were improved they would be ready for Christianity. One adviser had told him that unless he did so, he would never give a farthing to the mission. Crowther answered with a sharp irony. Look at England, he said, the first nation in the world in wealth, science, and invention. Had all these advantages made the men who gave such advice more willing to receive the gospel? “I fear there are no such effects. Neither themselves, nor many who maintain such an opinion, are found near the doors of the places where the Gospel is preached: it is to them foolishness.” Material progress did not make people Christians. Only “the faithful preaching of the Gospel, which is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth,” could change hearts, “both at home and abroad.” Preaching Like Christ How should the gospel be preached? His model was Christ himself: the Sermon on the Mount, the parables, the discourses. “Sublime and lofty as the sentiments therein expressed are; yet they are so simple, that every heathen can understand them; and so appropriate, that every one can see himself represented in them.” He told his clergy: “Imitate Christ, then, to reach the understanding, and not to move the feelings only; speak to the people as they are able to bear it.” Then came the heart of his method: Again, in preaching, divest yourself of a disposition to dispute with Mahometans, or to censure heathens; rather be possessed with the feelings of sympathy with all classes of hearers. The missionary should “take advantage of any principles which they themselves admit.” The sacrifices that the people offered to their gods, which many missionaries simply condemned, were for Crowther “a foundation for our preaching.” People who already understood that sin required a sacrifice could be shown the sacrifice of Christ. fields.title: Cotton Gins and Gin
fields.body_html:
“And he will judge between the nations, and will decide concerning many peoples; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning-hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.”

— Isaiah 2:4, ASV

The Gospel and the Plough

Crowther believed that honest trade could help to end the slave trade. It was not an original idea. Thomas Fowell Buxton had argued it in the 1830s, and David Livingstone would make it famous with his call, at Cambridge in 1857, for “commerce and Christianity.” The reasoning was simple. The African rulers who sold captives to the coast did so because captives were the one thing European buyers would pay for. If they could sell palm oil, cotton, ivory, and shea butter instead, and get the same guns, cloth, and salt in return, they would have less reason to raid their neighbours for slaves. And a people who could grow and sell their own produce would be less easily exploited.

Crowther took this seriously and practically. In 1851, at Abeokuta, he began a small experiment with cotton. The mission bought a saw gin, a machine for separating cotton fibre from its seeds, and a deaf and dumb boy named Thomas Craig turned out to love working the gin, which everyone else avoided as too laborious to turn all day. He worked most of the five hundred pounds that were the first clean cotton produced at Abeokuta. From that small beginning, Crowther wrote nine years later, the chiefs and people of Abeokuta had begun “consigning their cotton to merchants in England of their own choice, being taught … to develop the resources of their own country.”

On the Niger he did the same. At the mission station at Gbebe there were cotton gins and a press for making bales. When a messenger came from the Nupe king, who suspected the mission of hostile intentions, Crowther showed him the schoolroom, the gins, and the bales, and sent him back with a message:

that we are Anasara; there, pointing to the schoolroom, we teach the Christian religion; pointing to the cotton gin, I said this is our gun; and to the clean cotton puffing out of it, that is our powder; and I said the cowries which are the proceeds of the operation are the shots which England, the warmest friend of Africa, earnestly desires she should receive largely.

“This is our gun.” It is a vivid picture of the prophet’s vision at the head of this chapter, in which the nations “beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning-hooks.” Crowther had seen what guns had done to the Yoruba country. He wanted the peoples of the Niger to fight with cotton gins instead.

The Royal Geographical Society

By the 1870s he knew the Niger better than any other living person, African or European. On 11 June 1877 he read a paper on the river to the Royal Geographical Society in London. He described its geography, its peoples, its trade routes, and its politics, and gave a survey of thirteen languages met along the Niger and the Benue. Hausa, he said, was “to Africa, what the French is to Europe,” a common tongue of trade that could carry the gospel far. He described the Fulani wars and the Nupe kingdom, and told the society that he had given a Hausa trader a letter for an old white man he had heard of far to the south-east, hoping it might reach David Livingstone. The trader brought it back undelivered; the white man, he had heard, was dead. “Whoever it might be,” Crowther said, “the trial to communicate was worth making.”

He argued that legitimate commerce would in time be “a silent but a sure death blow” to the domestic slavery of the interior, and gave as evidence that more than a thousand slaves had bought their freedom with money earned in the Lagos trade. The society later gave him a gold watch.

He also did not hesitate to criticise European traders. The closing of the river’s outlets by the Delta chiefs, he said, was partly the fault of “civilized interested influence also.” Some of the Europeans on the coast were no better than the people they called savages. Years before, in his journals, he had written of an English captain who ill-treated his Kru sailors: “what recommendation can it be to the character of civilized Englishmen, who come to civilize … Africa? … ‘Physician, heal thyself.’”

The Henry Venn

For years he had asked for a mission steamer, so that he would not have to travel in trading ships and gunboats. In March 1878 one was sent out, named after the man who had made him a bishop. The Henry Venn was built on the Clyde and launched as a “temperance ship,” carrying no alcohol. It was managed by a lay agent of the society named J. H. Ashcroft, who also took charge of the mission’s business affairs. That arrangement, as we shall see, would bring trouble.

Gin

The greatest evil of the trade on the Niger, in Crowther’s view, was not slaves but spirits. European traders, with spirits shipped mostly from Hamburg, poured cheap gin and rum into the Delta and up the river. It was the easiest thing to sell and the most profitable. Crowther had seen what drink did in the villages. In 1886 a town on the Niger complained that he had not brought a case of gin to open a meeting, as the traders did. “I told them plainly,” he wrote, “that it is against God’s religion to give them poison to drink, therefore they must never expect any from me.” The prophet had pronounced a woe on the man who did exactly what the traders were doing: “Woe unto him that giveth his neighbor drink, to thee that addest thy venom, and makest him drunken also” (Habakkuk 2:15, ASV).

He was not alone among African rulers in his view. The Muslim Emir of Nupe, Maliki, sent Crowther a letter, through one of Crowther’s African clergy, which was translated from the Hausa and preserved:

Salute Crowther, the great Christian minister. … it is about Barasa (rum or gin), Barasa, Barasa, Barasa — my God, it has ruined my country, it has ruined our people very much, it has made our people become mad!

The Emir had forbidden its sale in his kingdom. He begged Crowther to ask the society to ask the Queen to stop the traders bringing it. “For God and the prophet’s sake,” he wrote, “he (Crowther) must help us in this matter.” In December 1884 the society sent a deputation to the Foreign Office to plead against the liquor trade on the Niger. Little came of it. The liquor traffic was too profitable, and it paid too much of the cost of governing the coast.

It is a striking scene: a Muslim emir and an Anglican bishop, united against the gin of Christian Europe.

The Company

Crowther’s hopes for commerce were not entirely fulfilled. The trade that came up the Niger in the 1870s and 1880s was dominated by British firms, and after being merged into a single company they were chartered in 1886 as the Royal Niger Company, with power from the British government to govern the river. The company’s interest was profit, not the welfare of the peoples of the Niger. It fought wars, imposed monopolies, and in time handed over its territory to the colony of Nigeria. The trade that Crowther had hoped would free Africa from the slave trade became, in part, the road by which Africa was brought under colonial rule.

He did not live to see all of that, and it is not fair to blame him for it. His vision was of African farmers and traders freely selling their own produce, “consigning their cotton to merchants … of their own choice.” What came instead was a trading monopoly under a foreign flag. The prophet’s vision of swords beaten into ploughshares was not fulfilled on the Niger in his lifetime. But the vision was right, and so was his refusal to bring gin.

fields.title: The Delta Churches
fields.body_html:
“Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee: The residue of wrath shalt thou gird upon thee.”

— Psalm 76:10, ASV

Dandeson

The work in the Niger Delta became, in the 1870s and 1880s, the most fruitful part of Crowther’s diocese, and much of it was done by his youngest son. Dandeson Coates Crowther was named after a lay secretary of the missionary society in London. He had shared his father’s captivity at Abokko’s village and refused to leave him. On 19 June 1870, in St. Mary’s Church, Islington, in London, the parish where his father had gone to school as a young man, Samuel Crowther ordained his son deacon. The text was Paul’s word to Timothy: “Suffer hardship with me, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.” Page called it “the first time that a black Bishop had ordained his black son.” In 1878, by Stock’s account (1876 in some modern accounts), Dandeson became Archdeacon of the Lower Niger, which meant chiefly the Delta, with his base at Bonny.

The Delta was a hard field. Its trading towns, Bonny, Brass, New Calabar, and Okrika, were rich and proud, ruled by great trading Houses whose heads were among the most powerful men on the coast. Their wealth had once come from the slave trade and now came from palm oil. They were suspicious of anything that might upset the order on which their power rested, and Christianity, with its refusal of the town’s jujus and its insistence that slaves and masters were equal before God, threatened that order at its root.

Persecution at Bonny

In Bonny the chiefs turned against the Christians in the 1870s. Converts were beaten, starved, and killed. When the persecution was at its height, Crowther went to Bonny himself. He sat for hours under a tree waiting for the chiefs to meet him, and when they did, he spoke plainly. “I struck at the root at once,” he wrote. Some of the English traders, among them a captain named Boler, took the side of the mission. Slowly the persecution eased.

The converts’ faith was simple and strong. One of them said: “Jesus has taken charge of my heart, and padlocked it. The key is with Him.” A persecuting chief named Hart, on his deathbed, warned his people against the idols. St. Stephen’s Church at Bonny, first opened on New Year’s Day 1872, was reopened in 1880, and a chief named Squiss gave it a clock.

The Bonny chiefs also passed a law that twins, who had been killed there as elsewhere in the Delta, should be handed over to the mission instead. When one set of twins was born, a crowd came to seize them, and Dandeson stood at the door facing them while the pastors escaped through a window with the babies. The surviving twin was baptised Theodora Kezia Powell. Later the juju priest who had led the crowd was himself baptised.

Brass and Akassa

At Brass, further west, a chief named Thomas Spiff held firm through years of persecution. One of the persecutors, a chief named Oruwari, was eventually converted, and explained his change of heart with rueful honesty: “Those whom we persecuted … are growing fat, … we … are growing lean.” At Akassa, at the mouth of the Nun, the chiefs declared: “God be true, Juju be lie.”

The greatest event at Brass was the conversion of its king. Ockiya had renounced his household gods at the end of 1876 and handed three of them over to the mission. For three more years he prepared for baptism. He was required to keep only one wife, and he did. On Advent Sunday 1879 he was baptised, taking the name Josiah Constantine. He died two weeks later, calling on Christ. In 1883 Dandeson went to England to buy two iron churches for Brass, and when they arrived, two of the Christian chiefs, William Kennmer and Christopher Iwowari, fixed the first plates.

At Okrika, the Christian wife of a chief named Atorodibo refused to be chalked by the juju priest. That night enemies from Okoni ambushed the market women and killed nearly all of them. She was taken captive, and when she told her captor of the God of heaven he secretly paddled her home. In June 1881 Crowther confirmed converts at Nembe. In a village called Ayambo, the missionaries reported, there were no idols left at all, and they called it “the land of Israel.”

Onitsha

On the upper river, the work was harder. Onitsha, the first station, went through many troubles. In 1875 Crowther found some of the men at the trading posts, some European and many of them educated Africans, arguing from the Old Testament that polygamy was allowed, and some of the women converts hiring out their slaves as prostitutes. He preached against the traders from the pulpit. He also sent home some of the teachers from Sierra Leone whose “former habits” had made them unfit for the work. The mission was not a church of saints, and he knew it.

At one point the chiefs of Onitsha demanded that he order the Christian converts to go back to their old religion. He stood before them with a Bible in his hand and said: “to command these converts to return to idolatry is out of my power. I cannot do it, and I dare not do it.” It was the answer Peter and John had given the rulers of Jerusalem: “Whether it is right in the sight of God to hearken unto you rather than unto God, judge ye” (Acts 4:19, ASV).

In October 1879, after attacks on British traders, a Royal Navy gunboat, HMS Pioneer, shelled and burned Onitsha. The mission moved for a time across the river to Asaba. It was another of the episodes that tied the mission, in the minds of the Niger peoples, to British power, and it was not one that Crowther could prevent.

He went on working at translation. He had begun learning Igbo in the 1850s. In 1875 he chose the Isuama dialect as the standard for Igbo translation, because it seemed to be understood most widely. The choice was debated, and later translators chose differently, but it was the beginning of Igbo as a written language of the church. At Kipo Hill, a new station far up the river near Egga, the bishop, now nearly seventy, made bricks with his own hands.

The Wrath of Man

The verse at the head of this chapter is one that Crowther quoted about Bonny. It comes from a psalm celebrating God’s victory over the enemies of his people. “Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee: The residue of wrath shalt thou gird upon thee.” The persecution meant to destroy the church had in the end made it stronger. The persecutors had become converts, and the martyrs had become seeds.

It would be too simple to say that the Delta churches grew only through persecution, or only through the courage of their members. They grew also because Christianity offered things that the old order did not: education, contact with the wider world, a religion in which slave and master stood equal, and freedom from the fear of the jujus. Some people came to church for those reasons and not for love of Christ, and Crowther knew it. But the courage was real. Men like Joshua Hart, the protomartyr of Bonny, and women like the chief’s wife at Okrika, paid for their faith with their lives or risked them. Years before in Freetown, Crowther had been silenced by a Shango drummer who charged that the Christians there lived no better than the heathen, and he had admitted that “the charge was too true.” The Christians of the Delta were answering that charge.

By the 1880s the Delta churches were largely supporting themselves. They were led, under the bishop, by an African archdeacon, and staffed by African clergy and teachers. They were, as nearly as any church in Africa at the time, what Henry Venn had dreamed of. They would soon be tested in a way that no one expected.

Their wealth had once come from the slave trade and now came from palm oil. They were suspicious of anything that might upset the order on which their power rested, and Christianity, with its refusal of the town’s jujus and its insistence that slaves and masters were equal before God, threatened that order at its root. fields.title: Asano
fields.body_html:
“Set me as a seal upon thy heart, As a seal upon thine arm: For love is strong as death; Jealousy is cruel as Sheol; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of Jehovah. Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can floods drown it: If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, He would utterly be contemned.”

— Song of Songs 8:6-7, ASV

The Other Half of the Story

Most of this book has followed Samuel Crowther up rivers, into kings’ courts, and across the sea to England. It has said little about the woman who stayed behind. That is partly the fault of the sources. Crowther’s journals are the journals of a travelling man, and his wife appears in them mostly as someone he left on the shore. We have none of her letters. But the silence does not mean that she was unimportant. For fifty-one years the missionary’s journeys rested on her.

Asano had been a slave child like him, rescued from a slave ship like him, and landed in Sierra Leone the same year as him. They had grown up in the same mission world, learned in the same schools, and married in 1829 when he was a young schoolmaster of about twenty-two. From 1830 the society’s reports list her as “Susanna Crowther, school-mistress.” She taught in the schools of the colony while he taught, and later kept the home at Abeokuta and at Lagos while he travelled. When he sailed with the Niger Expedition in 1841, he left her, as he wrote, “near her confinement, and four children.” When he went to England for ordination, and again and again up the river, she stayed.

Jesse Page, who wrote with the help of the family, put it simply. During her husband’s long journeys as explorer and as bishop, “Mrs. Crowther felt her part was to spare him, and faithfully fulfil the not less sacred ministry of home and children.”

The Children

They had six children, usually listed as Samuel, Abigail, Susan, Josiah, Juliana, and Dandeson. We have met some of them already. Samuel, the eldest, drew the little map that his father showed to the Queen. Juliana, as a small girl, was carried on the march up to Abeokuta in 1846, and a letter she wrote from there in 1849 survives. Dandeson shared his father’s captivity in 1867 and became Archdeacon of the Delta. Abigail married Thomas Babington Macaulay, an African clergyman who founded the CMS Grammar School at Lagos. It was Abigail who nursed her grandmother at the end, and Abigail who was with her father when he died. Her son, Herbert Macaulay, born in 1864, became a pioneer of Nigerian nationalism, and is often called its father. The slave boy from Osogun was the grandfather of one of the first men to demand that Nigeria govern itself.

The family remembered the home as a strict one. Crowther’s household, they told Page, was “very strict in discipline and in the observance of religious truths, which may be said to be bordering on a puritanic method.” No one missed church, class, or prayer meeting without giving a reason. Once one of the sons disobeyed his schoolmaster, was punished, and ran home in tears expecting sympathy. His father took him back to school himself, found out what had happened, and had the schoolmaster give him a dozen strokes of the birch in front of the other pupils, with a lecture that a schoolmaster was to be obeyed “in all things lawful and right.” It is not a story that modern parents will admire. It is typical of Victorian households, black and white, and it was told by his family with pride.

The Blucher Shoes

But the same father was, as Page put it, “a bright and entertaining father among his children.” In the evenings they gathered round his knees to hear stories of Osogun: of monkeys and rats, of the great family farm where he had hoed his heaps for the yams and then sat in the shade laughing at the slower boys. He taught them Yoruba proverbs and the fables that the language is full of.

Their favourite story was about his first shoes. At Fourah Bay (the family’s account dates it to the 1830s, which cannot be quite right, since by then he had been to London and was a married schoolmaster), he and three other students were made monitors, and to mark their new dignity they were given shoes, heavy army boots from the soldiers’ barracks called “Blucher shoes,” to wear to church every Sunday. None of them had ever worn shoes. When they laced them up in the dormitory that evening, none of them could take a step, and the pupils laughed at them. Crowther, as he told it, crawled to a corner, knelt, and then stood up holding on to the wall, and walked round and round the room with his hand on the wall until he could let go. The others followed. For months afterwards they would walk barefoot to church, carrying the shoes, and put them on at the church porch. Later they bought their own boots, “and were careful to buy those that made noise and creaked as we stepped with them, to our great delight and the admiration of our pupils.” He acted it out, and the children clapped and shouted.

It is a small story, but it tells us something. The bishop who was received by the Queen and given a doctorate by Oxford never forgot that he had once been a boy who could not walk in shoes. He did not tell the story with embarrassment. He told it as a joke against himself.

Eighteen Months

In the late 1870s Susan fell seriously ill. For eighteen months, as he wrote in 1880, his mind was “exercised … at the bedside of my dear sick wife.” He had hoped that she would recover in time for him to make his annual visitation of the Niger. She did not, and he faced the hardest choice of his ministry. On the one hand was his duty to his dying wife. On the other was the mission, which, as he wrote, was at that very time “disorganized in various ways which threatened its prosperity.” He chose his wife. “I was obliged to perform the first duty of charity at its proper place, for ‘charity begins at home.’”

For a man who had given his life to the mission, and who had so often left his family to go up the river, it was a significant decision. The mission could wait. His wife could not. He saw the illness, too, as part of God’s dealing with them both, “a rod in the Father’s hand to correct and cure the soul.”

They celebrated their golden wedding. Page, writing later, says that after it she was taken ill again while her husband was up the Niger on the Henry Venn, and that when he returned to Lagos he found her at the point of death. “It was,” he said, “one of her earnest wishes, during her long illness, that she might die in my arms, and this was granted her, though she never knew it, for she lay unconscious till her death.” Susan Crowther died at Lagos on 19 October 1880. Page says that he “mourned her loss with secret tears, and went about his work again.”

The words at the head of this chapter come from the Song of Songs, the Bible’s great poem of married love. “Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can floods drown it.” Asano and Ajayi had both been carried across the waters in slave ships. The waters had separated them from their homes and families. They had not separated them from each other. The Proverbs describe the worthy wife in words that Crowther’s children might have used of her: “Her children rise up, and call her blessed; Her husband also, and he praiseth her” (Proverbs 31:28, ASV).

The timing of her death was cruel. In the same weeks, a report on the state of the Niger Mission, written by a European missionary, reached Lagos for the bishop’s comments. It was the beginning of the long trial that would darken the last decade of his life. He had to face it without her.

His Mother

Three years later another death followed. His mother, Afala, baptised Hannah, had lived her last years under his roof at Lagos. She had kept to the end the resolution she had made when he found her again in 1846: that her son was “no longer my son, but the servant of God,” and that he must go about his work without worrying about her. He was up the Niger when she died, in October 1883, at an age thought to be ninety-seven. Abigail, her granddaughter, was with her. The old woman told Abigail not to write to her father about her illness, for fear of troubling his mind in his work. Near the end she said to her: “You are as good as your father’s being at home; keep near to me, you have a great work to do.”

He learned of her death when he came down the river. Writing in February 1884, he was thankful that she had been “spared to us so long in the midst of so many adverse changes in her course of life,” and that she had come at last “to know the Saviour in whom she placed her trust as her Good Shepherd to the end of her life.” He told the story of her last words, he said, “that you may know what value she placed on my missionary work among our heathen countrymen.”

Caleb’s Prayer

Between these two griefs he wrote one of the most hopeful letters of his life. On 26 February 1883, at Bonny, he wrote to his clergy of the good way the Lord had led him. He was about seventy-five. “I have been blessed with unbroken health,” he wrote, “that I have not been laid aside any day, week, month, or year from pursuing my duty, which is a rare blessing.” It was not quite true, since his journals record fevers, but it was how the years felt to him.

He told them that he had often made two “timid requests” in prayer, which he feared might “savour of selfishness.” The first was Caleb’s. When the Israelites divided the promised land, Caleb, at eighty-five, reminded Joshua of the promise that Moses had made him forty-five years before, when he had been one of the spies: “And now, behold, Jehovah hath kept me alive, as he spake, these forty and five years … As yet I am as strong this day as I was in the day that Moses sent me” (Joshua 14:10-11, ASV). And Caleb asked for the hill country, where the giants lived in great fortified cities.

Crowther had first gone up the Niger in 1841, a little over forty years before. The mountain he asked for, he said, was “the countries of the Niger territory.” The great fenced cities were “the strongholds of Mohammedanism and heathenism, fenced with deluding religions and strong shackles of slave system.” His second request was that before he was laid aside, every station should have a good and permanent church, so that his successors would be able to build a church that supported itself.

It is the prayer of an old man who does not think of himself as old. He had lost his wife. He would soon lose his mother. The trial of his mission had begun. And he asked God, like Caleb, for more hill country.

fields.title: The Gathering Storm
fields.body_html:
“Brethren, even if a man be overtaken in any trespass, ye who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to thyself, lest thou also be tempted.”

— Galatians 6:1, ASV

A Mission Stretched Thin

This chapter and the next tell the hardest part of Crowther’s story. They are hard in two ways. They are painful, because they end with an old man’s life’s work taken apart around him. And they are difficult to tell fairly, because the two sides have been told very differently. The missionary society’s own historians, writing soon after, presented a necessary if regrettable cleansing of a corrupt mission. Nigerian historians, and in time the Church of England itself, have presented a betrayal. The truth, as best it can be found, includes things that both sides would rather leave out.

Begin with the problem, which was real. By the late 1870s the Niger Mission stretched from the Delta to Lokoja and beyond, over some three hundred miles of river, among many peoples and languages. Its stations were staffed almost entirely by African clergy, catechists, and schoolmasters, most of them recruited from Sierra Leone. Some were men of great devotion. Others were not. They lived far from any supervision, among trading posts where money, drink, and women were easily had, and where the example set by many European traders was bad. The bishop visited each station at most once a year, and for years he had no boat of his own. Paul had written of “that which presseth upon me daily, anxiety for all the churches” (2 Corinthians 11:28, ASV). Crowther knew the feeling. It was impossible for one man, however faithful, to know what was happening in every station.

He was also, by temperament, lenient. He found it hard to believe the worst of the men he had trained, and hard to dismiss them when he did. Where the evidence was uncertain, he gave them the benefit of the doubt. Where a man had fallen, he hoped for his repentance. Some of his letters from these years show both his seriousness about sin and his instinct for mercy. Of converts who had been drawn, under pressure from the chiefs, into heathen rites, he wrote in 1885 that “our severe punishment to maintain Christian discipline must be moderated with sympathy and guided by due allowance for the measure of knowledge and experienced Christian principle which the converts possessed.” That is the spirit of the verse at the head of this chapter: “restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.” But gentleness can become weakness, and some of his own friends thought it had.

Ashcroft and Wood

The first sign of trouble came through the mission’s business affairs. In 1878 the society sent out the steamer Henry Venn with a European lay agent, J. H. Ashcroft, to manage it and to take charge of the mission’s money and supplies. Then came a scandal that could not be explained away. He agreed that the mission needed better men, and said so. “None but the best and well qualified of the sons of the African churches,” he wrote in 1884, “whose hearts are fired with ardent zeal,” should be employed as agents. “They should be decided spiritual men, because spiritual men can only teach spiritual things.” But he would not accept that the answer was to replace African agents with Europeans. In February 1884, in a letter that shows how deeply the criticism had hurt him, he offered to step aside. “If others are delicate to tell me of my incompetency in the superintendence of the Niger Mission,” he wrote, “it is my duty to relieve their minds of that delicacy. I am willing, as long as my health lasts, to labour as a pioneer in opening fresh grounds, while the already established stations can be worked by superior intellects and better managers.” The society would not hear of it.

For a few years things improved. In place of Phillips the society sent James Hamilton, an older missionary who had served in Sierra Leone and understood African work. Paul’s instruction to the Galatians has two halves. The first is about the one who has fallen: “restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.” The second is about the one who restores: “looking to thyself, lest thou also be tempted.” Crowther’s critics accused him of neglecting the first half, of letting fallen men stay fallen, and to some extent they were right. But they were soon to neglect the second half entirely. Those who judged his mission most harshly did not look to themselves. They did not ask whether their own certainty, their own zeal, or their own assumptions about Africans might lead them into sin.

fields.title: Onitsha, 1890
fields.body_html:
“For it was not an enemy that reproached me; Then I could have borne it: Neither was it he that hated me that did magnify himself against me; Then I would have hid myself from him: But it was thou, a man mine equal, My companion, and my familiar friend. We took sweet counsel together; We walked in the house of God with the throng.”

— Psalm 55:12-14, ASV

A New Generation

In the late 1880s a new kind of missionary began to arrive in Africa. They were young, well educated, and intensely earnest. Many came from Cambridge. Many had been shaped by the holiness movement associated with the Keswick Convention, with its call to a life of complete consecration, and by a fresh wave of missionary zeal in the English universities. They were ready to give up everything for Christ, and many of them did, dying of fever within months of landing. They also had very high standards, for themselves and for everyone else, and very little patience.

Two of them came to the Niger. John Alfred Robinson, a Cambridge graduate, became secretary of the mission in 1887. Graham Wilmot Brooke, a former cadet of the Royal Military Academy at Woolwich, longed to reach the Sudan, the great Muslim belt of Africa north of the Niger, and planned to reach it from the river. Together they drew up a plan for a new mission to the Hausa and the Muslim north. They meant to live as simply as the people, in local dress, and to renounce any claim to British protection. Their courage and self-denial were real. So was their low opinion of the African Christians they found at Lokoja.

The society accepted their plan and reorganised the Niger Mission around it. The Upper Niger, from Lokoja northwards, became the base for the new Sudan party. The Lower Niger and the Delta became a separate mission, with three English missionaries, one of whom, F. N. Eden, was its secretary. Both were to remain, in name, under the bishop. Some African agents on the upper river were moved or removed to make room for the new arrangements. Archdeacon Henry Johnson was asked to go to Lagos to await instructions.

On 20 January 1890, at a great valedictory meeting at Exeter Hall in London, the new missionaries were sent out. Crowther, who had been in England while the plans were made, was on the platform, and gave them his blessing. In February they all sailed for West Africa together, the old African bishop and the young Englishmen who would take his mission apart.

Lokoja

At Lokoja the Sudan party set to work with great energy. Stock, who admired them, described their work as partly “a work of correction.” They judged the Lokoja congregation unsatisfactory, and believed, in phrases they borrowed from the prophet Jeremiah, that they must “root out” and “pull down” before they could “build” and “plant.” They examined the African agents, kept some whom they judged truly godly, and got rid of others. Their letters home, printed in the society’s magazine, were full of zeal and full of criticism.

Their standard was that of the committee’s own words: missionaries must be “vessels meet for the Master’s use.” The phrase comes from Paul: “If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honor, sanctified, meet for the master’s use, prepared unto every good work” (2 Timothy 2:21, ASV). No one could object to the standard. The question was who was to judge, and how, and with what mercy.

The Meeting at Onitsha

In August 1890 the new committee for the lower mission met at Onitsha. Its members included the English missionaries, Bishop Crowther, Archdeacon Dandeson Crowther, and another African clergyman, the Rev. J. Boyle. Stock’s account of what happened is brief and careful. The two sides “entirely failed to agree as to either the policy or the personnel of the Mission.” The English members succeeded in carrying the dismissal of certain agents. They did not think it enough. So “the Secretary, acting for the C.M.S., gave separate notice, in its name, of suspension of some others from its employment.” Stock adds: “It is needless now to mention names.”

Nigerian historians, working from the society’s own archives, have filled in what Stock left out. Among those suspended were African clergy whom Crowther had himself ordained, and they were suspended in his presence. Among them was a veteran clergyman, Charles Paul, who had served the mission for decades. And among them was the bishop’s own son, the Archdeacon of the Delta, Dandeson Crowther. The English secretary, it seems, claimed the power to act for the society regardless of the committee. The old bishop, by these accounts, rose trembling to his feet to dissociate himself from what had been done, and withdrew from the committee.

He did not resign as bishop, and he was not removed. Popular accounts sometimes say that he was deposed or forced out. He was not. He remained Bishop of the Niger until he died. But he had seen his clergy suspended over his head by young men who had been in Africa a few months, and his authority over the mission that he had founded had been badly broken.

The psalm at the head of this chapter is David’s lament over betrayal by a friend. “For it was not an enemy that reproached me; Then I could have borne it.” Crowther had faced enemies all his life: the raiders who burned Osogun, the slave-dealers of Lagos, the chiefs of Bonny, Abokko. He had borne them. What he found hardest to bear came from his own side, from members of his own society and his own church, men he had blessed at Exeter Hall and sailed with to Africa. “We took sweet counsel together; We walked in the house of God with the throng.”

The Report

The news caused a storm on the whole West African coast, and deep division in London. The society’s committee sent a solemn letter to all its agents and congregations in West Africa, promising an impartial inquiry and restating its principles. A special sub-committee sat for many weeks. Eden and Brooke came to England to explain themselves. Stock, who was there, wrote that in twenty-five years there had been no question on which the committee had been so divided.

The report was issued in January 1891. On the individual cases, the action taken in Africa was “confirmed in some cases and reversed in others.” On the state of the mission, it made admissions on both sides. It confessed “the inadequacy of the provision made for the superintendence of the Mission.” It found that “the moral and spiritual condition of the congregations generally has in it at the present time much that is extremely lamentable.” And it added: “it is but just to the Bishop to say that from the commencement of the Mission most serious difficulties have beset him and surrounded every station.”

“Both sides on the Niger,” Stock wrote, “were grievously disappointed.” The young Englishmen thought the society had not gone far enough. The Africans thought it had endorsed an injustice. Crowther, according to Stock, “was also deeply dissatisfied with the Society’s decisions, although it was his full purpose to accept and act upon them.”

“Too Severe”

The young men did not live long. Robinson died in June 1891. Brooke died in March 1892. Eden resigned at the end of 1891. Their Sudan mission collapsed.

Eight years later Stock gave his judgement. “Robinson and Brooke — Brooke especially — were severe in their judgment of their African fellow-workers,” he wrote. “They were, indeed, too severe. They did not make sufficient allowance for racial weaknesses, and they were not patient enough with those who, like the venerable bishop himself, honestly differed from them. Their campaign against the evils on the Niger undoubtedly alienated the minds of many West Africans from the C.M.S., and it was long before confidence was restored.”

It is a revealing sentence. Stock thought the young men were wrong to be so harsh, though in the next breath he defended them, crediting their severity with the mission’s later improvement. But even in correcting them he speaks of “racial weaknesses,” as if Africans as a race were weaker than Europeans. That assumption, held even by the kind, was the real enemy of Crowther’s work. When Venn had made him a bishop in 1864, the society had believed that Africans could lead their own churches. By 1890 many in the society no longer believed it. The historian J. F. Ade Ajayi called these years “the turning of the tide.” The problems on the Niger were real. But the way they were handled, by young Englishmen overruling an old African bishop and his clergy, showed that something had changed in the way the society thought about Africans.

There were Christians on both sides who acted in good faith, and there was sin on both sides. Some of the African agents had been unfit for their work, and some had done great wrong. Crowther had been too slow to act. But the society had also failed him, by giving him an impossible task, by leaving him without support for years, and then by allowing young men who barely knew Africa to humiliate him and his clergy in public. The report of 1891 admitted part of this. It would take more than a century for the Church of England to admit the rest.

There were Christians on both sides who acted in good faith, and there was sin on both sides. Some of the African agents had been unfit for their work, and some had done great wrong. Crowther had been too slow to act. But the society had also failed him, by giving him an impossible task, by leaving him without support for years, and then by allowing young men who barely knew Africa to humiliate him and his clergy in public. The report of 1891 admitted part of this. It would take more than a century for the Church of England to admit the rest.

fields.title: The Delta Pastorate
fields.body_html:
“Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thy habitations; spare not: lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes.”

— Isaiah 54:2, ASV

The Delta Answers

The Christians of the Niger Delta did not accept what had happened at Onitsha quietly. Their archdeacon, by the Nigerian accounts, had been suspended. Their bishop had been humiliated. Many of them had suffered persecution for their faith, and had built and paid for their own churches. They did not see why a committee of young Englishmen should now decide who was fit to be their pastor.

Their answer was not to leave the Church. It was to stop taking the society’s money. The congregations of Bonny and the neighbouring towns, led by Archdeacon Dandeson Crowther, declared that they would support their own churches and clergy themselves. With some help from sympathisers in Lagos, they raised the funds, and, as Stock recorded some years later, “they have never again looked to the Society for pecuniary help.”

They asked their bishop to make it official. After consulting the members of the churches, they put a formal application into his hands, asking that the Delta be made a self-supporting native pastorate, like the pastorates that already existed in Sierra Leone and Lagos. Crowther sent it on to London with his full approval. Some modern historians say he had drafted the scheme himself in the spring of 1891. His letter supporting it spoke of the opportunities opening in the Delta, and of its unhealthiness for Europeans, and concluded that the suggestion “is providential that the Delta district should be made a native pastorate to be worked entirely through native agency, towards the expenses of which they resolved to contribute.”

It was, in fact, exactly what Henry Venn had hoped for thirty years before. Page himself quoted Venn’s hope “that in course of time the churches in the Niger Mission shall become self-supporting, as those in the Colonies are.” Venn had called it the “euthanasia” of a mission: the point at which the missionaries could step aside because the church they had planted could stand on its own. The Delta churches had reached it, not in the peaceful way Venn had imagined, but in the midst of a quarrel.

Not a Secession

The society’s leaders in London were not pleased. Page, who wrote as the society’s friend, admitted “a little natural regret” that the proposal “should come at a time when some misunderstanding was felt on the Niger.” Stock wrote that “coming just then, it had more the appearance of a secession than was pleasant.”

But he was careful to add: “it was in no sense a secession from the Church of England, and only a temporary alienation from the Society.” This matters, because the Delta Pastorate is sometimes described today as the first African breakaway from the Anglican Church. It was not. The Delta Christians had no wish to leave the Church of England, its Prayer Book, its creeds, or its bishops. They asked for the Archbishop of Canterbury’s counsel, and received it. They left the control of a missionary society, not the Church.

Other African Christians in those years did leave. In Lagos the Native Baptist Church was formed in 1888, and in 1891 a group of Lagos Christians left the mission churches to form the United Native African Church. The treatment of Crowther was one of the grievances that fuelled that movement. Crowther himself never encouraged it. The Delta Pastorate was his answer to the same pain: to stay in the Church, and to take responsibility for it.

Bonny, 1892

Crowther did not live to see the pastorate inaugurated. On 29 April 1892, four months after his death, it was formally begun at Bonny, with services of thanksgiving at St. Stephen’s Church and St. Clement’s. The preachers were the Rev. J. Boyle, who had sat beside the bishop at Onitsha, and Archdeacon Dandeson Crowther.

Dandeson’s sermon has survived in part. He said that God seemed to wish “in these latter days to extend the name and knowledge of His beloved Son by simple, inexpensive means, using local instruments to carry it into the interior.” By forming the pastorate, he said, “the people make the religion their own, and are already feeling the responsibility of taking the Gospel with them everywhere they go.” The ordinary Christians of the Delta, traders and fishermen and canoe-men, were carrying the gospel up the creeks where the missionaries could not easily go. “It may be said that they are weak, yet they act as pioneers for us.”

It is the voice of his father. Samuel Crowther had always believed that Africa would be won chiefly by Africans, and that the strength of a church lay not in its buildings or its foreign support but in its members’ sense that the faith was their own.

Reconciliation

The breach with the society did not last. When Joseph Sidney Hill, chosen as the next bishop, was sent out by the Archbishop before his consecration to visit the stations and ascertain the position of the new pastorate, the Delta Christians received him warmly. It received his successor, Herbert Tugwell, in the same way. Both, according to Stock, were “loyally received by them as their ‘overseers.’” In 1896, after conferences in London and Lagos, a formal constitution was agreed, setting out the pastorate as a self-supporting branch of the Church of England, governed by its own church councils under a bishop. Page credited the settlement to Bishop Hill, Bishop Tugwell, Archdeacon Crowther, and James Johnson of Lagos, who would himself become an assistant bishop a few years later. In time the pastorate came back into closer relations with the society.

Dandeson Crowther remained Archdeacon of the Delta for decades, and lived until 1938. Stock, writing in 1899, called the Delta Pastorate “the most encouraging thing” in the Niger region, “a practically independent African Church.” By then even the society’s own historian could see it as a success.

The Planter and the Increase

The prophet’s words at the head of this chapter are addressed to a barren woman, told to prepare for more children than she can imagine. “Enlarge the place of thy tent … spare not: lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes.” A century earlier, William Carey had preached on the same text when he called English Baptists to send missionaries to the world. The churches of the Niger Delta were one of the answers. From a handful of converts at Bonny in 1864, persecuted and despised, had grown a church that paid for its own clergy, sent its own members as evangelists into the interior, and stood firm when its founders were wronged.

Crowther did not see the full harvest. Few pioneers do. Paul said of the church at Corinth: “I planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6, ASV). Crowther had planted. Dandeson and the pastors of the Delta watered. The increase was yet to come.
