fields.title: “Good Night”
fields.body_html:
“I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith:”

— 2 Timothy 4:7, ASV

The Stroke

Samuel Crowther had been remarkably strong. He had survived the fevers that killed so many of his European companions, the wreck at Jebba, the captivity with Abokko, and fifty years of travel by canoe and steamer in one of the unhealthiest climates on earth. In 1883 he had thanked God for “unbroken health.” He was now in his eighties, as nearly as anyone could tell, and still travelling.

In the summer of 1891, at Bonny, it ended. As he got up from his desk, he had a stroke. In October he described it in a letter to a friend in England: “I was laid aside by a sudden attack of paralysis, as I got up from my desk, which paralyzed my right hand and leg and affected my speech for many days, so that I could not speak audibly.” The doctor ordered a change of air, and he left Bonny on 25 September and reached Lagos three days later, to stay at the house of his daughter Abigail Macaulay. “I am thankful to say that I am improving,” he wrote, “hoping to be all right again in a few weeks. … Wishing soon to recover my health, to spend the remainder of my days in the service of our Divine Master.” In a later letter he apologised for his shaky handwriting.

A missionary who called on him found him slowly recovering but not himself. For hours he would sit in thought, looking out across the sea.

Stock, the society’s historian, was frank about the cause. “In his case,” he wrote, “as in Robinson’s, death was certainly hastened by anxiety and disappointment. For he on his part was also deeply dissatisfied with the Society’s decisions, although it was his full purpose to accept and act upon them.”

The Last Weeks

He did not stop working. On Christmas morning he walked to Christ Church, Lagos, for the last time. In the last days of December Archdeacon Hamilton, his old friend from the years of reform, landed at Lagos and spent an hour with him. Then he took the bishop on his arm to a meeting to send out seven schoolmasters from the training institution. At the end, the old man stood up and gave them his blessing, as Page put it, “tenderly, fatherly, with slow and faltering speech.” It was his last act of public service. The next day he spent much of the time on diocesan business with his visitors. He spoke of going back to Bonny in the first week of January, and wrote to the British consul for the Oil Rivers, who happened to be in Lagos, to ask for a passage in his steamer.

Hamilton and another visitor from the society brought him, in those last days, what Stock called “the assurance of the Committee’s unabated respect and affection.” There had been a letter from the society’s secretary in London, too, which his daughter read to him more than once. In an old diary, after his death, was found the draft of a reply, written in a feeble hand and never sent. A pencil note said that the doctor had forbidden him to write any more.

The letter is confused in places, as a letter written after a stroke might be. But its last lines are clear. The secretary seems to have sent him a memorandum about his good character, and he wrote that it was an answer to his prayer, that the God who had called him first from among his people “may give me grace to set a good example for others to follow.” And then: “Since my appointment to the superintendent of the Niger Mission in 1857 to the present I never refuse any suggestion made by the committee for the improvement of the Niger Mission. Though I am single-handed, I like to be improved by the ideas of others.”

It is a humble ending to a long correspondence. He did not defend himself. He did not accuse anyone. He simply said that he had always been willing to learn.

“Good Night”

Abigail Macaulay, in whose house he spent his last days, wrote down afterwards what happened on the last day of the year. Here is her account, in part.

He was up as usual on the morning of the 31st, dressed, and went through the morning devotions as he did every day; then had his tea after seven o’clock. About eight o’clock he sent to call me to read a letter to him. I took the letter and read it, and said: “Father, I have read this letter to you several times.” He said: “I have read it too.”

She left him sitting at the table with his Prayer Book, his hymn book, and some papers, and went to see about his breakfast. Later that morning an old Christian woman named Emma Taiwo came to visit him, and came back in haste to say that something was wrong. Abigail ran in just in time to catch him before he fell from the sofa. It seems he had had another stroke. The doctor was sent for. He spoke little after that, but answered when spoken to. In the afternoon he was helped to his bedroom. He took his medicine patiently, and when she asked about his cough he said, “No pain.”

At midnight when I came in to give him his medicine he sat up and said he hoped it was the last dose. He lay down, and as I covered him I said, “Good night, father,” and he said, “Good night.” Half an hour later I heard movements in his room and saw father just lying down, and I jumped on the bed, for I saw he was dying. “Father! father!” I cried. He heaved a sigh, and all was over. He passed away at a quarter to one in the morning.

His daughter’s account places his death, strictly, in the first hour of 1 January 1892. His memorial, his biographers, and the church calendars that remember him all give the date as 31 December 1891. Either way, he died at the turn of the year, quietly, in his daughter’s house, with his daughter beside him.

His last word was “Good night.” It is a word of trust. The psalmist said: “In peace will I both lay me down and sleep; For thou, Jehovah, alone makest me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:8, ASV). The boy who had lain awake in chains the night before he was taken to market, and the old man who had slept on a ridge of earth in Abokko’s camp with his cap under his head, lay down at last in peace.

The Funeral

He was buried on 1 January 1892, at Lagos. The funeral service was held at Christ Church, and the address was given by the Rev. James Johnson, one of the most outspoken African clergymen of his generation. The Governor of Lagos and most of the senior European officials attended. Ten clergymen, African and European, walked before the coffin, which was strewn with ferns and frangipani. He was laid in the grave beside his wife and his mother, and the mourners sang together, “Hush, blessed are the dead.”

Six years later a marble monument was unveiled over the grave by the Governor. Its inscription called him “a native of Osogun,” the first student of Fourah Bay College, and a servant of the Church Missionary Society for sixty-two years. It gave his age as “about 89 years.” No one knew his birthday. The inscription’s estimate would put his birth around 1802, several years earlier than most modern historians think likely. The uncertainty is itself part of his story. He had been born into a world without written records, and had spent his life giving that world a written language.

The Successor

The society chose an Englishman to succeed him. Joseph Sidney Hill, a gentle and able man who had served in West Africa and New Zealand, was consecrated in St. Paul’s Cathedral on 29 June 1893, twenty-nine years to the day after Crowther’s consecration at Canterbury. The diocese was enlarged to take in the Yoruba country, and renamed Western Equatorial Africa. With Hill two African clergymen, Charles Phillips and Isaac Oluwole, were consecrated as assistant bishops. It was a gesture of goodwill, and it was received as one. But it was also a sign of what had changed. In 1864 an African had been made the bishop. In 1893 Africans were made the assistants.

Hill barely began the work. He sailed in November 1893, reached Lagos in December, and within a month he and his wife were both dead, as so many Europeans before him had died. It would be many decades before another African was made a diocesan bishop in the Anglican Church in Nigeria.

Paul wrote to Timothy near the end of his life, in the words at the head of this chapter: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith.” He was writing from prison, with many of his friends gone and some of them turned against him. It was not a triumphant ending, in the world’s eyes. But he knew what he had done, and to whom he had done it. So did Samuel Crowther.

fields.title: A Weaned Child
fields.body_html:
“Jehovah, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty; Neither do I exercise myself in great matters, Or in things too wonderful for me. Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul; Like a weaned child with his mother, Like a weaned child is my soul within me.”

— Psalm 131:1-2, ASV

The Man Himself

We have followed Samuel Crowther’s life from Osogun to Lagos. Before we ask what it meant, it is worth pausing to look at the man himself: what he was like to live with, how he prayed, and what kept him going. The sources are uneven. Much of what we know of his character comes from his family and admirers, and they remembered what they wanted to remember. But there is also his own voice, in fifty years of journals and letters, and it is consistent.

Humility

Everyone who knew him spoke first of his humility. It was not a pose. It showed itself in small things. When he was addressed in letters as “My Lord,” as English bishops were, he had his son add a postscript to his reply: “Please address me Right Reverend Bishop, and never as My Lord.” If there was only one chair in a room and a schoolmaster came in, the bishop would get up and give him his seat. Dandeson once asked him why. “People, seeing me standing,” he said, “will very soon go and get me another seat, but will not be so quick, if ever they did think of getting one for a schoolmaster.”

He answered every letter himself, by hand, however trivial, and kept copies of both his letters and the replies. Looking up once from a pile of letters from people he did not know, he said: “These sort of letters should be carefully answered to lead the writers to a higher aim and nobler thoughts.” He taught his children to say “thank you” for the smallest kindness.

Paul told the Philippians to do “nothing through faction or through vainglory, but in lowliness of mind each counting other better than himself” (Philippians 2:3, ASV). Crowther took the instruction almost literally. The psalm at the head of this chapter is one of the shortest in the Bible. “Jehovah, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty.” The psalmist compares his soul to a weaned child with its mother: no longer crying for what it wants, but content to be near her. It is a picture of a man who had stopped demanding things of God and of others, and had learned to rest.

“I Know My Place”

His humility had a harder side, and it should not be passed over. In January 1884, in the middle of the troubles over the mission, he wrote to the society’s secretary a letter that is painful to read today:

I know my place as negro, but I have ever paid my respects to Europeans, whether old or young, missionaries or those in secular occupations, as the race of our benefactors, to whom we owe our bodily freedom and the spiritual privileges of the glorious liberty of the Christian religion.

He went on to ask for more European missionaries, to be “the chief workers under the superintendence of the European secretary,” because “the Europeans are better managers, their actions and report will be better confided in both out here and in England. How should we read this? It would be too simple to say that Crowther had absorbed the racism of his age and believed Africans inferior. But it would also be too simple to say that the letter meant nothing. It was written by a man under great pressure, trying to save his mission by conceding what he could. And it reflects something real in him: a deep and lasting gratitude. He had been taken off a slave ship by English sailors, taught his letters by an Englishwoman, and made a bishop by English churchmen. “I owe so much to their fathers,” he said, when asked why he was so respectful to Europeans of every kind. That gratitude was genuine and honourable. But it also made it hard for him to stand up to Europeans when they were wrong, and some of them took advantage of it. The man who knew his place was surrounded, at the end, by younger men who were quite sure of theirs.

Prayer

He prayed constantly, and in the manner of an Anglican of his day: morning and evening prayer from the Prayer Book, family prayers, the Psalms. On the last morning of his life he went through his devotions as usual, and sat at his table with his Prayer Book and hymn book beside him. But he also prayed in the moment, silently, in times of danger. Once, when he feared that the Nupe king was about to order the mission out of Lokoja, he prayed, again and again, the prayer that Nehemiah prayed before the king of Persia. Nehemiah, asked by the king what he wanted, “prayed to the God of heaven” before he answered (Nehemiah 2:4, ASV). “The silent ejaculation of Nehemiah before Artaxerxes,” Crowther wrote, quoting Nehemiah’s words, “‘Grant him mercy in the sight of this man,’ was most applicable in my case, and was frequently offered.” To his surprise, the king raised the matter himself, and told him that the mission should stay. Crowther wrote in his journal: “This is an instance of an answer to prayer: ‘Before they call I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear.’”

He believed that prayer was the chief tool of a missionary. As he had told the Christians of Freetown in 1864, just after his consecration, “the habit of prayer for help from above” is the weapon that prevails most in the work of the ministry, and “we are better fitted when we feel our incompetency to change a sinner’s heart.” It was the conviction of a man who had tried for decades to change hearts and knew he could not.

Patience

His patience was remarkable, and some thought excessive. A young African clergyman, J. Boyle, remembered an occasion in 1874 when he and another new missionary, fresh from college, accompanied the bishop on a visit to a king. They had sent word ahead, but no one came to meet them. They were shown to a verandah and kept waiting for a long time. The young men were indignant at the insult to their bishop. Crowther was calm. “My young friends,” he said, “you have to bear and forbear with these people. … In dealing with them you have to be armed with a threefold coat of mail called Patience.”

He also said, in the same breath, that the people were at best “nothing better than children” in some of their actions. It is the language of his time, and he used it of the people he loved and served. But the heart of the remark was not contempt. It was patience, and patience was the virtue that his critics lacked. The young men of 1890 had many virtues, but patience was not among them.

Scripture and Humour

His Bible was the foundation of everything. He knew it so well that in Abokko’s village, with no book to read, he and Dandeson took comfort on the Sunday by repeating passages of it from memory. His letters and journals are full of it, not as decoration but as the natural language of his thought. When something good happened, he raised his Ebenezer, the stone that Samuel set up after a victory, saying “Hitherto hath Jehovah helped us” (1 Samuel 7:12, ASV). When something bad happened, he looked, as he wrote in 1868, “above to the Hand which has ever overruled similar affairs.”

He was also funny, in a quiet way. His children remembered the performance of the Blucher shoes. His answer at Bonny, when he was offered a haunted patch of bush for a mission, was a joke: “leave us and juju to settle the remaining palaver.” He knew when not to take himself seriously, which is rarer in bishops than it should be.

An Eli?

Stock, in his history, admitted that Crowther might have been “an Eli in exercising discipline too lightly.” Eli was the old priest of Shiloh whose sons behaved disgracefully and whom he failed to restrain. It was a pointed comparison. But Stock added at once: “he was an Eli, too, in simplicity and sincerity of character.” And he wrote that Crowther “lived in an atmosphere of suspicion and scandal, yet no tongue, however malicious, of white man or black man, ventured to whisper reproach against his personal reputation.”

There is another side of Eli worth remembering. When the boy Samuel came to him with a hard message from God, Eli did not argue. He said: “It is Jehovah: let him do what seemeth him good” (1 Samuel 3:18, ASV). According to his son, those were the words that Crowther used in 1864, when Venn pressed the bishopric on him. They were the words of a weaned child.

fields.title: Essentially African, Essentially Missionary
fields.body_html:
“After these things I saw, and behold, a great multitude, which no man could number, out of every nation and of all tribes and peoples and tongues, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, arrayed in white robes, and palms in their hands;”

— Revelation 7:9, ASV

Collapse

For a few years after Crowther’s death, it looked as if his life’s work had failed. In 1890, Stock recorded, the Niger Mission had “a Bishop, nine Native clergy, and nine English missionaries.” By 1893, after the suspensions, the resignations, the deaths, and the withdrawal of the Delta churches, its staff was listed as three Englishmen, one of whom soon went home, and three African clergymen. “So disastrous a change,” Stock wrote, “was unparalleled in the Society’s history since the fatal early days of Sierra Leone.” The young men’s mission to the Sudan had collapsed with them. The first African bishop of modern times in the Anglican Church had been succeeded by an Englishman, and the Englishman had died soon after reaching Africa.

Stock, who belonged to the side that had judged Crowther, still wrote in hope that the Master Himself would perhaps have said, “The Mission is not dead, but sleepeth.”

What Remained

It was not dead. Much of what Crowther had built could not be undone by a committee.

There was the Yoruba Bible, completed in 1884 by the team he had led and inspired, and the written Yoruba language that he, more than anyone, had given its shape. There was the beginning of written Igbo, and of Nupe, and word lists and grammars of a dozen other languages. There were the churches of the Delta, self-supporting and self-governing, which had survived persecution and would survive the quarrel with the society. There were congregations along the Niger, small and often struggling, from Onitsha to Lokoja. There were African clergy he had trained and ordained. And there was the example of his life, which nobody could take away.

Stock recorded a small incident from 1894. A missionary of the society was preaching in a street in Calcutta, in India, when an African man appeared in the crowd and began begging the people to accept Christ, of whom he had learned, he said, from “the sweet words of a black bishop called Crowther.” It is the kind of story that missionary histories like to tell, and we cannot know more about the man. But it is a reminder that the seed Crowther sowed travelled further than anyone could trace.

The Historians

In the century after his death, as the missionary era ended and Africa’s nations became independent, historians began to look at Crowther again. The Nigerian historian J. F. Ade Ajayi, in a study of the Nigerian missions published in 1965, showed how the crisis of 1890 had grown out of a change in European attitudes to Africans, and how Crowther’s generation of African Christians had become the educated elite of a new Nigeria. E. A. Ayandele, another Nigerian historian, admired Crowther but did not flatter him, judging him weak as an administrator and a disciplinarian. The Scottish historian Andrew Walls called him probably the most widely known African Christian of the nineteenth century. Lamin Sanneh, the Gambian-born scholar of mission, made him the great example of his argument that Bible translation, by treating African languages as worthy of the word of God, dignified African cultures and prepared the way for African churches to stand on their own.

These historians did not agree on everything. But they agreed that Crowther’s personal integrity was never in question, that the mission had real weaknesses, and that the way the crisis of 1890 was handled was unjust and had lasting consequences. Walls summed up Crowther’s legacy in a phrase: a Christian faith that was “essentially African and essentially missionary.” Crowther was African through and through, and never pretended otherwise. And he was a missionary through and through, who believed that the faith that had set him free must be carried to others.

“It Was Wrong”

In 2014, a hundred and fifty years after Crowther’s consecration, a service of thanksgiving and repentance was held in Canterbury Cathedral, where he had been made a bishop. The Archbishop of Canterbury, Justin Welby, preached. He called Crowther “the apostle of Nigeria,” and said: “We in the Church of England need to say sorry that someone was properly and rightly consecrated Bishop and then betrayed and let down and undermined. It was wrong.”

It had taken more than a century, and it came from the same church and the same cathedral. Crowther would probably have been embarrassed by it. He never asked for an apology, and never spoke publicly against those who had wronged him. But the apology was not really for his sake. It was for the sake of the truth, and of the African churches who had carried the memory of his treatment for generations.

The Harvest

The greatest change came after all the historians and archbishops. When Crowther was born, there were hardly any Christians in the lands that are now Nigeria. When he died, there were a few thousand, in scattered congregations, many of them nominal. Today Nigeria has one of the largest Christian populations in the world, and its Anglican church is among the largest provinces of the Anglican Communion, with many more worshippers on a Sunday than the Church of England. Most of the world’s Christians now live in the global South, and Africa has more Christians than any other continent. The churches of Africa send missionaries of their own across the world, including to Britain.

Crowther did not cause all this, and it would be foolish to claim that he did. Many other people, African and European, and many other movements, from independent African churches to the great revivals of the twentieth century, played their part. But in a real sense he stood at its beginning. He was the first African bishop of the Anglican Church in modern times, and the man through whom many Africans first heard the gospel in their own language. The pattern he believed in, of African churches led by Africans, supported by Africans, and carrying the gospel to their neighbours, is the pattern that prevailed.

Jesus said: “Except a grain of wheat fall into the earth and die, it abideth by itself alone; but if it die, it beareth much fruit” (John 12:24, ASV). Crowther’s work seemed to fall into the earth and die in 1891. The fruit came later.

He is remembered today in many ways. The Episcopal Church in the United States and the Church of Nigeria commemorate him on 31 December, the traditional date of his death. There is a university in Oyo that bears his name. His grandson, Herbert Macaulay, is honoured as a father of Nigerian nationalism. And every Sunday, in Yoruba and Igbo and a hundred other languages, African Christians read the Scriptures in their own tongue, as he spent his life to make possible.

Every Nation and Tongue

Crowther used a verse from the Psalms which many African Christians of his century took as a promise for their continent: “Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall haste to stretch out her hands unto God” (Psalm 68:31, ASV). In the Bible, Ethiopia stood for the lands of Africa beyond Egypt, and he believed he was living to see the promise fulfilled.

The vision at the head of this chapter goes further. It is John’s vision of heaven, of “a great multitude, which no man could number, out of every nation and of all tribes and peoples and tongues, standing before the throne and before the Lamb.” Every tongue: Yoruba and Igbo, Nupe and Hausa, Ijaw and English. Every people: the Egba and the Oyo, the chiefs of Bonny and the slaves of Brass, the Emir of Nupe’s people and the congregations of Islington. In that multitude, the distinctions that divided the Niger Mission in 1890 will count for nothing.

Samuel Ajayi Crowther was taken from his home in chains, sold six times, and put on a slave ship bound for the Americas. He was set free by strangers, taught by strangers, and made a Christian by people who did not know his language. He spent the rest of his life making sure that his own people would hear the gospel in theirs. He was wronged at the end, and did not complain. He died saying “Good night.” He was essentially African and essentially missionary. And he is, we may believe, somewhere in that multitude, with a palm in his hand.

fields.title: Appendix A: Lessons from the Life of Samuel Ajayi Crowther
fields.body_html:
“Remember them that had the rule over you, men that spake unto you the word of God; and considering the issue of their life, imitate their faith.”

— Hebrews 13:7, ASV

The lessons below gather the themes of this book so that readers can return to them. Samuel Crowther would have been uncomfortable being held up as an example. He preferred to point, as he so often did, to “the Hand which has ever overruled.” Each lesson therefore rests on Scripture, not on his example alone. The letter to the Hebrews tells us to consider how those who went before us lived and died, and to imitate their faith, not every detail of their lives.

1. God Writes Straight With Crooked Lines

The day he was taken from Osogun in chains was, Crowther wrote, the “unhappy” day which he was later taught “to call blessed.” He never pretended that the slave trade was good. He saw that God had brought good out of it. “As for you, ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20, ASV).

2. God Sees the Fatherless

A boy who lost his home, his family, and his name at about thirteen was not lost to God. Twenty-five years later he found his mother again. “Thou hast been the helper of the fatherless” (Psalm 10:14, ASV).

3. Freedom Is for Service

He was set free from one kind of slavery and gave himself to another, the service of Christ, which he called “perfect freedom.” “For freedom did Christ set us free: stand fast therefore, and be not entangled again in a yoke of bondage” (Galatians 5:1, ASV). The freedom was never for himself alone.

4. Gifts Are Received, Not Earned

When he was praised as proof of what an African could achieve, he turned Paul’s question on himself: “who maketh thee to differ? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7, ASV). Humility is simply the truth about where our gifts come from.

5. People Need the Word in Their Own Language

He spent his life giving the Yoruba, and then other peoples of the Niger, the Scriptures in their own tongue. At Pentecost every hearer asked, “how hear we, every man in our own language wherein we were born?” (Acts 2:8, ASV). The gospel is meant to be heard as a mother tongue, not a foreign one.

6. Preach With Sympathy, Not Scorn

He told his clergy not to dispute with Muslims or to mock the worshippers of the old gods, but to speak “with the feelings of sympathy with all classes of hearers.” “Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt” (Colossians 4:6, ASV).

7. Africa by Her Own Children

He believed, from 1841 onwards, that Africa would be evangelised chiefly by Africans. Every church, in every land, is meant to grow its own leaders. “The little one shall become a thousand, and the small one a strong nation” (Isaiah 60:22, ASV).

8. Hard Providences Are Not the End

Wrecked at Jebba, robbed and held for ransom by Abokko, burned out at Onitsha and Gbebe, he kept writing: “though it is night with us now daylight shall come.” “We are pressed on every side, yet not straitened; perplexed, yet not unto despair” (2 Corinthians 4:8, ASV).

9. Home Is Also a Calling

When his wife was dying, he gave up his annual visitation of the Niger to stay with her, and let the mission wait. “Charity begins at home,” he said. “If any provideth not for his own, and specially his own household, he hath denied the faith” (1 Timothy 5:8, ASV).

10. Gentleness Must Not Become Neglect

His mercy to men who had fallen was real, but it allowed some unworthy men to stay, and a mission run on mercy without close oversight once employed men who did terrible wrong. Leaders are called to restore the fallen gently and to guard the flock faithfully. “Restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1, ASV).

11. Zeal Without Patience Does Harm

The young men who judged his mission were sincere, devoted, and ready to die. They were also, as the society’s own historian later wrote, “too severe.” Zeal for purity that forgets humility becomes its own sin. “The wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (James 1:20, ASV).

12. Suffer Wrong Without Bitterness

He was wronged at the end of his life by his own side. He protested and withdrew from the committee, but he did not turn bitter. His last letter, a draft he never sent, said only that he had always been willing “to be improved by the ideas of others.” “Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1 Peter 2:23, ASV).

13. Churches Can Repent

More than a century later, the Church that had wronged him said, in the cathedral where he was consecrated, “It was wrong.” Institutions, like people, can confess their sins. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9, ASV).

14. The Seed Is Not the Harvest

At his death his mission seemed to have collapsed. A century later, the churches of Nigeria were among the largest in the world. Faithfulness is measured by God, not by what the faithful live to see. “Except a grain of wheat fall into the earth and die, it abideth by itself alone; but if it die, it beareth much fruit” (John 12:24, ASV).

fields.title: Appendix B: Chapter-by-Chapter Study and Reflection Guide
fields.body_html:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deluding your own selves.”

— James 1:22, ASV

This guide is for personal reflection, small groups, or a reading course of about twenty-four weeks. Its purpose is not to make Samuel Crowther an object of admiration, but to let his life hold up a mirror in which readers can examine their own discipleship under Scripture. Groups may find it helpful to begin each session with the chapter’s opening verse and to end with prayer. Several chapters raise hard questions about slavery, race, mission, and the failures of the Church. They are meant to be discussed honestly, not settled quickly.

Introduction - The Bishop and His Biographers

Central idea

Crowther’s own letters and journals are the surest guide to his life; later biographers added legend on one side and prejudice on the other.

Scriptures to revisit

Habakkuk 2:2; Proverbs 18:17.

Reflection

1. Why does it matter whether a Christian biography is accurate? 2. How can we honour a hero without hiding his faults or his wrongs?

Chapter 1 - Ajayi of Osogun

Central idea

God knew and shaped a boy born into a world of war and slave-raiding, before anyone recorded his birthday.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 139:13-16; Acts 17:26-27.

Reflection

1. What does it mean that God knows us before anyone else does? 2. What in your own background has God used that you once thought was only a loss?

Chapter 2 - The Unhappy, Blessed Day

Central idea

The day he was enslaved was the day God began to lead him, though he did not know it.

Scriptures to revisit

Genesis 50:20; Matthew 6:13; Romans 8:28.

Reflection

1. Crowther called the day of his capture both “unhappy” and “blessed.” Can both be true? 2. How should we speak about great evils that God has brought good out of?

Chapter 3 - Myrmidon

Central idea

Freedom came to him through strangers on a British warship, an act of justice he never forgot.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18.

Reflection

1. Who has been an instrument of freedom in your life? 2. What does it mean to “proclaim liberty to the captives” today?

Chapter 4 - Samuel Crowther

Central idea

In Sierra Leone the rescued boy became a new person in Christ, with a new name, a new calling, and a wife who shared his story.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Corinthians 5:17; John 8:36.

Reflection

1. What changed, and what did not change, when Ajayi became Samuel? 2. Why did he call the service of Christ “perfect freedom”?

Chapter 5 - The Niger, 1841

Central idea

A disastrous expedition convinced him that Africa must be evangelised chiefly by Africans.

Scriptures to revisit

Acts 1:8; 1 Corinthians 1:27-29.

Reflection

1. What can be learned from a mission that failed? 2. Who are the people best placed to carry the gospel in your own community?

Chapter 6 - “Who Maketh Thee to Differ?”

Central idea

His ordination made him a sign of what Africans could do, and he answered praise by pointing to grace.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Corinthians 4:7; Luke 14:22.

Reflection

1. How do you respond to praise? 2. What did the Shango drummer’s charge teach Crowther, and what does it teach the Church?

Chapter 7 - The Helper of the Fatherless

Central idea

God brought him back to his own people and gave him his mother again after twenty-five years.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 10:14; Psalm 68:5-6.

Reflection

1. Have you seen God restore something you thought was lost for ever? 2. What did his mother mean when she said, “You are no longer my son, but the servant of God”?

Chapter 8 - In Our Own Language

Central idea

He gave the Yoruba the Scriptures in their mother tongue and a written language to read them in.

Scriptures to revisit

Acts 2:8; Revelation 7:9.

Reflection

1. Why does it matter to hear God’s word in your own language? 2. How might translation be a form of love?

Chapter 9 - The Pleiad

Central idea

A voyage in which no one died showed the Niger could be opened, and showed his patient method with chiefs and Muslims.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 121:7-8; Colossians 4:5-6.

Reflection

1. How did Crowther speak with Muslims and with chiefs? 2. What can we learn from his patience?

Chapter 10 - Wrecked at Jebba

Central idea

A shipwreck left him stranded for a year, and he kept working.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Corinthians 4:8-9; Philippians 4:11-13.

Reflection

1. How did Crowther use his time while stranded? 2. What would it look like for you to keep faith through a long interruption?

Chapter 11 - Africa’s Own Children

Central idea

Venn and Crowther shared a vision of African churches supporting, governing, and extending themselves.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 60:22; 2 Timothy 2:2.

Reflection

1. What is a “self-supporting, self-governing, self-extending” church? 2. Is your church raising up its own leaders?

Chapter 12 - “I Am Not Worthy”

Central idea

He accepted the bishopric reluctantly, and his consecration was both a triumph and a sign of limits.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Samuel 2:8; 1 Peter 5:2-3.

Reflection

1. Why did Crowther refuse at first? 2. What do the newspaper reactions reveal about the prejudices of the time, and of ours?

Chapter 13 - A Bishop in a Canoe

Central idea

As bishop he lived dangerously, and in captivity he was fed by slaves.

Scriptures to revisit

Acts 20:24; 1 Kings 17:6.

Reflection

1. What did the kindness of Abokko’s slaves mean to him? 2. Why did he wish he had died instead of Fell?

Chapter 14 - Sympathy with All Classes

Central idea

His charges to his clergy taught the gospel first, preaching like Christ, and sympathy instead of scorn.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Peter 3:15; Genesis 18:25.

Reflection

1. What does it mean to preach “with sympathy” to people of other religions? 2. Where does his teaching show him to be a man of his time?

Chapter 15 - Cotton Gins and Gin

Central idea

He hoped honest trade would end the slave trade, and he fought the liquor traffic alongside a Muslim emir.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 2:4; Habakkuk 2:15.

Reflection

1. Why did Crowther call the cotton gin “our gun”? 2. Where do trade and faith meet in your own life?

Chapter 16 - The Delta Churches

Central idea

Persecution in the Delta produced strong, self-supporting churches.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 76:10; Acts 4:19-20.

Reflection

1. How did persecution strengthen the Delta churches? 2. Where might you need to say, “I cannot do it, and I dare not do it”?

Chapter 17 - Asano

Central idea

Behind his journeys stood a wife and family who made them possible.

Scriptures to revisit

Song of Songs 8:6-7; Proverbs 31:28-29; Joshua 14:10-11.

Reflection

1. Who made your own work possible, unseen? 2. What is the “hill country” you are still asking God for?

Chapter 18 - The Gathering Storm

Central idea

The mission had real problems, and his gentleness was both a virtue and a weakness.

Scriptures to revisit

Galatians 6:1; 2 Corinthians 11:28.

Reflection

1. When does mercy become neglect? 2. Why is it important not to leave the Onitsha crime out of the story?

Chapter 19 - Onitsha, 1890

Central idea

Young missionaries humiliated an old African bishop and his clergy, and the society’s own historian later called them “too severe.”

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 55:12-14; 2 Timothy 2:21; James 1:19-20.

Reflection

1. What went wrong at Onitsha, on both sides? 2. How can zeal for purity become a sin?

Chapter 20 - The Delta Pastorate

Central idea

The Delta churches answered injustice by taking responsibility for themselves, not by leaving the Church.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 54:2; 1 Corinthians 3:6.

Reflection

1. Why does it matter that the Delta Pastorate was not a secession? 2. How should Christians respond when their church wrongs them?

Chapter 21 - “Good Night”

Central idea

He died humbly, without bitterness, still willing to learn.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Timothy 4:7; Psalm 4:8.

Reflection

1. What do his last letter and his last words tell you about him? 2. How would you like to finish your own course?

Chapter 22 - A Weaned Child

Central idea

His character was marked by humility, prayer, patience, and gratitude, though his deference to Europeans had a cost.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 131:1-2; Philippians 2:3; Nehemiah 2:4.

Reflection

1. How do you read his letter “I know my place as negro”? 2. What is the difference between humility and letting others wrong you?

Chapter 23 - Essentially African, Essentially Missionary

Central idea

His work seemed to die with him, but it bore fruit in the churches of Africa.

Scriptures to revisit

Revelation 7:9; John 12:24; Psalm 68:31.

Reflection

1. What does Archbishop Welby’s apology teach about institutional repentance? 2. What seed are you sowing that you may not see grow?

fields.title: Appendix C: Chronology of the Life and Times of Samuel Ajayi Crowther
fields.body_html:
“So teach us to number our days, That we may get us a heart of wisdom.”

— Psalm 90:12, ASV

The dates below are meant as orientation. Dates taken from Crowther’s own letters and journals, or confirmed by the missionary society’s records, are given plainly. Where the sources disagree, the disagreement is noted. Dates given only by Jesse Page are followed unless they are plainly wrong.

c. 1807 - Birth

Ajayi is born at Osogun, in the Oyo country of the Yoruba, in what is now south-western Nigeria. The year is unknown. Estimates range from about 1802 (his gravestone) to about 1810; this book follows the common estimate of about 1807. His mother, Ibisomi, bore the title Afala.

1821 - Captured

Early in the year, as he dated it, Osogun is attacked by raiders in the wars that follow the collapse of the Oyo empire. He is enslaved and passed from owner to owner, and eventually sold to Portuguese slavers at Lagos.

7 April 1822 - Rescued

The slave ship carrying him is stopped off Lagos by HMS Myrmidon and HMS Iphigenia of the Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron.

17 June 1822 - Sierra Leone

He is landed at Freetown and sent to the mission village of Bathurst, under Mr. Davey. Mrs. Weeks, the wife of a missionary, teaches him.

11 December 1825 - Baptism

Baptised Samuel Crowther by the Rev. J. Raban.

1826-1827 - England

He visits England with the Daveys and attends the parish school in Liverpool Road, Islington.

1827 - Fourah Bay

He becomes, as tradition records, the first student entered at the new Christian Institution at Fourah Bay, Freetown.

21 September 1829 - Marriage

He marries Asano, baptised Susan Thompson, a Yoruba girl freed from another slave ship in October 1822.

1829-1841 - Teacher

Schoolmaster at Regent and Wellington; from 1834 a tutor at Fourah Bay. In February 1837 he writes the letter describing his capture and rescue.

1841 - The Niger Expedition

He sails as a catechist with J. F. Schön on the government expedition up the Niger. Forty-two Europeans die within about two months. At Fernando Po on 2 November he writes that Africa can chiefly be benefited “by her own Children.”

1842-1843 - Ordination

He studies at the Church Missionary College, Islington. His Vocabulary of the Yoruba Language is published. He is made deacon by the Bishop of London on 11 June 1843, and ordained priest in October.

December 1843 - Return to Africa

He lands at Freetown on 2 December 1843 and preaches his first sermon in Africa the next day. On 9 January 1844 he leads the first public service in Yoruba.

17 January 1845 - Badagry

He reaches Badagry with Henry Townsend and C. A. Gollmer.

August 1846 - Abeokuta

He enters Abeokuta on 3 August. On 21 August he is reunited with his mother after twenty-five years.

February 1848 - His Mother’s Baptism

His mother is baptised Hannah, among the first converts of the Abeokuta mission. Sources give the day as 5 or 6 February.

1851 - England Again

He meets Lord Palmerston, and on 18 November is received at Windsor by Queen Victoria and Prince Albert, and recites the Lord’s Prayer in Yoruba. In December the Royal Navy attacks Lagos.

1854 - The Pleiad

He sails with Dr. W. B. Baikie up the Niger and the Benue. The voyage returns on 4 November without a single death.

1857 - The Dayspring

He sails on 29 June to found the Niger Mission, with an all-African staff. Onitsha is reached on 26 July and a station founded. On 7 October the Dayspring is wrecked near Jebba, and the party is stranded for a year.

14 September 1862 - First Fruits

The first baptisms of the Niger Mission, at Gbebe near the Confluence.

29 June 1864 - Consecration

Consecrated in Canterbury Cathedral as bishop of “the countries of Western Africa beyond the limits of our dominions,” after receiving the degree of Doctor of Divinity from Oxford. He holds his first ordination at Lagos on 22 August, and begins the mission at Bonny.

1866 - The First Charge

His first charge to his clergy is printed in London. Further charges follow in 1869, 1874, and 1885.

1867 - A Year of Troubles

Easter Day: the chiefs of Bonny renounce the worship of the sacred lizard. In September he and Dandeson are held for ransom by Abokko near Idda; on 28 September they escape, and William Fell is mortally wounded. In October the missionaries are expelled from Abeokuta.

19 June 1870 - Dandeson Ordained

He ordains his son Dandeson deacon at St. Mary’s, Islington.

1873 - Death of Henry Venn

Venn, his friend and patron, dies.

1875-1876 - Igbo and the Delta

He chooses the Isuama dialect as the standard for Igbo translation. Dandeson becomes Archdeacon of the Lower Niger (1876 in modern accounts; Stock gives 1878). King Ockiya of Brass gives up his household gods.

c. 1877 - Crime at Onitsha

A girl dies after cruel treatment by two African employees of the mission, one of them a dismissed teacher whom the bishop had re-employed. The case comes to trial in 1882.

11 June 1877 - Royal Geographical Society

He reads a paper on the Niger to the Society in London.

1878 - The Henry Venn

The mission steamer arrives, with J. H. Ashcroft as lay agent in charge of the mission’s business affairs.

1879 - Brass and Onitsha

Onitsha is shelled and burned by HMS Pioneer in October. King Ockiya of Brass is baptised on Advent Sunday.

1880 - Wood’s Report; Susan’s Death

J. B. Wood reports unfavourably on the mission. Susan Crowther dies at Lagos on 19 October, after fifty-one years of marriage.

1881 - Madeira

A conference at Madeira agrees reforms, including an English secretary to live on the Niger.

1882 - Phillips

He ordains Thomas Phillips priest in England, the first ordination of an Englishman by an African bishop. In September the London papers report the conviction at Sierra Leone in the Onitsha case.

1883 - Attacks and Losses

On 26 February he writes his “Caleb” letter from Bonny. On 12 April the Duke of Somerset attacks the society in the House of Lords. Several agents are let go. His mother dies at Lagos in October.

1884 - The Yoruba Bible

The complete Bible in Yoruba is published. In January and February he writes the letters “I know my place as negro” and “I am ready to yield place to others”; the society declines. In December the society protests to the Foreign Office against the liquor trade.

1886 - The Royal Niger Company

The British trading firms on the Niger are chartered as the Royal Niger Company.

1887 - Robinson

J. A. Robinson becomes secretary of the Niger Mission.

1890 - The Crisis

On 20 January, at Exeter Hall, he blesses the new missionaries; all sail in February. In August, at a committee meeting at Onitsha, African agents and clergy are dismissed or suspended, among them Archdeacon Dandeson Crowther. The bishop withdraws from the committee.

January 1891 - The Report

The society’s report confirms some suspensions and reverses others, admits inadequate supervision, and declares the situation on the Niger “extremely lamentable.”

1891 - Stroke

Robinson dies in June. In the summer the bishop suffers a stroke at Bonny. He moves to Lagos, arriving on 28 September, and stays with his daughter Abigail Macaulay. The Delta churches decline further money from the society and ask to become a self-supporting pastorate; the bishop forwards their request with his approval.

31 December 1891 - Death

He dies at Lagos, at a quarter to one in the morning according to his daughter’s account, which would strictly make the date 1 January 1892. He is buried on 1 January beside his wife and mother.

29 April 1892 - The Delta Pastorate

The self-supporting Niger Delta Pastorate is inaugurated at Bonny.

1893-1894 - The Successor

Joseph Sidney Hill is consecrated Bishop in Western Equatorial Africa on 29 June 1893, with Charles Phillips and Isaac Oluwole as African assistant bishops. Hill dies at Lagos in January 1894.

1896 - The Pastorate Constitution

A formal constitution settles the Delta Pastorate as a self-supporting branch of the Church of England.

4 August 1898 - Memorial

A marble monument is unveiled over his grave at Lagos.

1938 - Death of Dandeson

Archdeacon Dandeson Coates Crowther dies at Freetown.

2014 - Repentance

At a service of thanksgiving and repentance in Canterbury Cathedral, 150 years after the consecration, Archbishop Justin Welby says of Crowther’s treatment: “It was wrong.”

fields.title: Appendix D: Notes on Sources and Method
fields.body_html:
“it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write unto thee in order … that thou mightest know the certainty concerning the things wherein thou wast instructed.”

— Luke 1:3-4, ASV

This appendix explains where the story told in this book comes from, how the sources were weighed, and which popular claims have been corrected. It is written for readers who want to check the story for themselves, and for anyone who will retell it.

Crowther’s Own Writings

Samuel Crowther is unusual among the missionaries of his century in that so much of his own voice survives. Wherever possible, this book has let him speak for himself. The principal writings used are these, all now in the public domain:

  • His letter of February 1837 to the Rev. William Jowett, describing his capture, enslavement, and rescue. It was printed as an appendix to the Journals of the Rev. James Frederick Schön and Mr. Samuel Crowther, who, with the Sanction of Her Majesty’s Government, Accompanied the Expedition up the Niger, in 1841 (London, 1842). The same volume contains his own journal of the 1841 expedition and his letter from Fernando Po on native agency. Jesse Page later reprinted the 1837 letter with a number of small errors, so this book quotes it from the 1842 printing.
  • Journal of an Expedition up the Niger and Tshadda Rivers (London, 1855), his account of the Pleiad voyage of 1854.
  • The Gospel on the Banks of the Niger (London, 1859), with J. C. Taylor, the journals of the Dayspring expedition and the founding of the Niger Mission.
  • A Charge Delivered on the Banks of the River Niger in West Africa (London, 1866), his first charge to his clergy.
  • His paper on the Niger read to the Royal Geographical Society on 11 June 1877 and printed in its Proceedings.
  • His letters and later charges, as quoted by Jesse Page and Eugene Stock.

The Biographers

Jesse Page wrote two popular lives, Samuel Crowther: The Slave Boy Who Became Bishop of the Niger (1888) and The Black Bishop: Samuel Adjai Crowther (London: Hodder and Stoughton, 1908). The second was written with the help of Crowther’s family, and it preserves many letters and family memories that are found nowhere else, including Abigail Macaulay’s account of her father’s death and the story of the Blucher shoes. Page is indispensable, but he must be read with care. He wrote at the family’s request, but with the society’s co-operation and as its friend, and he smooths over the crisis of 1890, giving almost no names and no details. He sometimes paraphrases letters rather than quoting them exactly, and several of his dates are wrong or inconsistent. He also imagines Crowther’s inner feelings freely, and writes in the language of racial superiority common in his time. This book has used Page for facts and quotations that can be checked or that are plausible, and has marked family stories as family stories.

Eugene Stock’s History of the Church Missionary Society (3 volumes, London, 1899) is the society’s official history, written by a man who was on its staff through the crisis. It is generally reliable on dates and on what the society decided, and it is honest in places, admitting that the young missionaries were “too severe.” But it tells the story from the society’s side, and it too uses the racial language of its time. A short American missionary booklet on Crowther, published at Hartford, Connecticut, in 1903, has not been relied on, as it contains too many errors.

Modern Historians

This book has drawn facts and interpretations, but not text, from the work of modern historians, especially:

  • J. F. Ade Ajayi, Christian Missions in Nigeria 1841-1891: The Making of a New Élite (1965), and his edition of the 1837 letter in P. D. Curtin, ed., Africa Remembered (1967).
  • E. A. Ayandele, The Missionary Impact on Modern Nigeria 1842-1914 (1966).
  • Andrew F. Walls, “The Legacy of Samuel Ajayi Crowther,” International Bulletin of Missionary Research 16:1 (1992).
  • Lamin Sanneh, Translating the Message: The Missionary Impact on Culture (1989).
  • Jehu Hanciles, Euthanasia of a Mission (2002), and his work on Dandeson Crowther.
  • G. O. M. Tasie, Christian Missionary Enterprise in the Niger Delta 1864-1918 (1978).
  • P. R. McKenzie, Inter-religious Encounters in West Africa (1976), on Crowther’s approach to Islam and African religion.
  • Emmanuel Egbunu, “Racial Tension in Mission,” Anvil 36:3 (2020).

These scholars have been read for what they establish, and are named in the text where their judgements are reported. Nothing from their books has been reproduced beyond short phrases.

Corrections to Popular Accounts

Crowther’s story is often retold, and some common claims are wrong or uncertain. This book has taken the following positions.

  • His birth year is unknown. Popular accounts give 1806, 1807, 1809, or 1810 with confidence. His gravestone implies about 1802. No record exists. This book says “about 1807” and means it as an estimate.
  • “The first African bishop.” He was the first African bishop of the Anglican Church, and the first African consecrated a bishop by the Church of England. He was not the first African bishop in history; the ancient churches of North Africa and Ethiopia had African bishops for centuries.
  • “The first African Anglican priest.” He was not. Philip Quaque of Cape Coast was ordained in the Church of England in 1765. Crowther was, in Stock’s words, “the first African clergyman of our day,” and the first African ordained for the Church Missionary Society’s work in West Africa.
  • The name of the slave ship. It is usually given as the Esperança Feliz. Crowther’s own letter does not name it. The name rests on mission tradition.
  • He did not meet Asano on the slave ship. She was freed from a different ship, some months later.
  • His mother’s baptism. Sources disagree on whether it was 5 or 6 February 1848, and on who baptised her. This book says only February 1848.
  • “Never ill.” Page wrote that Crowther’s constitution was proof against fever. His own journals record bouts of fever and dysentery.
  • The kidnapping by Abokko took place in September 1867, as his diary and the letters of the time show, not 1868, as he said himself ten years later.
  • The Onitsha crime was real. Some modern retellings present all the charges against the Niger Mission as racist fabrications. A girl was killed at Onitsha by two of the mission’s African employees, about 1877, and they were convicted at Sierra Leone in 1882. No source suggests that the bishop knew of the crime, but one of the men, dismissed by him, had later been re-employed out of pity.
  • He was not deposed. Popular accounts sometimes say that he was removed from his bishopric in 1890. He was not. He withdrew from the mission’s finance committee in protest, and remained bishop until his death.
  • Numbers of clergy dismissed. A figure of “twelve of fifteen African pastors” dismissed circulates widely. This book has not been able to verify it, and does not use it. Stock’s own figures for the collapse of the mission’s staff between 1890 and 1893 are given in Chapter 23.
  • The Delta Pastorate was not a secession from the Anglican Church. It was a withdrawal from the financial control of the missionary society. It remained part of the Church of England, and in time came back into closer relations with the society.
  • The date of his death. His memorial and his church commemorations give 31 December 1891. His daughter’s account puts his death at a quarter to one in the morning, strictly 1 January 1892.
  • The 2014 apology. Archbishop Justin Welby’s words at Canterbury were spoken in a sermon at a service of thanksgiving and repentance. This book has not found a separate formal resolution of apology by the Church Missionary Society, though the society’s own journal has since published a Nigerian archbishop’s account of the crisis as a racial injustice.
  • Commemoration. The Episcopal Church in the United States and the Church of Nigeria commemorate him on 31 December. He does not appear in the national calendar of the Church of England.

Language

The nineteenth-century sources describe Africans in terms that are offensive today, and some of them, including Page and at times Stock, assume that Africans are an inferior race. Crowther himself sometimes used the language of his time, speaking of “heathen” and “savages” and of the people as “children.” This book has quoted such language only where it was necessary to show what Crowther faced or how he thought, and has tried to make clear where it stands. The terms “heathen” and “idolatry” are used, as Crowther used them, to describe religious practice from a Christian point of view, not to judge the worth of the people who practised it.

Scripture

All Scripture quotations are from the American Standard Version (1901). Crowther himself read the Authorized (King James) Version in English, and where he quotes Scripture in his own words, his wording has been kept.

Method

This book is not a work of original research in archives. It is an attempt to tell a true story accurately, for general readers, from the published sources. Where the sources are uncertain, the book says so. Where they disagree, it has preferred Crowther’s own contemporary writings to later recollections, and contemporary records to family memory. Where a detail rests only on a family story or on Page’s imagination, it has been marked as such or left out. No conversations have been invented. Every quotation attributed to Crowther or to anyone else comes from the sources named above, except Archbishop Welby’s words, which are from his sermon at Canterbury on 29 June 2014 as reported by Anglican News and quoted in Anvil.
